lessons.title: What you are actually running
lessons.summary: GNU coreutils 9.4 on Ubuntu, the info manual, and the shell builtins that pretend to be the same tools.
objectives: Identify the installed coreutils package and the manual that matches it
Tell a shell builtin from the coreutils binary on PATH
Read an exit status as data, including the commands the manual calls out as special
Name the Ubuntu binaries that the GNU manual documents but this package does not own
lessons.gnuVsBsd: macOS and the BSDs ship a different userland. `ls --version` is a GNU question and fails on BSD ls. Homebrew and similar systems often install the GNU tools under a `g` prefix (`gls`, `gdate`, `gstat`) so they do not replace the BSD ones. This course ran only the Ubuntu GNU binaries. BSD notes later in the course are documented differences, not captured output.
lessons.markdown:
GNU coreutils is one package that absorbed the old textutils, fileutils, and shellutils collections. On this machine it is the set of programs that copy, list, sort, checksum, and format ordinary files. It is not the kernel, not the compiler, and not the shell. A C++, Rust, or Android build uses it constantly anyway: `install` places a binary, `nproc` suggests a job count, `sha256sum` checks an NDK archive, and `timeout` stops a hung test. Those are coreutils jobs. `grep`, `find`, `make`, and `adb` are not.

The introduction in the installed info file says the utilities are mostly compatible with POSIX, and that the info manual is the documentation the project maintains. It also says the man pages are no longer maintained. When a man page and the info node disagree, follow the info node for coreutils 9.4, then confirm the flag still exists in `--help` on the binary you will run. The HTML manual on gnu.org tracks newer releases. A flag you saw on the web and cannot find in `--help` is not a flag you have.

The shell sits in front of every command line. Bash provides its own `echo`, `printf`, `test`, `[`, `true`, `false`, and `pwd`. Those builtins do not have to match `/usr/bin` of the same name. The manual says this explicitly for `echo`: an unadorned `echo` may not be the program the chapter describes, and `env echo` is one way to skip the shell's version. This course uses absolute paths when the difference matters, and it shows `type` so you can see the shadowing on your own prompt.

Exit status is how these short programs talk back. The manual's rule for almost every command is that zero means success and non-zero means failure. It then lists exceptions whose statuses mean something narrower: `chroot`, `env`, `expr`, `ls`, `nice`, `nohup`, `numfmt`, `printenv`, `runcon`, `sort`, `stdbuf`, `test`, `timeout`, and `tty`. `sort -c` uses 1 to mean "not in order" and 2 to mean "I could not run the check". `timeout` uses 124 when it kills the child. `test` uses 1 as the answer "false". Reading a bare non-zero as "the tool is broken" will make you mis-handle all three.

Ubuntu does not install every name the GNU manual has a chapter for. On this image, `hostname` belongs to the hostname package, `kill` and `uptime` belong to procps, and `find` belongs to findutils. Teaching those binaries as if they were this coreutils 9.4 build would be a lie about the system you develop on. The reference marks them as companions. The lessons that need them say so in the example badge.

Performance shows up later as a property of a bottleneck: locale collation, a sort that spills, a pipe that block-buffers, a copy that cannot reflink. Nothing in this orientation lesson is a speed ranking. The useful habit is to ask which resource is scarce before you add a flag.

## Worked examples

### Package and version

```example
{"id": "orientation-01", "title": "The coreutils package you have", "companion": "", "script": "dpkg-query -W -f 'coreutils ${Version}\\n' coreutils\n/usr/bin/ls --version | /usr/bin/head -n 1\n", "stdout": "coreutils 9.4-3ubuntu6.3\nls (GNU coreutils) 9.4\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/orientation-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Builtin versus binary

```example
{"id": "orientation-02", "title": "echo is usually the shell", "companion": "", "script": "type -a echo\necho --help\n/usr/bin/echo --version | /usr/bin/head -n 1\n", "stdout": "echo is a shell builtin\necho is /usr/bin/echo\necho is /bin/echo\n--help\necho (GNU coreutils) 9.4\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/orientation-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Exit status is the value

```example
{"id": "orientation-03", "title": "true and false from the package", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/true\n/usr/bin/printf 'true:%s\\n' $?\n/usr/bin/false\n/usr/bin/printf 'false:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "true:0\nfalse:1\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/orientation-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Names the manual mentions that this package does not own

```example
{"id": "orientation-04", "title": "Who owns hostname, kill, and uptime", "companion": "", "script": "dpkg -S /usr/bin/hostname\ndpkg -S /usr/bin/kill\ndpkg -S /usr/bin/uptime\n", "stdout": "hostname: /usr/bin/hostname\nprocps: /usr/bin/kill\nprocps: /usr/bin/uptime\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/orientation-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Before a script depends on a GNU flag, print the version and the `type` of the command. In a Rust `build.rs` or a CMake custom command the `PATH` may not be your interactive shell, and a builtin is not involved there at all: the exec'd binary is coreutils. In an interactive bash function, the builtin is involved. Check both places if the script is sometimes pasted into a prompt.

When you file a bug, the introduction asks for the version, the architecture, the input, what you expected, and what you got. `sort --debug` and `date --debug` are the two places the manual tells you to look before you write that report.

## Tips and pitfalls

`echo --help` from the builtin prints the two words `--help`. That is not a documentation viewer failing. It is the builtin treating every operand as text. `/usr/bin/echo --help` is the manual page for the binary.

`ls --version` on macOS is not a quiet no-op. It is an error from BSD ls, which reads `--version` as an illegal option. A script that starts by asserting GNU should check the version line, not merely the exit status of an unrelated command.

Do not parse `ls` to decide what a build tree contains. The next lessons show why. This lesson's only listing is the version line, which is a single predictable stream.

## Performance

Starting a coreutils process is cheap next to reading a multi-gigabyte artifact, and expensive next to a Rust function that already has the bytes in memory. The orientation question is not "which command is fastest". It is "is this work a process, a pipe, or a library call?" Checksums of a firmware blob belong in `sha256sum`. Splitting a string you already hold in a Rust `&str` does not belong in `cut`. The benchmark page measures a few cases where the process is the right tool and the cost is visible. It does not claim a winner for every machine.

lessons.title: Quoting, globs, pipes, and status
lessons.summary: The shell rewrites the command line before coreutils sees it. Quoting, globs, pipes, and exit status are the four rewrites that matter.
objectives: Predict when the shell splits words, expands globs, and leaves quotes alone
Read a pipeline status with and without pipefail
Stop option parsing with -- when a file name starts with a dash
Notice ARG_MAX as a limit on globs, not as a property of ls
lessons.gnuVsBsd: Quoting and pipelines are POSIX shell behavior, not a coreutils feature. `$'...'` ANSI-C quoting is bash and is not available in a strict POSIX `sh` such as dash. BSD shells differ the same way. `pipefail` is a bash/ksh option, not a coreutils flag. The coreutils programs themselves then run the same on GNU and, where they exist, on BSD; the shell in front of them does not.
lessons.markdown:
Coreutils programs receive an argument vector and, if you connect them, a stream of bytes. They do not see the quotes you typed. Bash parses those quotes, expands globs against the directory, splits unquoted variables on `IFS`, and only then calls `exec`. If a lesson command "does the wrong thing", the first question is whether the shell already changed the request.

Single quotes are literal. Double quotes allow `$` and backslash escapes. Unquoted text splits on spaces and expands `*`, `?`, and `[]`. A file named `a b.txt` is one argument only when it is quoted or when a glob produces it as one match. The glob `box/*.txt` is safe for spaces in the matched names because each match becomes one argument. It is unsafe for a name that starts with `-`, and it never matches a leading dot.

A pipe connects stdout of one process to stdin of the next. The default status of a pipeline is the status of the last process. `set -o pipefail` changes that: the status is the rightmost non-zero status. GNU `false` in the middle of a pipeline is invisible unless pipefail is on. SIGPIPE is the other half of this. A writer whose reader exits early receives SIGPIPE and, under pipefail, the pipeline often ends at 141, which is 128 plus signal 13. `yes | head` is the small version of that story. The later `yes` lesson measures it directly; here you only need the rule.

`--` ends options. `cat -- -n` reads a file whose name is `-n`. Without `--`, many GNU tools treat `-n` as a flag. The common-options node describes this convention. It is not universal in the outside world (`echo` is the famous exception, covered with `printf`), but it is the habit to use in this package.

The shell also has a size limit on the argument vector. `getconf ARG_MAX` is not coreutils. It is still the number that explains why `printf '%s\n' *` dies in a directory of build products while `find` streaming names does not. Coreutils can read NUL-separated names with `--files0-from` on `sort`, `wc`, and several checksum tools. That is the escape hatch when the glob no longer fits.

## Worked examples

### Quotes and splitting

```example
{"id": "shell-quoting-globs-pipes-01", "title": "Three arguments or one", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '%s\\n' 'a b' \"a b\" a b\n", "stdout": "a b\na b\na\nb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/shell-quoting-globs-pipes-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A glob keeps the space inside one match

```example
{"id": "shell-quoting-globs-pipes-02", "title": "Glob matches are single fields", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir box\n/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > 'box/a b.txt'\n/usr/bin/printf '%s\\n' box/*.txt\n", "stdout": "box/a b.txt\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/shell-quoting-globs-pipes-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### pipefail sees the middle failure

```example
{"id": "shell-quoting-globs-pipes-03", "title": "Pipeline status with and without pipefail", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\nbash -c '/usr/bin/printf a | /usr/bin/false | /usr/bin/true'\n/usr/bin/printf 'nopf:%s\\n' $?\nbash -c 'set -o pipefail; /usr/bin/printf a | /usr/bin/false | /usr/bin/true'\n/usr/bin/printf 'pf:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "nopf:0\npf:1\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/shell-quoting-globs-pipes-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A name that looks like an option

```example
{"id": "shell-quoting-globs-pipes-04", "title": "End option parsing with --", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'secret\\n' > ./-n\n/usr/bin/cat -- -n\n", "stdout": "secret\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/shell-quoting-globs-pipes-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Pass file names from a Rust or C++ driver as separate `exec` arguments, not as one string you hope the shell will split. If you must go through `sh -c`, quote with `printf '%q'` from the coreutils `printf`, which the printf lesson demonstrates.

For a directory you do not control, prefer a NUL-safe producer. `ls --zero` is GNU coreutils. `find -print0` is findutils, and the safe-pipelines lesson shows both, labeled. Do not `ls | while read` a build tree. `read` splits on whitespace and the newline in a hostile name ends the record early.

## Tips and pitfalls

The runner for this course sets `pipefail` around every captured script. A script you paste into an interactive bash does not, until you set the option. When a captured pipeline exits 141 and your terminal exits 0, that is the option, not a different coreutils.

Unquoted `$var` is not a coreutils bug. If `var='a b'`, then `cat $var` asks cat for two files. Quote `"$var"`.

A failed glob in bash, with default settings, stays as the literal pattern if nothing matches. `nullglob` turns it into zero arguments, and `ls` with zero path arguments lists the current directory. That surprise is worse than an error. Leave `nullglob` off unless you have handled the empty case.

The number is 1.", "hint": "`printf` one name per line, then `wc -l`.", "solution": "The space stays inside the match, so wc sees one line.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'z\\n' > 'my file.txt'\n/usr/bin/printf '%s\\n' *.txt | /usr/bin/wc -l\n", "stdout": "1\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/shell-quoting-globs-pipes-ex02.sh"}

Do not let `set -e` abort the script before the printf.", "hint": "Toggle `set +e` around the ls, or use an `if`.", "solution": "A missing operand path is status 2 for GNU ls. The script then returns to a strict shell.", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/ls ./missing-name\nstatus=$?\nset -e\n/usr/bin/printf 'saw:%s\\n' \"$status\"\n", "stdout": "saw:2\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/ls: cannot access './missing-name': No such file or directory\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/shell-quoting-globs-pipes-ex03.sh"}


## Performance

Quoting costs nothing you can measure against file I/O. The performance failure mode is accidental work: a glob of a million object files builds a huge `argv`, the kernel rejects it with `E2BIG`, and the command never starts. Streaming names avoids that allocation. `getconf ARG_MAX` reports the limit on this machine; it is a kernel parameter, not a coreutils constant, and it is not a reason to claim one `ls` flag is faster than another.

```example
{"id": "shell-quoting-globs-pipes-05", "title": "The argument-size ceiling on this host", "companion": "getconf", "script": "getconf ARG_MAX\n", "stdout": "2097152\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/shell-quoting-globs-pipes-05.sh", "truncated": false}
```

lessons.title: Redirections, streams, and stdbuf
lessons.summary: stdout and stderr are separate, FILE buffering is not the kernel pipe buffer, and stdbuf cannot change programs that never use FILE streams.
objectives: Redirect stdout and stderr independently and explain which stream a diagnostic uses
Describe full buffering versus line buffering when stdout is a pipe
State why stdbuf does not affect cat or dd, and why it rejects line-buffered stdin
Point at libstdbuf.so as the mechanism on this ELF build
lessons.gnuVsBsd: Redirection syntax is the shell. `stdbuf` is GNU coreutils and is absent on stock macOS and most BSDs. The manual says it exists only on ELF platforms that support a constructor attribute, so a portable script must not require it. The `gstdbuf` name from a GNU prefix package is the usual macOS install. Nothing in this lesson was executed on BSD.
lessons.markdown:
A coreutils process has the three standard descriptors the C library expects. The shell wires them up before `exec`. `>` redirects file descriptor 1. `2>` redirects file descriptor 2. `>/tmp/out 2>&1` makes both descriptors share the destination, and the order of those redirections matters because `2>&1` copies the current meaning of descriptor 1. None of that logic lives in `cat`. `cat` writes bytes to whatever descriptor 1 already is.

Buffering is a second mechanism, inside the process, on top of the kernel pipe. The C standard library accumulates `printf` output in a user-space buffer. When stdout is a terminal it is typically line buffered. When stdout is a pipe it is typically fully buffered, often 4 KiB or 8 KiB, so a reader sees nothing until the buffer fills or the process exits. That delay is not the kernel holding the bytes. The bytes have not been written yet. Tools that call `write` directly never enter this path.

`stdbuf` exists to change the FILE buffering mode before the command's `main`. On this Ubuntu build the `stdbuf` binary contains the strings `LD_PRELOAD` and `libstdbuf.so`, and the library is installed at `/usr/libexec/coreutils/libstdbuf.so`. The preload constructor runs first and calls `setvbuf`. The manual then lists two reasons the setting may not stick. `dd` and `cat` do not use FILE streams for their I/O. `tee` sets up its own buffering and overwrites the stdbuf choice. Line buffering on stdin is rejected because it is meaningless; this 9.4 build exits 125 and says so.

A latency difference is real for programs that do use `printf` and then wait. The benchmark page times a four-line C harness, not `cat`. If that sample's medians separate, the note says they separated on that harness. It does not say `stdbuf -oL` makes coreutils filters faster. Throughput and time-to-first-byte are different questions. Full buffering can be the faster way to push a large file through a pipe, and the wrong way to watch a progress line.

## Worked examples

### Split the two output streams

```example
{"id": "redirections-and-buffering-01", "title": "stdout and stderr land in different files", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/ls . missing-stream > out.txt 2> err.txt\nstatus=$?\nset -e\n/usr/bin/printf 'status:%s\\n' \"$status\"\n/usr/bin/printf 'stdout-file:\\n'\n/usr/bin/cat out.txt\n/usr/bin/printf 'stderr-file:\\n'\n/usr/bin/cat err.txt\n", "stdout": "status:2\nstdout-file:\n.:\nerr.txt\nout.txt\nstderr-file:\n/usr/bin/ls: cannot access 'missing-stream': No such file or directory\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/redirections-and-buffering-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### stdbuf refuses line-buffered input

```example
{"id": "redirections-and-buffering-02", "title": "-iL is rejected", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/stdbuf -iL /usr/bin/true\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "/usr/bin/stdbuf: line buffering stdin is meaningless\nTry '/usr/bin/stdbuf --help' for more information.\n", "exitCode": 125, "download": "/downloads/examples/redirections-and-buffering-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### The helper library is on disk

```example
{"id": "redirections-and-buffering-03", "title": "libstdbuf.so shipped with this package", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/ls -l /usr/libexec/coreutils/libstdbuf.so\n", "stdout": "-rwxr-xr-x. 1 root root 14632 Aug 25 15:09 /usr/libexec/coreutils/libstdbuf.so\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/redirections-and-buffering-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### cat still runs under stdbuf, and that proves nothing about buffering

```example
{"id": "redirections-and-buffering-04", "title": "stdbuf does not stop cat, and does not document a new cat mode", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'ab\\n' | /usr/bin/stdbuf -o0 /usr/bin/cat | /usr/bin/od -An -tx1\n", "stdout": " 61 62 0a\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/redirections-and-buffering-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

When a long pipeline looks stuck, check whether the producer is fully buffering. A progress line from a C or C++ tool that uses `printf` and no `fflush` will sit in the FILE buffer until it fills. `stdbuf -oL` is the non-invasive experiment, and only if the program uses FILE streams and does not reset them. If the program is Rust and it wraps stdout in a `BufWriter`, stdbuf does nothing: Rust is not the C library.

For logs you want to keep, redirect in the shell rather than asking every tool for an output flag. `tool >run.log 2>run.err` keeps diagnostics out of the byte stream you will checksum.

## Tips and pitfalls

`stdbuf -oL` on `cat` is a no-op in the sense the manual describes. The pipeline still copies bytes. You cannot conclude from a successful exit that buffering changed.

Status 125 means stdbuf itself failed. Status 126 means the command was found but could not be executed. Status 127 means it was not found. Those numbers are in the stdbuf node. Do not treat them as the command's own status.

`LD_PRELOAD` is ignored for setuid binaries. stdbuf will not change a privileged program, which is what you want.

## Performance

The kernel pipe has a capacity. The FILE buffer is in the writer. Filling an 8 KiB stdio buffer and then one `write` system call is fewer transitions than one `write` per line. That is why fully buffered output can use less CPU for a bulk copy, and why it feels late when you are watching a build log. `stdbuf -o0` forces a write per FILE operation and can raise system time on a chatty producer. Measure that with the buffering benchmark, which reports time-to-first-byte for a harness that sleeps between `printf` calls. Do not copy its medians onto `cp` or `dd`. The manual already told you those two ignore stdbuf.

lessons.title: Locale, collation, and LC_ALL=C
lessons.summary: LC_COLLATE decides what "sorted" means. LC_ALL=C is byte order, not a universal speedup, and it changes joins and checksums of nothing but the order of text.
objectives: Show that en_US.UTF-8 and C order the same bytes differently
Explain which tools consult LC_COLLATE, LC_CTYPE, and LC_NUMERIC
Use LC_ALL=C when the contract is bytes, and say so in the script
Refuse a speed claim that was not measured on a fixed input
lessons.gnuVsBsd: Both GNU and BSD userlands honor POSIX locales, but the collation tables are not the same data. `LC_ALL=C` is the portable way to ask for byte order on either side. GNU `sort` adds `-V`, `--parallel`, and `-S`, which BSD sort does not match flag for flag. macOS `sort` is not GNU sort. This lesson's captured order is the GNU 9.4 order on this Ubuntu locale set.
lessons.markdown:
A locale is a bundle of rules for characters, collation, numbers, dates, and messages. Coreutils does not invent a private alphabet. The sort node says that unless you ask otherwise, comparisons use `LC_COLLATE`, and a line's trailing newline is not part of the comparison. Under `en_US.UTF-8` the letters `a` and `A` are primary-equal and the case difference is a later pass, so they group together. Under `LC_ALL=C` the order is the unsigned byte order: `A` (0x41) before `a` (0x61), and `B` before `a` as well.

`LC_ALL` overrides the individual `LC_*` variables. Setting only `LC_COLLATE=C` while leaving `LC_CTYPE` as UTF-8 is a sharper knife, and it is easy to get half-wrong. For a byte-oriented contract, set `LC_ALL=C` on that one command. Exporting it for an entire desktop session also switches messages and number formats, which is more than a sort script needs.

Tools that look at locale in ways people forget: `sort` and therefore anything that requires sorted input (`uniq` after a locale sort, `join`, `comm`); `tr` character classes such as `[:upper:]`, because `LC_CTYPE` defines which bytes are letters; `sort -n` and `seq`, because `LC_NUMERIC` can make the decimal point a comma; `date`, because `LC_TIME` names months; `wc -m`, because a character is not a byte once the encoding is UTF-8. Checksums do not consult collation. `sha256sum` of a file is the same in C and in en_US. If a checksum changed when you exported `LC_ALL`, you changed the bytes, not the hash.

`LC_ALL=C` is often faster for `sort` of large text because the collation is a simple comparison instead of a multi-level Unicode weight. The manual does not promise a ratio. The benchmark page runs a fixed 100000-line file under both locales and reports medians. If they separate, the note says they separated on that file in a warm cache. If they do not, the note says the run cannot rank them. Either result is allowed. Do not paste a blog's "C is always 10x" into a build script.

Byte order is also the wrong order for humans reading a dictionary, and the wrong order for version numbers (`sort -V` is its own lesson). Pick the order that matches the consumer. A `join` requires both files to be sorted by the same rule. Sorting one file in C and the other in en_US produces a disorder diagnostic, not a merged table.

## Worked examples

### The same four lines, two orders

```example
{"id": "locale-and-byte-order-01", "title": "UTF-8 collation groups case together", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'A\\na\\nB\\nb\\n' | /usr/bin/sort\n", "stdout": "a\nA\nb\nB\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/locale-and-byte-order-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "locale-and-byte-order-02", "title": "C locale is unsigned byte order", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'A\\na\\nB\\nb\\n' | /usr/bin/sort\n", "stdout": "A\nB\na\nb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/locale-and-byte-order-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Character count is not the byte count

```example
{"id": "locale-and-byte-order-03", "title": "wc -m and wc -c on U+00E9", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '\u00e9' | /usr/bin/wc -m -c\n", "stdout": "      1       2\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/locale-and-byte-order-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A checksum ignores collation

```example
{"id": "locale-and-byte-order-04", "title": "sha256sum of abc in two locales", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abc' | /usr/bin/sha256sum\n", "stdout": "ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad  -\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/locale-and-byte-order-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Put `LC_ALL=C sort -u` in front of a manifest of file names when the manifest is a byte contract, for example a list of object files a linker will consume. Put the locale sort only when a person will read the list as a dictionary.

If a `join` fails with "not sorted", do not reach for `--nocheck-order` first. Re-sort both inputs with the same `LC_ALL`. The join lesson shows what the nocheck flag hides.

For numbers that must use a dot, run `LC_ALL=C sort -n` or `LC_ALL=C numfmt`. A teammate whose `LC_NUMERIC` uses a comma will otherwise see a different parse. This sandbox's locale uses a dot; the flag is still worth writing down so the script does not depend on that accident.

## Tips and pitfalls

`sort --debug` prints which locale rules it used, on stderr. That line is part of diagnosing a "wrong" order. It is not corruption.

`uniq` compares adjacent lines in the locale's equality, unless you set C. Case-folding with `uniq -i` is a further fold. Sort and uniq have to agree or the adjacency is meaningless.

Setting `LC_ALL=C` does not make UTF-8 data ASCII. It makes comparisons and some classifications byte-wise. `wc -m` under `LC_ALL=C` counts bytes rather than decoded characters. That is useful when you mean bytes, and surprising when you meant letters.



```exercise
{"id": "locale-and-byte-order-ex02", "title": "Ask sort what it used", "prompt": "Run `sort --debug` on the single line `a` and keep both streams. The status is 0.", "hint": "The locale note is on stderr. The sorted line is on stdout.", "solution": "The diagnostic names the collation. That is the manual's suggested first step when order looks wrong.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\n' | /usr/bin/sort --debug\n", "stdout": "a\n_\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/sort: text ordering performed using \u2018en_US.UTF-8\u2019 sorting rules\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/locale-and-byte-order-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "locale-and-byte-order-ex03", "title": "Hash both locales", "prompt": "Print `sha256sum` of the bytes `abc` with `LC_ALL=C` and with `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8`.", "hint": "Two pipelines. The digest is a property of the bytes.", "solution": "The two digests match the known SHA-256 of abc. Locale did not enter the hash.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abc' | LC_ALL=C /usr/bin/sha256sum\n/usr/bin/printf 'abc' | LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 /usr/bin/sha256sum\n", "stdout": "ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad  -\nba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad  -\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/locale-and-byte-order-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

Collation cost grows with the number of comparisons, which for a comparison sort grows like N log N times the cost of one comparison. A heavier comparison therefore shows up on large N, not on a ten-line example. The locale benchmark uses 100000 lines so the comparison work is at least visible next to process startup. Read the median gap against the trial spread before you keep `LC_ALL=C` as a speed hack. Keep it as a correctness hack whenever the next program assumes byte order, even if the medians tie.

lessons.title: Spaces, newlines, NULs, and binary bytes
lessons.summary: File names are byte strings. Newlines and leading dashes break line-oriented tools. NUL is the delimiter that cannot appear in a name.
objectives: Show a name containing a space and a name containing a newline
Use --quoting-style=shell-escape and --zero on GNU ls
Explain why line-oriented pipes corrupt binary and hostile names
Pass -- when an operand begins with a dash
lessons.gnuVsBsd: `ls --zero` and `--quoting-style` are GNU. BSD `ls` has no `--zero`. The portable NUL-safe producer outside coreutils is `find -print0` (findutils) together with `xargs -0`. BSD `ls -b` shows C-style escapes on some systems and is not the same flag set. This lesson captured GNU ls 9.4 only.
lessons.markdown:
A Linux file name is a sequence of bytes, not a Unicode string and not a line. The only bytes that cannot appear are NUL and `/`. Space, newline, quote, leading dash, and invalid UTF-8 are all legal names. Tools that split input on whitespace or newline are assuming a subset of that space. The assumption holds for a tree you created with boring names and fails for a tree you downloaded, unpacked, or let a user name.

GNU `ls` can show the danger instead of hiding it. `--quoting-style=shell-escape` prints a name you could paste back into bash, including `$'...` for a newline. `--zero` ends each name with a NUL and does not escape the bytes inside the name, because NUL cannot occur there. Those two options answer different questions. The first is for a human. The second is for the next program.

`wc --files0-from=-` reads a NUL-delimited list of paths. `sort --files0-from` and the checksum tools have the same idea. The producer and the consumer must agree. `ls --zero | wc -l` is wrong: `wc -l` counts newlines, and the NUL list may contain none. The safe-pipelines lesson connects the pieces. Here the point is the delimiter.

Binary files are the same issue one level down. `cat -A` is a text visualization: tab becomes `^I`, a newline becomes `$`, a NUL becomes `^@`. It is not a reversible dump. `od -An -tx1` is the dump. `sort` will read binary input because the manual says GNU utilities do not restrict the bytes inside a line, but a "line" still ends at newline, and a missing final newline is silently supplied by `sort`. A file that is one huge line becomes one record. That is a memory question, not a character-set question.

Android build trees and Gradle caches do contain spaces (`Application Support` is a macOS problem; `My Documents` style names and NDK paths with spaces show up on Linux too). Rust `OUT_DIR` is usually safe. A test fixture that only uses `file1` never exercises the bug your user will hit.

## Worked examples

### A space is one name

```example
{"id": "filenames-and-binary-01", "title": "shell-escape quoting", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir box\n/usr/bin/touch 'box/a b'\n/usr/bin/ls -1 --quoting-style=shell-escape box\n", "stdout": "'a b'\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/filenames-and-binary-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A newline in the name

```example
{"id": "filenames-and-binary-02", "title": "A newline is visible in shell-escape style", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir -p nest\nname=\"$(/usr/bin/printf 'nest/a\\nb')\"\n/usr/bin/touch \"$name\"\n/usr/bin/ls -1 --quoting-style=shell-escape nest\n", "stdout": "'a'$'\\n''b'\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/filenames-and-binary-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### NUL-delimited names

```example
{"id": "filenames-and-binary-03", "title": "ls --zero keeps the space inside the field", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/touch 'a b' c\n/usr/bin/ls -1 --zero | /usr/bin/od -An -tx1\n", "stdout": " 61 20 62 00 63 00\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/filenames-and-binary-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### NUL is data, not a line ending

```example
{"id": "filenames-and-binary-04", "title": "cat -A marks a NUL", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\0b\\n' | /usr/bin/cat -A\n", "stdout": "a^@b$\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/filenames-and-binary-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

When a shell loop must visit names, use `find -print0` (companion) and `read -d ''`, or stay inside coreutils with `ls --zero` only if you accept that `ls` is not a recursive inventory tool. `ls` without `-A` hides dotfiles. `ls` without a path argument lists `.`, which is a different set from the files you thought you passed.

For a checksum manifest of arbitrary names, GNU `sha256sum --zero` writes NUL-terminated records. Matching check mode can read them back. The checksum lesson shows the text format first, because that is what download pages publish. Switch to `--zero` when names are allowed to contain newlines.

## Tips and pitfalls

Creating the newline name with an unquoted command substitution is itself a quoting hazard. The example quotes the substitution. Copy the quotes.

`ls` output is not a stable API. Columns, color, and quoting depend on whether stdout is a terminal. In this capture, stdout is a pipe, so you get the non-terminal format. A screenshot of an interactive `ls` will not match.

Binary-safe does not mean "use cat". It means "do not treat the stream as newline-delimited text unless you have decided that is the format".

Use od.", "hint": "`printf 'a\\nb'` writes exactly those three bytes. `od -An -tx1` prints them.", "solution": "You should see 61, 0a, 62. The 0a is the newline that text tools would treat as a record boundary.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb' > bytes\n/usr/bin/od -An -tx1 bytes\n", "stdout": " 61 0a 62\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/filenames-and-binary-ex02.sh"}

The total line is about the files' contents (empty files have 0 lines) plus a total. Read it as a name list that survived the space, not as a line count of the listing.", "solution": "wc opened both names. A space-splitting loop would have looked for a file named `a` and a file named `b`.", "script": "/usr/bin/touch 'a b' c\n/usr/bin/ls -1 --zero | /usr/bin/wc -l --files0-from=-\n", "stdout": "0 a b\n0 c\n0 total\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/filenames-and-binary-ex03.sh"}


## Performance

NUL-delimited streams are not slower in any way that matters next to `stat` calls. The costly bug is correctness that forces a retry: a script that splits names, misses a file, and reruns a link. `ls` itself is a poor recursive walker because it stats every name to decide how to print, which is a syscall per entry. If you only need names, a dedicated walker (`find`, which is not coreutils) can do less. If you need sizes, you were going to stat anyway, and `du` or `stat` is the honest tool. Do not "optimize" by parsing `ls -l`.

lessons.title: Listing names with ls
lessons.summary: ls prints names and, when asked, metadata. The format depends on the destination, the quoting style, and which names you asked to include.
objectives: Choose -1, -A, -F, -l, and -S on purpose
Read --quoting-style and --zero as output contracts
Tell dir and vdir apart from ls
Keep color and columns out of scripts
lessons.gnuVsBsd: GNU `ls --color` is BSD `ls -G` on macOS. GNU `ls -T` sets tab stops; BSD `ls -T` sets a time format. `--group-directories-first`, `--quoting-style`, and `--zero` are GNU. Human-readable `-h` exists on both, with different details. `dir` and `vdir` are GNU names. Captured output is GNU ls 9.4 writing to a pipe, so it uses the non-terminal format.
lessons.markdown:
`ls` answers "what names are here, and optionally what metadata the kernel will tell me about them." It is a presentation program. The info node spends most of its length on which names are included, how they are sorted, and how they are printed. Those are three separate choices, and the defaults change when stdout is a terminal: columns and, depending on the build and aliases, color. In a pipe, this GNU ls writes one name per line if you pass `-1`, and a compact format otherwise. Scripts should pass the format they need and not inherit an alias. `command ls` or `/usr/bin/ls` skips an alias. It does not skip a shell function of the same name; `type ls` tells you.

`-a` includes names that start with `.`, including `.` and `..`. `-A` includes dot names and skips `.` and `..`. That is the useful inventory of a directory you intend to copy. `-F` appends a classifier: `/` for a directory, `@` for a symlink, nothing for a regular file. The classifier is a character on the end of the name. Do not feed `-F` output to another tool as a path.

`-l` is the long format: mode, link count, owner, group, size, time, name. `-h` prints powers-of-1024 sizes with a suffix. The sort lesson's `-h` can order that output; `numfmt` can turn a raw byte column into the same idea with an explicit unit. `-S` sorts by size. None of these are a substitute for `stat -c` when you need one field.

`dir` and `vdir` are the same package. `dir` is an ls with a different default presentation. `vdir` is closer to `ls -l`. Scripts that call `vdir` because it "looks like" a long listing will confuse a reader who has only learned `ls`. Call `ls -l`.

`dircolors` prints shell code that sets `LS_COLORS`. Evaluating it is what makes `--color=auto` look like your theme. The colors are not in the file. They are in the terminal. A log file that captured color codes is full of escapes; pass `--color=never` when the consumer is not a terminal.

## Recipes

For a build directory you want to eyeball, `ls -l -h -S --group-directories-first` puts directories first and large artifacts at the top of the file list. That is a human view. For a program, use `stat` or `find` (findutils) with an explicit format.

If you must log a listing in CI, pin `--time-style=long-iso`, `--quoting-style=shell-escape`, `-1`, and `--color=never`. The log is then diffable except for timestamps you expected to change.

## Tips and pitfalls

`ls` without arguments lists the current directory. A script that does `ls $maybe_empty` when the variable is empty becomes "list `.`", which looks like success and shows the wrong tree. Pass `--` and quote, and handle the empty case.

`-R` is recursive presentation, not an archive and not a walk you can resume. It is also easy to mix with `-l` into a blob no parser should read.

Aliases in `~/.bashrc` such as `alias ls='ls --color=auto'` do not apply to `sh -c` scripts or to exec from Rust. They apply to your interactive prompt. Do not debug a script by comparing it with what you see after an alias.

## Performance

`ls -l` stats every name it prints. On a directory of hundreds of thousands of build outputs that is a lot of `stat` syscalls, and it is still the wrong interface if the next step parses the columns. The cost is metadata, not the printing. `ls` of a single name is fine. Recursive `ls -lR` of a multi-gigabyte tree is an inventory you did not need if `du -s` or a build tool already knows the answer. No flag of `ls` changes the disk bandwidth of reading file contents, because `ls` does not read contents except when it must identify some special cases. Do not use it as a copy or a checksum.

lessons.title: stat, touch, and timestamps
lessons.summary: stat prints kernel metadata with a format string. touch sets timestamps. GNU and BSD spell those jobs with different flags, and ext4's type code confuses stat -f.
objectives: Print size, mode, owner, and mtime with stat -c
Set an explicit timestamp with touch -d and copy one with touch -r
Distinguish stat on a file from stat -f on a filesystem
Explain why stat -f can say ext2/ext3 on an ext4 volume
lessons.gnuVsBsd: This is the sharpest everyday split. GNU `stat -c '%s'` is BSD `stat -f %z` (the format letters differ too). GNU `stat -f` means filesystem, not format. BSD `touch` does not accept GNU `-d`; it uses `-t` with a different timestamp grammar. Scripts that try `stat -c` on macOS fail immediately. Nothing here was run on BSD. The captured `stat -f` line is this host's GNU coreutils reading this filesystem.
lessons.markdown:
`stat` reads the inode (and, with `-f`, the filesystem) and prints what you ask. The default multi-line layout is for a person. `stat -c` is for a script. Format sequences include `%s` size in bytes, `%a` mode in octal, `%A` mode in symbolic form, `%U` and `%G` owner names, `%u` and `%g` ids, `%F` file type, `%y` human mtime, `%Y` mtime as seconds since the epoch, `%n` the name, `%h` the link count, `%b` the number of allocated blocks, and `%B` the block size those blocks are counted in. `%b` times `%B` is the allocated space, which is not `%s` for a sparse file. The du lesson uses that pair.

`touch` creates an empty file or updates timestamps. `touch -d '2020-01-02 03:04:05 UTC'` sets both times to that instant on GNU touch. `touch -r other file` copies timestamps from `other`. `touch -c` will not create a missing file. None of this writes your data. A reproducible build that needs `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` still has to pass that into the compiler; `touch` only fixes the inode clock after the fact.

Filesystem identity is where this host is a good teacher. `df -T` on the capture disk reports `ext4`. `stat -f -c '%T'` reports `ext2/ext3`. GNU stat is not confused about the mount in a vague way: the kernel's statfs type code for ext2, ext3, and ext4 is the same historic magic, and the format sequence prints that shared name. Use `df -T` or `findmnt` (findmnt is util-linux, not coreutils) when you need the type string a person means. Use `stat -f -c '%s'` when you need the filesystem block size.

Timestamps you copy from another machine are not a security log. They are metadata the owner can set, which is exactly why `touch -d` works without being root. Do not authenticate a file by its mtime. Checksum the bytes.

## Worked examples

### One field, not a paragraph

```example
{"id": "stat-touch-timestamps-01", "title": "Format strings for size, mode, and type", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'hello\\n' > notes.txt\n/usr/bin/stat -c 'size=%s mode=%a type=%F name=%n' notes.txt\n", "stdout": "size=6 mode=644 type=regular file name=notes.txt\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/stat-touch-timestamps-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### An explicit timestamp

```example
{"id": "stat-touch-timestamps-02", "title": "touch -d then read it back", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/touch -d '2020-01-02 03:04:05 UTC' stamped\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%y' stamped\n", "stdout": "2020-01-02 03:04:05.000000000 +0000\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/stat-touch-timestamps-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Copy a timestamp

```example
{"id": "stat-touch-timestamps-03", "title": "touch -r copies mtime", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/touch -d '2020-01-02 03:04:05 UTC' source\n/usr/bin/touch -r source copy\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%y %n' source copy\n", "stdout": "2020-01-02 03:04:05.000000000 +0000 source\n2020-01-02 03:04:05.000000000 +0000 copy\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/stat-touch-timestamps-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### The filesystem type string disagrees with df

```example
{"id": "stat-touch-timestamps-04", "title": "stat -f versus df -T on this disk", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/stat -f -c 'statfs_type=%T block_size=%s' .\n/usr/bin/df --output=source,fstype,target .\n", "stdout": "statfs_type=ext2/ext3 block_size=4096\nFilesystem     Type Mounted on\n/dev/vdc       ext4 /\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/stat-touch-timestamps-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

In a C++ or Rust release job, after you `install` a binary, record `stat -c '%s %a' ` on the installed path if the package format cares about mode and size. Record `sha256sum` if the package format cares about bytes. Do not record the default `stat` paragraph into a machine-readable bill of materials; the column widths are not a contract.

To see whether two builds produced the same bytes, ignore mtime. `cmp` is diffutils, not coreutils. `sha256sum` is the coreutils answer, and `install -C` is the coreutils way to avoid bumping mtime when the bytes already match.

## Tips and pitfalls

`stat file >` redirection is a different file from `stat`'s operand. People overwrite the file they meant to inspect by pointing a redirect at it. Put redirects on a log name.

`%Y` is seconds. `%y` contains a space and a timezone. If you sort on `%y` as text you are not sorting by time once the format varies. Print `%Y` and `sort -n`.

`touch` on a symlink updates the target unless you pass `-h`. The link-count and symlink lessons cover the distinction. If you only remember one rule: metadata operations follow symlinks unless a flag says `-h` or `--no-dereference`.

A newline would have made it 5.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abcd' > payload\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%s' payload\n", "stdout": "4\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/stat-touch-timestamps-ex01.sh"}

That integer is what you can sort and compare across machines that agree on UTC.", "script": "/usr/bin/touch -d '2020-01-02 00:00:00 UTC' when\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%Y' when\n", "stdout": "1577923200\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/stat-touch-timestamps-ex02.sh"}

## Performance

`stat` is one syscall per call for a file, plus formatting. It does not read the file. Calling it in a shell loop over tens of thousands of names is slower than a language that calls `stat` in-process, because you pay for a process per file. That overhead is real and it is still not a reason to parse `ls -l`. If you need many metadata records, use a program that can do the loop internally (`find -printf`, which is findutils, not coreutils) or call `stat` from Rust. `touch` is not a performance tool. Setting timestamps on an entire tree with a shell loop is dominated by process startup, the same way.

lessons.title: mkdir, rmdir, and empty trees
lessons.summary: mkdir -p builds parents under the umask. -m applies to the last component. rmdir only removes empty directories.
objectives: Create a nested directory and predict parent modes under umask 0022
Remove an empty directory and explain the two rmdir failures
Choose rmdir over rm -r when emptiness is the safety check
Know that mknod of a device node is a privileged operation this course does not perform
lessons.gnuVsBsd: `mkdir -p` and `mkdir -m` exist on BSD. GNU long options (`--parents`, `--mode`) do not. The parent-mode pitfall is shared: `-m` does not apply to parents created along the way. `rmdir` is POSIX. `mknod` exists on both and is the wrong tool for ordinary directories. Captured modes assume the sandbox umask printed in the example.
lessons.markdown:
`mkdir` creates directories. `mkdir -p a/b/c` creates each missing component and succeeds if the final one already exists as a directory. The mode argument `-m 700` is applied to the directory that the invocation treats as the one being created at the end, not to every parent it had to materialize. Parents are created with the mode `0777` modified by the umask. This capture environment's umask is `0022`, so a parent lands at `0755` while the leaf you named with `-m 700` lands at `0700`. That is the bug behind a "private" cache directory whose parent is world-executable and world-readable. If the parent must be private too, `mkdir` it separately with `-m 700`, then create the child.

`rmdir` removes a directory only when it is empty. A regular file fails with "Not a directory". A directory that still has an entry fails with "Directory not empty". Those are different mistakes. `rmdir -p a/b/c` removes `c`, then `b`, then `a` if each becomes empty. It stops when one is not empty. It will not delete a file that happens to sit in the way. That is why it is safer than `rm -r` for tearing down a scratch tree you believe is empty. If `rmdir` fails, something is still there and you should look before you reach for `-r`.

`mkfifo` creates a named pipe and is covered with tee. `mknod` can create a fifo too, and it can create device nodes if you pass a major and minor number. Device nodes in `/dev` are not a coreutils exercise and they need privileges. The reference entry says so. This lesson does not call `mknod`.

Directories themselves have a size, but that size is the directory's own metadata storage, not the sum of the files inside. `du` is the tool that walks. `stat -c %s` on a directory is almost never the number you wanted in a disk-usage report.

## Worked examples

### Parent mode versus leaf mode

```example
{"id": "directories-01", "title": "-m does not lock down parents", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'umask:'\numask\n/usr/bin/mkdir -p -m 700 deep/leaf\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%a %n' deep deep/leaf\n", "stdout": "umask:0022\n755 deep\n700 deep/leaf\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/directories-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### rmdir refuses a file and a non-empty directory

```example
{"id": "directories-02", "title": "Two different rmdir errors", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/mkdir box\n/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > box/file\n/usr/bin/rmdir box\n/usr/bin/printf 'nonempty:%s\\n' $?\n/usr/bin/rmdir box/file\n/usr/bin/printf 'nota_dir:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "nonempty:1\nnota_dir:1\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/rmdir: failed to remove 'box': Directory not empty\n/usr/bin/rmdir: failed to remove 'box/file': Not a directory\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/directories-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Remove a chain that is actually empty

```example
{"id": "directories-03", "title": "rmdir -p removes emptied parents", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir -p a/b/c\n/usr/bin/rmdir -p a/b/c\n/usr/bin/ls -A\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/directories-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A directory's own byte size is not the tree

```example
{"id": "directories-04", "title": "stat on a directory is not du", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir -p tree/sub\n/usr/bin/printf 'hello\\n' > tree/sub/f\n/usr/bin/stat -c 'dir_size=%s' tree\n/usr/bin/du -b -s tree\n", "stdout": "dir_size=4096\n6\ttree\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/directories-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Create a cache root once: `mkdir -m 700 "$HOME/.cache/mytool"` and then `mkdir -p` the subdirectories if the root already has the mode you want. Do not expect a single `mkdir -p -m 700` of a brand-new deep path to privatize the whole chain.

In a test harness, build the tree under `mktemp -d` and remove it with `rm -r` only at the end, when destruction is the point. During the test, `rmdir` is the assertion that a directory you meant to empty is empty.

## Tips and pitfalls

`mkdir -p` on a path whose middle component is a file fails. `-p` does not replace a file with a directory. That failure is useful.

`rmdir` on a symlink to a directory is not "remove the directory through the link" in the way people hope. Do not point recursive deletion at a symlink you have not inspected. The link lesson shows how to see the target with `readlink`.

The umask is a process property. A systemd unit, a CI runner, and your interactive shell can disagree. Print `umask` in the job if the modes matter.

## Performance

`mkdir` of a deep tree is metadata writes. It is slow on a filesystem that journals metadata when you do it one process per directory from a shell loop. `mkdir -p` in one process is the better coreutils form. It is still not a bulk extractor: `tar` (not coreutils) creates a tree from an archive with far less shell traffic. Creating thousands of directories as a cache partition is a filesystem-layout question. Keep directories from becoming huge in entry count; many filesystems slow down on a single directory with hundreds of thousands of names, and `ls` or shell globs then dominate. That limit is the filesystem's, not a mkdir flag.

lessons.title: basename, dirname, readlink, realpath, pwd
lessons.summary: These tools rewrite path strings. They do not all require the file to exist, and the shell's pwd is not always /usr/bin/pwd.
objectives: Strip prefixes and suffixes with basename and dirname without reading stdin
Choose realpath -e, the default, and -m for missing components
Compare readlink -f with realpath
Call /usr/bin/pwd when you mean the coreutils program
lessons.gnuVsBsd: GNU `basename` accepts multiple names, `-a`, and `-s`. BSD basename is usually one name and a suffix. GNU `readlink -f` canonicalizes and allows a missing final component; older BSD `readlink` only printed a symlink target. macOS has gained flags over time; do not assume the GNU set. `realpath` was missing on older macOS. `/usr/bin/pwd` versus the shell builtin is a bash issue on every system. This lesson ran GNU tools only.
lessons.markdown:
Path tools are string and symlink resolvers. `basename /src/libfoo.a .a` prints `libfoo`. `dirname /src/libfoo.a` prints `/src`. Multiple arguments are allowed on GNU basename and dirname. `-z` changes the output separator to NUL. It does not switch the tools into a mode where they read NUL-separated stdin. If you have a NUL list, you still need something that splits it and passes arguments, or you stay in a language that has the bytes. People pipe `find -print0` into `dirname` and get "missing operand", which is what this package does.

`realpath` prints an absolute path. By default every component except the last must exist. `-e` requires the last component too. `-m` allows missing components in the middle, which is how you ask "what would this path be" before you create it. `--relative-to=DIR` prints the result relative to DIR. That is the form you want in a build log that should not embed the absolute sandbox path, when both paths share a root.

`readlink` without flags prints the immediate target of a symlink and fails on an ordinary file. `readlink -f` canonicalizes, following every symlink, and all but the last component must exist. On a missing final component it still prints a path and exits 0. `readlink -e` is the strict form. `readlink -m` allows missing components. If you only want "is this a symlink, and what does it store", do not pass `-f`. `-f` answers a different question: the canonical file name.

`pwd` is a builtin in bash. `/usr/bin/pwd` is coreutils. `-L` is logical and follows the shell's idea of `$PWD`. `-P` is physical and resolves symlinks. In a directory you entered through a symlink, they differ. Build scripts that compare paths should pick one and document it. `realpath -P` is the physical resolution if you already have a path in a variable.

None of these tools create or delete the file, except that your script might do that around them. `mkdir -p "$(dirname -- "$path")"` is the usual pairing, and the `--` matters when the path starts with a dash.

## Worked examples

### Suffix and directory

```example
{"id": "paths-01", "title": "basename and dirname on a library path", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/basename /opt/ndk/libfoo.a .a\n/usr/bin/dirname /opt/ndk/libfoo.a\n/usr/bin/basename -a /a/b /c/d.txt\n", "stdout": "libfoo\n/opt/ndk\nb\nd.txt\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/paths-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Missing paths

```example
{"id": "paths-02", "title": "realpath -m versus -e", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/realpath -m /tmp/does-not-exist-cu/child\nset +e\n/usr/bin/realpath -e /tmp/does-not-exist-cu\n/usr/bin/printf 'strict:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "/tmp/does-not-exist-cu/child\nstrict:1\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/realpath: /tmp/does-not-exist-cu: No such file or directory\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/paths-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### readlink -f allows a missing tail

```example
{"id": "paths-03", "title": "Canonical name of a missing final component", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/readlink -f /tmp/missing-final-component\n/usr/bin/printf 'exit:%s\\n' $?\n", "stdout": "/tmp/missing-final-component\nexit:0\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/paths-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A relative answer from the coreutils pwd

```example
{"id": "paths-04", "title": "realpath --relative-to and /usr/bin/pwd", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir -p proj/src\n/usr/bin/realpath --relative-to=proj proj/src\n/usr/bin/pwd -P\n", "stdout": "src\n/tmp/cuwb-lz19dzik\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/paths-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

In a script that receives a path from a user, run `realpath -e -- "$path"` when the file must already exist, and fail the build if it does not. Use `realpath -m` only when you are about to create the path and you need the absolute form for a log line.

`basename -- "$0"` is a common way to get a program name. The `--` is load-bearing if the name can start with a dash. Pair `mkdir -p -- "$(dirname -- "$dest")"` with `install -D` when you would otherwise recreate the parent logic by hand. `install -D` creates leading components itself; the permissions lesson prefers it for placing a binary.

Build systems should store relative paths in committed files. `--relative-to` the repository root keeps a CI workspace prefix out of the artifact.

## Tips and pitfalls

`dirname` of a name with no slash prints `.`. Feeding that to `mkdir -p` creates a directory in the current working directory, which may be correct and may be a surprise.

Command substitution deletes trailing newlines. A path that legitimately ends in a newline, which is rare and legal, will be damaged by `path=$(realpath -- "$path")`. NUL-delimited APIs avoid that. Coreutils `realpath -z` ends the output with NUL.

The builtin `pwd` can be a shell function's view of the world. If a script's shebang is bash, `pwd` is the builtin even when `/usr/bin` is first on `PATH`. Type the absolute path when you are teaching or testing the coreutils behavior.

The path is not read from disk.", "script": "/usr/bin/basename /build/libfoo.a .a\n", "stdout": "libfoo\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/paths-ex01.sh"}

The file does not need to exist.", "hint": "`realpath ./no-such-leaf` is enough on GNU realpath because the final component may be missing. The current directory exists.", "solution": "You get an absolute path ending in `no-such-leaf`. `-e` would have failed.", "script": "/usr/bin/realpath ./no-such-leaf\n", "stdout": "/tmp/cuwb-5_m8kn3_/no-such-leaf\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/paths-ex02.sh"}

The builtin would usually match here because this directory was not entered through a symlink.", "script": "/usr/bin/pwd -P\n", "stdout": "/tmp/cuwb-e_17lrc6\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/paths-ex03.sh"}


## Performance

These tools are string and symlink operations. `realpath` may call `lstat` on each component. That is noise next to compiling a crate, and it is the whole cost if you call `realpath` once per file from a shell loop over a million paths. Resolve a root once, then join relative names in-process if you are in Rust or C++. Do not cache a `pwd` from a previous working directory across a `cd`. The slow bug is not realpath's algorithm. It is repeating it at process-per-file granularity, and following a symlink farm that an attacker or a broken install planted. `-e` failing closed is the performance win that matters: you find the bad path before a later tool walks the wrong tree.

lessons.title: cp, sparse files, and reflinks
lessons.summary: cp can share data, preserve holes, or read every byte. On this ext4 disk a reflink clone is refused and a sparse file is not.
objectives: Copy a file, a symlink as a symlink, and a symlink's target
Show that --reflink=always fails here and --reflink=auto falls back
Compare apparent size and allocated blocks after a sparse copy
Prefer --update=none over -n on coreutils 9.4
lessons.gnuVsBsd: GNU `cp --reflink` asks for a clone or copy-on-write when the filesystem supports it. macOS uses `cp -c` for a clonefile, which is a different flag. `--sparse` is GNU. `cp -a` is GNU's archive mode (`-dR --preserve=all`); BSD `cp -a` is not the same preserve set. GNU 9.4 warns that `-n` is non-portable and tells you to use `--update=none`. That warning was captured here. BSD was not executed.
lessons.markdown:
`cp` reads a source and writes a destination, unless the filesystem can do better. "Better" has two independent meanings. A reflink or clone is a new directory entry that shares the source's data blocks until one side writes. A sparse copy is a destination whose holes are not written out as zero bytes. Neither is a guarantee. Both depend on the filesystem and on the flags.

On this machine `cp --reflink=always` fails with "Operation not supported". The capture disk is ext4, which does not do reflink clones. `--reflink=auto` is the default-ish polite request: try a clone, and if the kernel refuses, copy the bytes. `--reflink=never` forces the byte copy. A script that requires a clone, because it is about to mutate one side of a huge image, must pass `--reflink=always` and treat a non-zero status as "do not pretend these files are independent". A script that only wants a copy should pass `--reflink=never` when a silent clone would surprise a later checksum of allocated blocks, or leave the default if either result is acceptable. Say which one you mean.

Sparse files are a different axis. `truncate -s 1M` creates a hole. `stat` shows a large `%s` and a small `%b`. `cp --sparse=auto` uses a heuristic to keep holes. `--sparse=always` tries to make a sparse destination even when it has to detect zero runs. `--sparse=never` writes the zeros. `du -B1` without `--apparent-size` reports allocated space. `du -b` reports apparent size. If those numbers match, you do not have a hole.

`-a` is archive mode: recursive, preserve links as links, and preserve attributes. Copying a symlink with `-a` copies the symlink. `cp -L` follows it and writes a regular file. That choice matters for a toolchain sysroot, where a symlink to a shared library must stay a symlink.

`-n` / `--no-clobber` on this 9.4 prints that the behavior is non-portable and may change. The replacement the help text names is `--update=none`. `mv -n` does not print the same warning and exits 1 when it refuses. Do not assume the two `-n` flags are one feature.

`--parents` recreates the source path under the destination directory, but the source path is interpreted relative to the current directory. The example `cd`s first. Running it from the wrong place looks like a missing `src`.

## Worked examples

### Reflink request versus fallback

```example
{"id": "copy-01", "title": "always fails here, auto copies", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abc\\n' > src\nset +e\n/usr/bin/cp --reflink=always src dest-always\n/usr/bin/printf 'always:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n/usr/bin/cp --reflink=auto src dest-auto\n/usr/bin/sha256sum src dest-auto\n", "stdout": "always:1\nedeaaff3f1774ad2888673770c6d64097e391bc362d7d6fb34982ddf0efd18cb  src\nedeaaff3f1774ad2888673770c6d64097e391bc362d7d6fb34982ddf0efd18cb  dest-auto\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/cp: failed to clone 'dest-always' from 'src': Operation not supported\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/copy-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A symlink stays a symlink under -a

```example
{"id": "copy-02", "title": "-a keeps the link, -L copies the target", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'data\\n' > target\n/usr/bin/ln -s target link\n/usr/bin/cp -a link copy-link\n/usr/bin/cp -L link copy-file\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%F %n' copy-link copy-file\n", "stdout": "symbolic link copy-link\nregular file copy-file\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/copy-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Sparse size versus allocated blocks

```example
{"id": "copy-03", "title": "A hole survives an auto sparse copy", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/truncate -s 1M hole\n/usr/bin/cp --sparse=auto hole hole-copy\n/usr/bin/stat -c 'src size=%s blocks=%b' hole\n/usr/bin/stat -c 'dst size=%s blocks=%b' hole-copy\n", "stdout": "src size=1048576 blocks=0\ndst size=1048576 blocks=0\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/copy-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Do not clobber, without -n

```example
{"id": "copy-04", "title": "--update=none leaves the destination", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'new\\n' > incoming\n/usr/bin/printf 'old\\n' > kept\n/usr/bin/cp --update=none incoming kept\n/usr/bin/cat kept\n", "stdout": "old\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/copy-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

For an Android `out/` tree or a Rust `target/` directory, `cp -a` is the blunt instrument that preserves symlinks and modes. It is not incremental. `rsync` is the incremental tool and it is not installed here and not coreutils. If you only needed a clone and the filesystem is btrfs or XFS with reflink, `--reflink=always` is the cheap copy. On this ext4 host it is not available, so the cheap copy does not exist and you pay the bytes.

`--parents` is how you lift `include/foo.h` into `dest/include/foo.h` without rewriting the path in the shell.

## Tips and pitfalls

`cp dir1 dir2` when `dir2` exists creates `dir2/dir1`. When `dir2` does not exist, it creates `dir2` as the copy. `-T` forces "destination is the directory itself, not a container". Use `-T` in scripts that must not nest by accident.

Preserving ownership requires privilege. `-a` asks to preserve it and, as an ordinary user, will keep the owner you already have and may warn about what it cannot copy. Read stderr. A zero status can still have skipped an xattr or a capability.

Confirm a copy with `sha256sum` of both names. Matching digests means the bytes match. They do not tell you whether the filesystem cloned the extents or wrote new ones; `stat` block counts are the clue for holes, and this ext4 host simply cannot reflink.

## Exercises

The flag only forbids a clone.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'xyz\\n' > a\n/usr/bin/cp --reflink=never a b\n/usr/bin/sha256sum a b\n", "stdout": "f34fe622a8fe7565fc15be3ce8bc43d7e32a0dd744ebef509fa0bdb130c0ac31  a\nf34fe622a8fe7565fc15be3ce8bc43d7e32a0dd744ebef509fa0bdb130c0ac31  b\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/copy-ex01.sh"}


```exercise
{"id": "copy-ex02", "title": "Require a clone and accept the failure", "prompt": "Create `a` and run `cp --reflink=always a b` on this filesystem. Leave the non-zero status in place.", "hint": "ext4 on the capture host returns \"Operation not supported\".", "solution": "A required clone that the filesystem cannot do must fail the script. Falling back silently is `--reflink=auto`, which is a different request.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'xyz\\n' > a\n/usr/bin/cp --reflink=always a b\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "/usr/bin/cp: failed to clone 'b' from 'a': Operation not supported\n", "exitCode": 1, "download": "/downloads/solutions/copy-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "copy-ex03", "title": "Keep an existing file", "prompt": "With `old` containing `keep` and `new` containing `replace`, copy `new` onto `old` using `--update=none`, then print `old`.", "hint": "The destination content should stay `keep`.", "solution": "`--update=none` is the GNU 9.4 spelling of \"do not overwrite\".", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'keep\\n' > old\n/usr/bin/printf 'replace\\n' > new\n/usr/bin/cp --update=none new old\n/usr/bin/cat old\n", "stdout": "keep\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/copy-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

A reflink is a metadata operation. A byte copy moves every byte through the page cache and may write them back. On a filesystem that supports reflinks, the difference is enormous for a multi-gigabyte image and irrelevant for a 4-byte file. This host does not support the clone, so there is no reflink number to report, and inventing one would be false. The copy benchmark compares `cp --reflink=never` with `dd` on an 8 MiB warm file and tells you if the medians even separate. Sparse copies save write bandwidth when the source is mostly holes. They do not save it when the source is a compressed APK full of non-zero bytes. Look at `%b` before you celebrate.

lessons.title: mv on one filesystem and across two
lessons.summary: mv is a rename when the destination is the same filesystem. Across devices it copies and then unlinks. -n refuses to replace and exits 1.
objectives: Rename a file and move it into a directory with -t
Show that -n exits 1 and leaves the destination bytes alone
Demonstrate a cross-device move from the ext4 disk onto tmpfs
Use -T when the destination must not be treated as a container
lessons.gnuVsBsd: POSIX `mv` across filesystems is copy-plus-unlink because `rename` returns EXDEV. GNU `mv -t` and `-T` are not portable to BSD mv. GNU `mv -n` on this version exits 1 when it refuses; do not assume BSD `-n` prints the same diagnostic. The cross-device example uses `/dev/shm` (tmpfs) and was captured here. No BSD host was involved.
lessons.markdown:
`rename(2)` changes a directory entry. It is atomic on one filesystem and it does not copy bytes. `mv` uses it when source and destination are on the same device. When they are not, the kernel returns EXDEV and `mv` copies, then unlinks the source. That second form is not atomic. A crash in the middle can leave both copies, or the new copy without the mode bits you expected. Scripts that move a finished artifact into place on the same filesystem get the atomic publish. Scripts that move from the build disk onto a tmpfs ramdisk, or onto another mount, do not.

You can see the device identity with `stat -c '%d'`. Two paths with the same device number can still be different mount points in exotic setups, but a different device number is enough to prove the move cannot be a pure rename. This sandbox lives on the ext4 root. `/dev/shm` is tmpfs. The example moves a small file between them and prints both device numbers, then deletes the tmpfs file. Do not leave scratch files in `/dev/shm`.

`-t DIR` means "every operand is a source, and DIR is the container". That is the form that works with `xargs` (findutils, not coreutils), because you can put `-t` before the names `xargs` appends. `-T` means "the destination is not a directory to move into, even if it is a directory". Without `-T`, `mv file existing-dir` puts `file` inside `existing-dir`. With `-T`, that shape is an error unless you are replacing a non-directory. Pick one explicitly in a script.

`-n` refuses to replace an existing destination. On this GNU mv it prints "not replacing" and exits 1. The source remains. `--update=none` is the related cp spelling; mv's `-n` did not print the cp portability warning in the probe for this course. Still prefer the long option you can explain. `--backup` makes a backup according to the version-control rules in the common-options chapter. It is easy to fill a directory with `~` files if you turn it on in a loop.

Trailing slashes matter. `mv file dir/` insists that `dir` is a directory. The trailing-slashes node in the manual is the reference. A script that adds the slash fails closed when `dir` was accidentally a file.

## Worked examples

### A same-filesystem rename

## Recipes

Publish a finished archive by writing it to a temporary name on the same filesystem and then `mv -T` it onto the public name. Readers see the old file or the new file, not a partial write. If the public name is on another mount, you cannot have that atomicity. Copy to a temporary name on the destination filesystem and `mv` there.

`mv -n` in a loop is a reasonable "do not smash an existing artifact" check because the status is non-zero. Test the status. A script with `set -e` will stop, which is what you want if replacement is a bug.

## Tips and pitfalls

`mv` of a directory onto another directory moves it inside, the same way as a file. `mv a b` when both are directories yields `b/a` if `b` exists. That surprise has eaten release directories. `-T` makes the intent visible.

Cross-device `mv` of a symlink copies the symlink or the content depending on flags, and it may not preserve every attribute an ordinary user cannot set. Read stderr.

The trap in the cross-device example removes the shm file even when a later command fails. Copy that pattern. The course runner also deletes its sandbox, but `/dev/shm` is outside the sandbox.

A same-filesystem `mv` is a directory update, constant in the size of the file. A cross-device `mv` costs as much as `cp` plus `unlink`, including page-cache traffic. People "speed up" a script by switching to `mv` and then point it at another mount, where it is suddenly a full copy. Check `stat -c '%d'` when a move of a large Android image is mysteriously slow. There is no flag that makes EXDEV cheap. Reflink copies, where the filesystem supports them, are a `cp` feature, not an `mv` feature. On this ext4 host you already saw that the clone is unavailable.
