lessons.title: rm, prompts, and shred's limits
lessons.summary: rm unlinks directory entries. -I can exit 0 without deleting. shred overwrites only when the device actually stores the new bytes in place.
objectives: Remove a normal file and a name that starts with a dash
Explain the captured behavior of rm -I when stdin hits EOF
State why --preserve-root exists without demonstrating a deletion of /
Describe the manual's limits on shred for journals, snapshots, and SSDs
lessons.gnuVsBsd: GNU rm defaults to `--preserve-root`. BSD rm historically did not have that guard; some current BSD rms added a similar check, and you must read the local man page rather than assume GNU's default. GNU `-I` prompts once in specific cases. `shred` is GNU. macOS has no coreutils shred in the base system. This lesson never ran `rm` against `/` and never ran a BSD rm.
lessons.markdown:
`rm` removes a name. When the link count hits zero and no process has the file open, the filesystem may reuse the blocks. It does not promise to erase them. `rm` of a file you have open in another process removes the name and leaves the data alive until the last file descriptor closes. That is why deleting a log that a daemon still has open does not free the space. The space shows up in `du` of the directory as gone and in `df` of the filesystem as still used. The du and df lesson is the measurement. The mechanism is the inode reference count.

`--` ends options, so `rm -- -rf` removes a file named `-rf` and does not recurse. Build this habit before you interpolate a variable. `rm -r -- "$dir"` is the shape. `rm -r $dir` is the shape that word-splits and glob-expands.

GNU rm treats `/` specially. `--preserve-root` is the default. `--no-preserve-root` turns the guard off. This course does not run either form against the real root. The help text is enough to show that the guard exists, and a demonstration that "probably refuses" is not something to type against `/`. The manual's node on treating `/` specially is the citation. If you need to empty a scratch directory, point `rm -r` at a path you created with `mktemp -d` and checked with `realpath`.

`-i` prompts for each removal. `-I` is less chatty: it prompts when you ask it to remove more than three arguments, or when you descend recursively. In this sandbox, `rm -I` on four files, with empty stdin, printed a question, deleted nothing, and exited 0. A `set -e` script will not notice. If you automate `-I`, you have not built a safety check; you have built a prompt that an empty pipe answers by keeping the files and looking successful. Prefer a dry run that lists names, then an explicit `rm` without `-I`, over a prompt nobody is watching.

`shred` overwrites a file's bytes and, with `-u`, unlinks it. The manual's assumption is that the filesystem and the hardware replace those blocks in place. It then lists designs that break the assumption: journaled data modes, copy-on-write and log-structured filesystems, snapshots, RAID, compressed filesystems, and wear leveling on SSDs, which write the new data somewhere else and leave the old data until garbage collection. ext4 in the default `data=ordered` mode is one of the cases the manual says still overwrites file data as usual, and `data=journal` is not. If you do not know the mount options, the manual tells you to assume shred cannot reliably operate on regular files. The example uses `-n 1` on a scratch file so you can see the name disappear. It is not evidence that a secret is gone from the device.

## Worked examples

### Remove a dash-leading name

```example
{"id": "remove-and-shred-01", "title": "-- keeps -n as a file name", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > ./-n\n/usr/bin/rm -- -n\n/usr/bin/ls -A\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/remove-and-shred-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### -I with nobody answering

```example
{"id": "remove-and-shred-02", "title": "Four files, empty stdin, nothing deleted", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/touch f1 f2 f3 f4\nset +e\n/usr/bin/rm -I f1 f2 f3 f4\n/usr/bin/printf 'status:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n/usr/bin/ls -1\n", "stdout": "status:0\nf1\nf2\nf3\nf4\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/rm: remove 4 arguments? ", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/remove-and-shred-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### The guard is visible in --help, and that is as close as we get to /

```example
{"id": "remove-and-shred-03", "title": "preserve-root is a default, not a demo on the real root", "companion": "grep", "script": "/usr/bin/rm --help | /usr/bin/grep -n preserve-root\n", "stdout": "14:      --no-preserve-root  do not treat '/' specially\n15:      --preserve-root[=all]  do not remove '/' (default);\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/remove-and-shred-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### shred -u removes the name after one overwrite pass

```example
{"id": "remove-and-shred-04", "title": "One pass, then the directory entry is gone", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'secret\\n' > note\n/usr/bin/shred -u -n 1 note\n/usr/bin/ls -A\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/remove-and-shred-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Delete a build scratch directory only after `realpath` shows it sits where you think. Compare the resolved path to the prefix you created. Then `rm -r -- "$scratch"`. The `mktemp` lesson gives you the directory.

For a secret on a laptop SSD, assume `shred` is not sufficient. The manual's own advice points at destroying media when the bytes must be unrecoverable, and at full-disk encryption so the deletion problem is "drop the key" rather than "overwrite the NAND". Encryption is not a coreutils feature. It is the reason not to oversell `shred`.

## Tips and pitfalls

`rm -I` exiting 0 with the files still present is the sharp edge. Test the listing, not only the status, if you ever script `-I`.

`grep` in the help example is the grep package, not coreutils. It is labeled. The same line is visible in `rm --help` without grep if you read it; the filter keeps the capture short.

`shred` of a symlink shreds the target if it follows the link. Know what the name points at before you pass `-u`.

The blocks may still exist on the device until reused.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > gone.txt\n/usr/bin/rm -- gone.txt\n/usr/bin/ls -A\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/remove-and-shred-ex01.sh"}

Print the status and then the remaining names.", "hint": "`set +e` around rm, because you need the listing afterward. Status may be 0 even when the files remain.", "solution": "The prompt received EOF. The files are still there. That is the captured GNU rm behavior you have to design around.", "script": "/usr/bin/touch a b c d\nset +e\n/usr/bin/rm -I a b c d\n/usr/bin/printf 'status:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n/usr/bin/ls -1\n", "stdout": "status:0\na\nb\nc\nd\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/rm: remove 4 arguments? ", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/remove-and-shred-ex02.sh"}

List the directory.", "hint": "`-n 1` is one pass, not a security proof. `-u` unlinks.", "solution": "The name is gone from the directory. The manual's caveats about SSDs and journals still apply to the blocks.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'temp\\n' > temp\n/usr/bin/shred -u -n 1 temp\n/usr/bin/ls -A\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/remove-and-shred-ex03.sh"}


## Performance

`rm` of a large tree is a metadata storm: one unlink per file, directory updates, journal traffic. It is often slower than people expect and almost never limited by "how fast rm the program is". `rm -r` of a tree of a million tiny files is seek and journal work. There is no parallel flag in GNU rm 9.4 that you should reach for to "speed it up" without understanding the filesystem. `shred -n` multiplies the write traffic by the pass count. Extra passes do not fix wear leveling. They make a false sense of security more expensive. One pass in the example is there to show the interface, not because one is a measured optimum.

lessons.title: Hard links, symlinks, ln, link, unlink
lessons.summary: A hard link is another name for the same inode. A symlink is a path stored as data. ln -r rewrites that path to be relative.
objectives: Create a hard link and watch the link count with stat
Create a symlink, retarget it with ln -sfn, and print it with readlink
Use GNU ln --relative and explain why absolute link text breaks when a tree moves
Show that link and unlink refuse directories for an unprivileged caller
lessons.gnuVsBsd: `ln -s` is POSIX. GNU `ln -r` / `--relative` is not on BSD ln. `link` and `unlink` exist widely as thin wrappers around the syscalls; diagnostics differ. macOS `cp -c` is unrelated. GNU `cp -a` preserving a symlink was captured in the copy lesson, not here. No BSD ln was executed.
lessons.markdown:
A hard link is a directory entry that points at an inode. Two names, one inode, one set of bytes, one link count. `stat -c '%h'` prints that count. When you `rm` one name, the count drops and the bytes remain while any name or open file descriptor remains. Hard links cannot span filesystems, because the inode number is local to the device. `ln` across devices fails. Hard links to directories are rejected for an unprivileged user; the kernel returns EPERM. `link` is the bare syscall wrapper and produces that error on a directory. `ln` is the tool with the useful flags.

A symbolic link is a file whose content is a path. The path is not checked when the link is created. It is interpreted when someone opens the link. `readlink` prints the stored path and does not follow further. `readlink -f` resolves it. If you store an absolute target, moving the tree to another prefix breaks the link. GNU `ln -s -r` / `ln -sr` stores a relative target computed from the link's location. That is what you want inside a project tree you will relocate. `cp -a` copies the symlink as a symlink. `cp -L` follows it. Those were captured in the copy lesson; the distinction belongs next to this one.

`ln -sfn new target-name` replaces a symlink even when the name already exists. Without `-f`, ln refuses. Without `-n`, some cases treat an existing symlink-to-directory as a directory to link inside. `-n` / `--no-dereference` is the "do not treat the destination as a directory" flag. The combination `-sfn` is the usual retarget.

`unlink` removes one name via `unlink(2)`. It does not take `-r` and it does not remove a directory. `rm` is the tool with those behaviors and with prompts. Use `unlink` when you mean exactly one non-directory name and you want a failure if that is not what you have.

`du` counts a hard-linked file once unless you pass `-l`. Two names are not two copies of the bytes. The disk-usage lesson measures that. Installing a binary with hard links to save space is a real packaging trick and a real surprise when you edit one name and the other changes.

## Worked examples

### Link count

```example
{"id": "links-01", "title": "Two names, one inode", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'same\\n' > a\n/usr/bin/ln a b\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%h %i %n' a b\n/usr/bin/unlink b\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%h %n' a\n", "stdout": "2 355552 a\n2 355552 b\n1 a\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/links-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A relative symlink

```example
{"id": "links-02", "title": "ln -sr stores a relative target", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir -p sub\n/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > sub/target\n/usr/bin/ln -sr sub/target the-link\n/usr/bin/readlink the-link\n", "stdout": "sub/target\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/links-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Retarget

```example
{"id": "links-03", "title": "ln -sfn replaces the stored path", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/ln -s old name\n/usr/bin/ln -sfn new name\n/usr/bin/readlink name\n", "stdout": "new\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/links-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Directories are refused

```example
{"id": "links-04", "title": "link and unlink do not remove or alias a directory", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir box\nset +e\n/usr/bin/link box box2\n/usr/bin/printf 'link:%s\\n' $?\n/usr/bin/unlink box\n/usr/bin/printf 'unlink:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "link:1\nunlink:1\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/link: cannot create link 'box2' to 'box': Operation not permitted\n/usr/bin/unlink: cannot unlink 'box': Is a directory\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/links-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Inside a repository, create tool symlinks with `ln -sr` so a checkout moved to another directory still resolves. For a system prefix, an absolute link under `/usr` can be correct because the target is supposed to stay at that absolute path. Decide which world the link lives in before you let `ln -s` store whatever string you were holding.

When a Rust `target` directory hard-links identical artifacts, `du -s` without `-l` is the honest disk usage and `du -l` is the sum of the names. Publish the one your capacity planning means.

## Tips and pitfalls

`ln -s target link` does not read `target`. A typo creates a dangling link and exits 0. `readlink -e` is the check that every component exists.

Replacing a symlink with `ln -sf` while a running program has already resolved the old target does not change what that process has open. Symlinks are resolved at open time.

`unlink` on a directory prints "Is a directory". `link` on a directory printed "Operation not permitted" in this sandbox. Those are different errno values. Do not collapse them into one handler if you are wrapping the tools.

Removing one name would drop it to 1 and keep the bytes.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'z\\n' > data\n/usr/bin/ln data alias\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%h' data\n", "stdout": "2\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/links-ex01.sh"}


Leave the non-zero status.", "hint": "unlink has no `-r`.", "solution": "The message says the name is a directory. `rmdir` is the empty-directory tool.", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir dir\n/usr/bin/unlink dir\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "/usr/bin/unlink: cannot unlink 'dir': Is a directory\n", "exitCode": 1, "download": "/downloads/solutions/links-ex03.sh"}


## Performance

Creating a hard link or a symlink is a small metadata write. It does not scale with the size of the target file. That is the performance reason to link identical multi-megabyte artifacts instead of copying them, and it is only available for hard links when both names are on the same filesystem. Symlinks are cheap everywhere and cost a resolution on every open: a chain of symlinks is extra `stat` traffic on process start, which shows up when a dynamic linker walks a long path. `ln -sr` does the resolution work once, at creation, and stores a short relative path. Prefer that to a deep absolute path that every later open must parse. There is no measured "ln is faster than cp" number in this lesson because the comparison is only interesting for large files on a filesystem that cannot reflink, and the copy lesson already showed this ext4 host cannot clone.

lessons.title: chmod, chown, and install
lessons.summary: chmod changes mode bits. chown changes ownership and fails here without privilege. install copies a binary into place and can skip the write when the bytes already match.
objectives: Set an octal mode and a symbolic mode with chmod
Copy a mode with chmod --reference
Explain a failed chown to root on this sandbox
Place a file with install -D and skip a rewrite with install -C
lessons.gnuVsBsd: Symbolic and octal chmod are POSIX. GNU `chmod --reference` and `chown --reference` are not BSD flags. GNU `install -D` creates leading directories and `-C` compares content before writing. BSD `install` uses a different set (`-S` for backups on some systems). `chown` to another user needs privilege on both. The failed chown below was captured as an unprivileged user. No BSD install was run.
lessons.markdown:
The mode is a set of bits stored on the inode: read, write, execute, for owner, group, and other, plus setuid, setgid, and sticky. `chmod 640 file` sets owner read-write, group read, other nothing. `chmod u=rw,go= file` is the same request in the symbolic grammar, which is what you want when you are editing rather than replacing the mode. `chmod --reference=other file` copies the mode. It does not copy the owner. The reference file is dereferenced if it is a symlink, so you copy the target's mode.

`chown user:group file` changes ownership. Only a privileged process can give a file to another user. In this sandbox `chown 0:0` fails with "Operation not permitted" and exits 1. That is the correct outcome, not a broken chown. `chgrp` can change the group to another group you belong to. `--from` on GNU chown avoids a race where you only want to change the owner if it is still the owner you think. `--reference` copies both user and group. None of these change the bytes.

`install` is `cp` plus the modes you want for a published binary, with a few extra contracts. `install -D -m 755 src dest/bin/tool` creates the parent directories of the destination and sets the mode. `install -C` compares the content and does not rewrite the destination if it already matches, which leaves the mtime alone. Build systems use that so a later step does not rebuild the world because a timestamp moved. `-s` strips symbols and needs a `strip` program; this lesson does not strip, because stripping is binutils, not coreutils, and it changes the bytes.

SELinux context is a third channel. `chcon` and `runcon` are coreutils, and they need a kernel with SELinux. `id -Z` on this host fails because the kernel is not SELinux-enabled. A mode of 644 is not a substitute for a context, and a context is not a substitute for a mode. On this machine you only have the mode.

Directories need the execute bit to be traversed. A directory mode of 600 lets the owner read the directory's names and not traverse it usefully in the way people expect from files. `chmod` on a tree with `-R` will happily clear execute on directories if you apply a file-shaped mode. Do not `chmod -R 644` a source tree.

## Worked examples

### Octal and symbolic

```example
{"id": "permissions-and-install-01", "title": "640 and u=rw,go= are the same end state", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > a\n/usr/bin/printf 'y\\n' > b\n/usr/bin/chmod 640 a\n/usr/bin/chmod u=rw,go= b\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%a %A %n' a b\n", "stdout": "640 -rw-r----- a\n600 -rw------- b\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/permissions-and-install-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Copy a mode

```example
{"id": "permissions-and-install-02", "title": "--reference copies mode only", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > src\n/usr/bin/printf 'y\\n' > dst\n/usr/bin/chmod 600 src\n/usr/bin/chmod --reference=src dst\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%a %n' dst\n", "stdout": "600 dst\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/permissions-and-install-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### chown to root fails closed

```example
{"id": "permissions-and-install-03", "title": "Unprivileged chown", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > mine\n/usr/bin/chown 0:0 mine\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "/usr/bin/chown: changing ownership of 'mine': Operation not permitted\n", "exitCode": 1, "download": "/downloads/examples/permissions-and-install-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### install -D and install -C

```example
{"id": "permissions-and-install-04", "title": "Place a tool and do not rewrite identical bytes", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '#!/bin/sh\\nprintf ok\\n' > tool\n/usr/bin/install -D -m 755 tool prefix/bin/tool\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%a %n' prefix/bin/tool\nbefore=$(/usr/bin/stat -c '%Y' prefix/bin/tool)\n/usr/bin/install -C -m 755 tool prefix/bin/tool\nafter=$(/usr/bin/stat -c '%Y' prefix/bin/tool)\n/usr/bin/printf 'mtime %s %s\\n' \"$before\" \"$after\"\n", "stdout": "755 prefix/bin/tool\nmtime 1794154153 1794154153\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/permissions-and-install-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

A Rust or C++ release script should `install -D -m 755` the binary into the prefix rather than `cp` plus a separate `chmod`. The mode is part of the publish. Use `install -C` when the same script may run twice and you do not want to bump mtimes that a package diff will treat as a change.

Do not chown build outputs to another user in CI. If the package format needs root ownership, that is a packaging step with privilege, outside this sandbox, and it should be explicit. A failed chown in the log is better than a script that ignores the status and ships a root-owned path it did not create.

## Tips and pitfalls

`chmod` follows symlinks to change the target's mode. `chmod -h` is not portable. GNU chmod's `--help` documents how symlinks are handled; do not assume a mode change on the link itself.

`install -d` creates directories. `install -D` on a file creates leading components of the file destination. Mixing them up produces a directory where you wanted a file, or the reverse.

The mtime comparison in the example prints two integers. If they match, `-C` did not rewrite the inode's mtime. If a filesystem's timestamp granularity ever made them match by accident, the content comparison is still what `-C` did; the printed integers are the observation on this run.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id": "permissions-and-install-ex01", "title": "Make a file owner-readable only", "prompt": "Create `secret` and set mode 600. Print the symbolic mode.", "hint": "`stat -c %A`.", "solution": "`-rw-------` is the symbolic form of 600.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'hide\\n' > secret\n/usr/bin/chmod 600 secret\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%A' secret\n", "stdout": "-rw-------\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/permissions-and-install-ex01.sh"}
```


```exercise

Do not hide the status.", "hint": "The sandbox user is not root.", "solution": "Operation not permitted, status 1. The file is still yours.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > mine\n/usr/bin/chown 0:0 mine\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "/usr/bin/chown: changing ownership of 'mine': Operation not permitted\n", "exitCode": 1, "download": "/downloads/solutions/permissions-and-install-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "permissions-and-install-ex03", "title": "Install into a prefix", "prompt": "Write a one-line file `tool` and `install -D -m 755` it to `opt/bin/tool`. Print the mode.", "hint": "`-D` creates `opt/bin`.", "solution": "The mode is 755 and the parent directories exist. That is the publish step a build should use.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'echo hi\\n' > tool\n/usr/bin/install -D -m 755 tool opt/bin/tool\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%a' opt/bin/tool\n", "stdout": "755\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/permissions-and-install-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

`chmod` and `chown` are metadata updates. They do not rewrite file contents. `install` without `-C` does rewrite the destination, which changes mtime and can cascade into rebuilds that dwarf the copy. `-C` exists so a repeated install of identical bytes stays cheap and quiet. The comparison itself reads both files, so `-C` is not free; it is cheaper than a false rebuild of a C++ target that depends on the installed header's timestamp. `install -s` runs `strip`, which is another process and another write. Do not strip in the hot loop of a debug build. None of these tools are the bottleneck of a link that reads gigabytes of objects. They are the bottleneck of a script that installs one file at a time in a shell loop over thousands of headers. Copy the tree with a tool that can do many files per process, or accept the process-startup cost knowingly.

lessons.title: dd, truncate, and sync
lessons.summary: dd copies blocks and can leave holes. truncate sets a size. sync asks the kernel to flush caches and does not prove the drive finished.
objectives: Copy a fixed number of blocks with dd and status=none
Create a sparse file with truncate and with dd conv=sparse
Read size and allocated blocks back with stat
Call sync -f on a file without claiming hardware durability
lessons.gnuVsBsd: GNU `dd` adds `status=progress` and `status=none`. BSD `dd` often reports progress on SIGINFO instead. `conv=sparse` is not identical across implementations. `truncate` is GNU and is missing from older macOS base systems. `sync -f` is GNU. This lesson only writes files inside the sandbox and never opens a disk device. No BSD dd was run.
lessons.markdown:
`dd` reads blocks and writes blocks. The historical interface is `if=`, `of=`, `bs=`, `count=`, and `conv=`. It is easy to destroy a device by pointing `of=` at the wrong node. Every example in this lesson uses a regular file in the scratch directory. There is no example with `/dev/sd` or `/dev/nvme`. If a real disk image job needs `dd`, the destination path should be a file you just created, and the script should print that path before it writes.

`status=none` keeps the statistics off stderr. `status=progress` prints them. GNU dd's `iflag=fullblock` accumulates a full input block when the reader returns short reads, which happens on pipes. Without it, `bs=1M count=1` on a pipe can stop after the first short read and produce a short file. Copying a regular file in this lesson does not hit that case. Know it before you `dd` from a pipe and think `count` means what it means for a disk.

`conv=sparse` tries to seek over NUL output blocks instead of writing them. A file of zeros produced that way has a large size and zero allocated blocks on a filesystem that supports holes. `truncate -s 1M file` creates the same shape without writing the zeros at all. `truncate -s 0 file` empties a file but leaves the directory entry, unlike `rm`. Shrinking discards the tail from the file's logical size. It does not shred it.

`sync` asks the kernel to write out cached data. With no arguments it applies broadly. `sync -f file` syncs the filesystem that contains `file`. `sync -d` limits itself to file data. None of these calls can promise that a drive's own cache has committed the bits to stable media. They are still the right call at the end of a snapshot script, followed by an honest sentence in the log: the kernel was asked to flush. Durability beyond that is a property of the hardware and the mount options, which this course does not tune and does not drop caches to measure.

`od` is how you look at a small `dd` result when you care about bytes. `stat -c '%s %b'` is how you look at sparseness. `du -b` versus `du -B1` is the same story from the disk-usage tools.

## Worked examples

### A counted copy

```example
{"id": "dd-truncate-sync-01", "title": "Four 1 KiB blocks from /dev/zero into a file", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/dd if=/dev/zero of=block.bin bs=1024 count=4 status=none\n/usr/bin/wc -c block.bin\n", "stdout": "4096 block.bin\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/dd-truncate-sync-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### conv=sparse on zeros

```example
{"id": "dd-truncate-sync-02", "title": "A hole instead of written zeros", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/dd if=/dev/zero of=sparse.bin bs=1024 count=8 conv=sparse status=none\n/usr/bin/stat -c 'size=%s blocks=%b block_unit=%B' sparse.bin\n", "stdout": "size=8192 blocks=0 block_unit=512\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/dd-truncate-sync-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### truncate extends without writing

```example
{"id": "dd-truncate-sync-03", "title": "truncate -s 1M", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/truncate -s 1M hole\n/usr/bin/stat -c 'size=%s blocks=%b' hole\n/usr/bin/du -B1 hole\n/usr/bin/du -b hole\n", "stdout": "size=1048576 blocks=0\n0\thole\n1048576\thole\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/dd-truncate-sync-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### sync the filesystem that holds the file

```example
{"id": "dd-truncate-sync-04", "title": "sync -f returns success and proves only the call", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'flushed-request\\n' > note\n/usr/bin/sync -f note\n/usr/bin/printf 'sync-ok\\n'\n", "stdout": "sync-ok\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/dd-truncate-sync-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Build a sparse disk image for a test with `truncate -s 64M image` only when 64 MiB is a size you are willing to create, and prefer a few megabytes in a sandbox. Fill a region later with `dd conv=notrunc` if you must write at an offset. `seek=` skips output. `skip=` skips input. Write both names down in the script so a reader does not swap them.

At the end of a backup that must survive power loss at the kernel level, `sync -f` the destination directory. Then say in the operator log that device firmware caches are outside that call.

## Tips and pitfalls

`/dev/zero` is not a coreutils invention. It is an infinite source of NUL bytes. `count=` is what makes `dd` stop. Forgetting `count` while reading `/dev/zero` fills the disk. The examples always pass `count`.

`status=progress` writes to stderr and will dirty a captured byte stream if you merge the descriptors. Keep it on stderr.

`truncate` on a missing file creates it. `truncate` on a symlink follows the symlink. Check `readlink` first if the name might not be a regular file.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id": "dd-truncate-sync-ex01", "title": "Write exactly 512 bytes", "prompt": "Use dd to put 512 zero bytes in `z` and print the size with wc -c.", "hint": "`bs=512 count=1 status=none`.", "solution": "The size is 512. status=none keeps the transfer stats off the output.", "script": "/usr/bin/dd if=/dev/zero of=z bs=512 count=1 status=none\n/usr/bin/wc -c z\n", "stdout": "512 z\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/dd-truncate-sync-ex01.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "dd-truncate-sync-ex02", "title": "Extend a file to 4096 without copying zeros by hand", "prompt": "Create `h` with truncate at 4096 bytes and print size and allocated blocks.", "hint": "`stat -c '%s %b'`.", "solution": "Size is 4096. Allocated blocks on this filesystem are 0 for a fresh hole.", "script": "/usr/bin/truncate -s 4096 h\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%s %b' h\n", "stdout": "4096 0\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/dd-truncate-sync-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "dd-truncate-sync-ex03", "title": "Ask for a flush", "prompt": "Write `n` and run `sync -f n`. Print `done` afterward.", "hint": "sync's success means the request was accepted.", "solution": "The kernel accepted the sync. That is the whole claim.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'n\\n' > n\n/usr/bin/sync -f n\n/usr/bin/printf 'done\\n'\n", "stdout": "done\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/dd-truncate-sync-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

`dd` with a tiny `bs` on a large file makes more syscalls than `bs` of 64 KiB or 1 MiB. The copy benchmark uses 64 KiB on an 8 MiB warm file and compares it with `cp`. Read the medians before you conclude anything. A larger block size can be slower if it causes a short-read bug on a pipe without `fullblock`, because you retry logic you did not write. Sparse conversion saves write I/O only when the output blocks are actually zero. A sparse `truncate` saves the writes entirely because nothing is copied. `sync` forces writeback, which makes a following read of "cold" data less cold and makes a benchmark that forgot about it lie. This course does not call `sync` inside the timing loops.

lessons.title: cat and tac
lessons.summary: cat streams bytes forward. tac reverses records. Neither one parses the file, and tac's separator stays glued to the record.
objectives: Show cat -A for tabs, line ends, and NULs
Squeeze blank lines with cat -s and number lines with cat -n
Reverse lines with tac
Explain tac -s using a hex dump of the separator
lessons.gnuVsBsd: BSD `cat -v -e -t` covers much of what GNU `cat -A` combines (`-A` is `-vET`). `tac` is GNU-only. The usual BSD substitute is `tail -r`, which is not the same program and was not run here. GNU cat is unaffected by stdbuf because it does not use FILE streams; that limit is in the stdbuf node and the buffering lesson.
lessons.markdown:
`cat` concatenates files to stdout. With no file, or with `-`, it reads stdin. It does not transform the bytes unless you ask. `-n` numbers lines. `-s` squeezes repeated blank lines into one. `-A` is the "show me the hidden bytes" mode: tabs as `^I`, ends of lines as `$`, and other nonprinting bytes in caret notation, including NUL as `^@`. The output of `-A` is not the original file. Do not checksum it and think you checksummed the input.

`tac` prints records in reverse. The default record is a line. It has to see the end of the input before it can print the last record first, so it is not a streaming tool in the way `cat` is. A multi-gigabyte file reversed with `tac` is a memory and temporary-space question. The manual does not give you a sort-style `-S` for it. If you need the last lines of a log, `tail` is the tool that seeks. `tac` is the tool that flips a small stream.

`-s` on `tac` sets the separator. The separator stays attached to the record. For the input `a,b,c` with separator `,`, the records are `a,`, `b,`, and `c`, and the reverse is `c` then `b,` then `a,`, which prints as `cb,a,` with no extra newline. That looks like corruption until you dump it. `od -An -tx1c` shows the commas are still there, attached to the following record in the reversed output. This is the behavior to teach, not a bug to "fix" by adding a newline and hoping.

A missing final newline is still data. `printf 'abc' | cat` writes three bytes and no newline. `wc -l` on that stream reports 0. `cat` did not eat a line. There was no newline to count. The wc lesson is the full version of that trap.

`cat` of a binary file to a terminal can scramble the terminal by writing control sequences. This course dumps binary with `od` or `cat -A` into a pipe, not onto a claimed tty. The capture environment's stdout is a pipe anyway.

## Worked examples

### Show the hidden bytes

```example
{"id": "cat-and-tac-01", "title": "cat -A", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\tb \\n' | /usr/bin/cat -A\n", "stdout": "a^Ib $\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cat-and-tac-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### NUL is ^@

```example
{"id": "cat-and-tac-02", "title": "cat -A on a NUL", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\0b\\n' | /usr/bin/cat -A\n", "stdout": "a^@b$\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cat-and-tac-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Squeeze blank lines

```example
{"id": "cat-and-tac-03", "title": "cat -s", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\n\\n\\nb\\n' | /usr/bin/cat -s\n", "stdout": "a\n\nb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cat-and-tac-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### tac and a separator that stays attached

```example
{"id": "cat-and-tac-04", "title": "Reverse comma-separated records", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a,b,c' | /usr/bin/tac -s,\n/usr/bin/printf '\\n---\\n'\n/usr/bin/printf 'a,b,c' | /usr/bin/tac -s, | /usr/bin/od -An -tx1c\n", "stdout": "cb,a,\n---\n  63  62  2c  61  2c\n   c   b   ,   a   ,\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cat-and-tac-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Number a snippet for a code review paste with `nl -ba` rather than `cat -n` when you also need the blank lines numbered in the style the nl lesson controls. `cat -n` is the quick version.

Reverse a short list of records you produced yourself, after you have decided the separator. Do not `tac` a log to "see the end". `tail` seeks. `tac` reads.

## Tips and pitfalls

`tac` on a file that does not end with the separator still prints the last partial record. The comma example has no trailing comma and no trailing newline. The dump is the authority.

`cat file1 file2 > file1` truncates `file1` before reading it. The shell opens the redirection first. Do not concatenate a file onto itself that way. Write to a new name and `mv` it on the same filesystem.

`stdbuf -oL cat` does not switch cat to line buffering. The buffering lesson says why. Repeating it here because people put stdbuf in front of cat in log pipelines and then argue about the flag.

## Exercises


## Performance

`cat` is a sequential read and write. For a warm cache and a destination that is another file, `cp` is the tool that can ask the filesystem for a reflink or a sparse layout. `cat` will read and write the bytes. Using `cat` in a pipeline (`cat file | tool`) adds a process and a pipe for no transformation. The tool can open the file. That extra process is small and measurable only when the work itself is small; the benchmark page does not pretend otherwise. `tac` is the one that becomes expensive for large inputs because reversal needs the records available from the end. `tail` is the constant-time-ish choice for "show me the end" on a regular file, subject to the kernel's ability to seek.

lessons.title: head and tail
lessons.summary: head prints a prefix, including GNU negative counts. tail prints a suffix or follows a file. Follow mode needs a bound.
objectives: Take the first lines or bytes, and all but the last lines, with GNU head
Start at line K with tail -n +K
Use NUL as a record separator with head -z
Bound tail -f with timeout so a capture cannot hang
lessons.gnuVsBsd: GNU `head -n -1` means "all but the last line". BSD head rejects a negative count. `tail -n +K` is the widely available "start at line K" form. GNU `tail -F` follows by name and retries when the file is replaced; BSD tails vary. `timeout` around `tail -f` is GNU coreutils. Negative head counts in this lesson are a GNU capture, not a portable script.
lessons.markdown:
`head` and `tail` cut a sequence of records. The default record is a line. `-n` selects lines and `-c` selects bytes. `head -n 2` keeps the first two lines. `head -n -1` keeps everything except the last line. That negative form is the GNU extension that deletes a trailer without a second pass you write yourself. `head -c -2` keeps all but the last two bytes. BSD head will not run these negative counts. If the script must be portable, do the trim another way and do not copy the GNU flag blindly.

`tail -n 1` is the last line. `tail -n +2` starts at line 2 and continues to the end, which is the usual "drop the header" operation. `tail -c 3` is the last three bytes. These are streaming from the point they start, except that finding the last N lines of a pipe requires buffering those lines because a pipe cannot be seeked. On a regular file, `tail` can seek near the end. That is why `tail` of a huge log is cheap and `tac` of the same log is not.

`-f` follows a file descriptor as it grows. `-F` follows by name: if the file is rotated and a new file appears under the same name, `-F` retries and switches. A capture that uses `-f` must stop. `timeout 1 tail -n +1 -f log` runs until the timer sends SIGTERM and then exits 124. The lines that were already in the file are printed first. Nothing in this course follows a log forever.

`-z` makes the record separator NUL. `head -z -n 1` keeps the first NUL-terminated record, including the NUL. That pairs with `sort -z` and `ls --zero` when names are the records. Mixing `-z` tools with newline tools splits the wrong places.

`head` closes the pipe early when it has enough input. The writer receives SIGPIPE. Under `pipefail`, a pipeline such as `yes | head` can exit 141. Without `pipefail`, you see head's status 0. The shell lesson introduced the rule. `yes` is where the 141 is captured on purpose.

## Worked examples

### All but the last line

```example
{"id": "head-and-tail-01", "title": "GNU head -n -1", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\n' | /usr/bin/head -n -1\n", "stdout": "a\nb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/head-and-tail-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Drop a header with tail

```example
{"id": "head-and-tail-02", "title": "tail -n +2", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'header\\na\\nb\\n' | /usr/bin/tail -n +2\n", "stdout": "a\nb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/head-and-tail-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### NUL records

```example
{"id": "head-and-tail-03", "title": "head -z keeps one record and its NUL", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\0b\\0' | /usr/bin/head -z -n 1 | /usr/bin/od -An -tx1\n", "stdout": " 61 00\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/head-and-tail-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Follow, but only for a second

```example
{"id": "head-and-tail-04", "title": "timeout bounds tail -f", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'boot\\n' > log\n/usr/bin/timeout 1 /usr/bin/tail -n +1 -f log\n", "stdout": "boot\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 124, "download": "/downloads/examples/head-and-tail-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Drop a CSV header with `tail -n +2` only when you have already accepted that the file is not quoted-CSV-safe. The cut lesson shows why a comma inside quotes breaks field tools. Dropping the first line is still valid for a log whose first line is a banner.

Watch a build log interactively with `tail -F` so a rotation does not freeze the view. In CI, copy the finished log. Do not leave `tail -f` as the last step of a job without `timeout`.

## Tips and pitfalls

`head -n -0` is not "give me nothing" in the way a casual reading suggests. Read the help text before you invent a negative zero. Prefer an explicit positive count when you can.

`tail -f` on a file that is not growing still holds the process. The timeout is not optional in a sandbox.

Combining `tail -f` and a pipe to `grep` (grep is not coreutils) reintroduces block buffering in grep. The lines exist and you do not see them. That is the buffering lesson, not a tail bug.

The newline after b remains.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\n' | /usr/bin/head -n 2\n", "stdout": "a\nb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/head-and-tail-ex01.sh"}


```exercise
{"id": "head-and-tail-ex02", "title": "Last three bytes", "prompt": "Print the last three bytes of `abcdef`.", "hint": "`tail -c 3`.", "solution": "The bytes are d, e, f. This is a byte count, not a character count.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abcdef' | /usr/bin/tail -c 3\n/usr/bin/printf '\\n'\n", "stdout": "def\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/head-and-tail-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "head-and-tail-ex03", "title": "Stop a follower", "prompt": "Write `hi` into `log` and run `timeout 1 tail -n 1 -f log`.", "hint": "The expected status is 124.", "solution": "You see `hi` and the status is timeout's 124, not tail's own success. The follower was stopped.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'hi\\n' > log\n/usr/bin/timeout 1 /usr/bin/tail -n 1 -f log\n", "stdout": "hi\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 124, "download": "/downloads/solutions/head-and-tail-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

`head` stops reading when it has enough. On a pipe, that saves the producer from generating the rest only if the producer honors SIGPIPE or a short write. A producer that ignores SIGPIPE and keeps computing wastes the work `head` tried to avoid. On a regular file, `tail -n 10` of a large log is a seek plus a small read. `cat | tail` throws the seek away and reads the whole file. Do not insert `cat`. Following a file is idle most of the time; the cost is the open file and the poll, which is fine for a person and wasteful as a permanent CI step. There is no timing number in this lesson because "how fast is head" on three lines is process startup, and the interesting case is the seek `tail` can do. Measure that on a file large enough to matter, on the filesystem you care about, with the benchmark method: repeated trials, warm or cold stated out loud.

lessons.title: Counting with wc
lessons.summary: wc counts newlines, words, characters, bytes, and the longest line. A missing final newline makes -l and your eyes disagree.
objectives: Separate wc -l, -w, -m, -c, and -L
Predict -l on a file that does not end in a newline
Count characters and bytes in a two-byte UTF-8 character
Pass names with --files0-from
lessons.gnuVsBsd: POSIX `wc` counts lines, words, and bytes. GNU adds `--files0-from`, `--total`, and a few output controls. `-m` is characters and depends on the locale. BSD wc exists and its extra flags differ. The missing-newline behavior of `-l` is POSIX: a line is a sequence ending in a newline. This capture is GNU wc 9.4 under en_US.UTF-8 unless a command overrides it.
lessons.markdown:
`wc` counts. It does not define a "line" as "what a text editor shows". `-l` counts newline bytes. A file that contains `hello` with no newline has a last line in an editor and a line count of 0 from `wc -l`. A file that contains `hello\n` has a line count of 1. This is the most common off-by-one in shell scripts that check "did the program print a line". Print the bytes with `od` when the count surprises you.

`-c` counts bytes. `-m` counts characters under the current locale. For the two bytes of UTF-8 `é` (U+00E9), `-m` reports 1 and `-c` reports 2 when the locale is UTF-8. The help text says the order of selected counts is newline, word, character, byte, maximum line length. So `wc -m -c` prints the character count and then the byte count. Under `LC_ALL=C`, the character classification collapses toward bytes and `-m` will not save you as a Unicode counter. Set the locale on purpose.

`-w` counts words: non-empty sequences of characters delimited by whitespace, with the locale deciding what is whitespace and what is printable. `-L` is the maximum display width of a line, not the byte length. A tab's display width is greater than one. Do not use `-L` as a buffer-size calculator.

With more than one file, `wc` prints a total unless you change `--total`. `--total=never` suppresses it. `--total=only` prints only the total. `--files0-from=F` reads NUL-separated names from F, or from stdin if F is `-`. That is how you count lines in files whose names contain spaces without the shell splitting them. Empty files contribute zeros and still appear as names.

`wc` reads the whole input. There is no "stop at the first match" flag. If you needed the first match, you wanted `grep` (not coreutils) or `head`.

## Worked examples

### The missing newline

```example
{"id": "counting-with-wc-01", "title": "wc -l counts newlines", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'hello' | /usr/bin/wc -l\n/usr/bin/printf 'hello\\n' | /usr/bin/wc -l\n", "stdout": "0\n1\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/counting-with-wc-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Bytes and characters

```example
{"id": "counting-with-wc-02", "title": "\u00e9 is one character and two bytes", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '\u00e9' | /usr/bin/wc -m -c\n", "stdout": "      1       2\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/counting-with-wc-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Words and the longest line

```example
{"id": "counting-with-wc-03", "title": "-w and -L", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a  b\\nc\\n' | /usr/bin/wc -w\n/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nabc\\n' | /usr/bin/wc -L\n", "stdout": "3\n3\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/counting-with-wc-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### NUL-separated names

```example
{"id": "counting-with-wc-04", "title": "--files0-from accepts a space in a name", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\n' > 'a b'\n/usr/bin/printf 'bb\\n' > c\n/usr/bin/printf 'a b\\0c\\0' | /usr/bin/wc -l --files0-from=-\n", "stdout": "1 a b\n1 c\n2 total\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/counting-with-wc-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Assert a generator produced a trailing newline by checking `wc -l` only after you have decided the format includes one. For "is the file empty", `test -s` is the predicate. `wc -c` is the measurement when you need the number.

Count lines in a selection of files with weird names by writing a NUL list. `ls --zero` is not a full recursive inventory. `find -print0` is the companion that walks. Either way, the consumer is `--files0-from=-`.

## Tips and pitfalls

`wc` with no flags prints lines, words, and bytes. Scripts that parse the default three columns break when someone adds `-l` and the columns shift. Pass the flag.

The total line says `total`. If you add `--total=only`, you lose the per-file lines. Pick the one the next parser expects.

`wc -l` on a directory fails. It is not `du`.


An empty file is not a missing file.", "script": ": > empty\n/usr/bin/wc -l -c empty\n", "stdout": "0 0 empty\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/counting-with-wc-ex02.sh"}

Use a redirect or a pipe so the filename does not appear... `wc -c` on stdin still may pad. Print the number in a stable way by taking the first field.", "hint": "`printf 'abc' | wc -c` prints a padded number and no name when reading stdin.", "solution": "The count is 3. There is no filename column when wc reads stdin.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abc' | /usr/bin/wc -c\n", "stdout": "3\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/counting-with-wc-ex03.sh"}


## Performance

`wc -c` can use the file size from metadata for a regular file in some cases, but you should not depend on a shortcut for a benchmark story. `wc -m` has to look at the encoding. `wc -l` has to look at every byte for newline. The wc benchmark runs `-c`, `-l`, and `-m` on a warm ASCII file of 200000 lines and reports whether the medians separate. On ASCII, `-m` and `-c` count the same quantity and `-m` may still do more work. If the run cannot separate them, that is the result. A file of multi-byte characters is a different experiment; do not reuse the ASCII medians for it.

lessons.title: split and csplit
lessons.summary: split cuts by size or into chunks. csplit cuts at a pattern. Round-robin mode distributes lines, so one line stays in one piece.
objectives: Split a file by line count with numeric suffixes
Distinguish split -n N from split -n r/N
Cut a file at a regex with csplit
Suppress empty pieces with csplit -z
lessons.gnuVsBsd: GNU `split` adds `-d`, `-a`, `--additional-suffix`, `--filter`, and `-n` with `l/` and `r/` forms. BSD split is a smaller tool. `csplit` is GNU and is not in the macOS base system. Chunk behavior below was captured with GNU split 9.4. Do not copy `-n r/3` into a script and assume byte-wise round robin.
lessons.markdown:
`split` writes pieces of a file. `-l 2` means two lines per piece. `-b` means bytes per piece. `-d` uses numeric suffixes instead of letters. `-a` sets the suffix width. The default prefix is `x`. Pieces land in the current directory unless you pass a prefix path. A script should `cd` to a scratch directory or pass an absolute prefix so it does not scatter `x00` files through a source tree.

`-n N` splits into N byte chunks as evenly as it can. `-n l/N` splits into N chunks without breaking lines. `-n r/N` round-robins lines across N files. The input `abcdef` with no newline is one line. `split -n 3` produces three pieces of two bytes. `split -n r/3` puts that single line into the first piece and leaves the other two empty, because there is only one record to hand out. People use `r/N` expecting byte striping and then checksum the empty files. The mode is about lines. Name the mode in a comment next to the command.

`--filter` runs a command for each piece, with `$FILE` set to the piece name. It is a way to compress pieces without a second pass you schedule yourself. The filter is a shell command. Quote it. This lesson does not need a filter to show the cuts; the sort lesson uses an external program for a different reason.

`csplit` cuts where a pattern matches. `csplit -f p - '/^FOOT/'` on a file that contains a header and a `FOOT` line writes the pieces and prints their byte counts to stdout. Those counts are the tool's report, not a `wc` you have to add. `-z` suppresses empty pieces, which matters when the pattern matches the start of the file or matches twice with nothing between. Patterns are basic regular expressions. They are not PCRE, and they are not a JSON splitter. A JSON line file splits cleanly with `split -l` only because each record is already one line. The moment a record contains a raw newline, line split is wrong.

## Worked examples

### Two lines per piece, numeric names

```example
{"id": "split-and-csplit-01", "title": "split -d -l 2", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\nd\\n' | /usr/bin/split -d -a 1 -l 2 - p-\n/usr/bin/ls -1\n/usr/bin/printf 'p-0:\\n'\n/usr/bin/cat p-0\n", "stdout": "p-0\np-1\np-0:\na\nb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/split-and-csplit-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Byte chunks versus line round-robin

```example
{"id": "split-and-csplit-02", "title": "-n 3 is not -n r/3", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abcdef' | /usr/bin/split -d -a 1 -n 3 - bytes-\n/usr/bin/printf 'abcdef' | /usr/bin/split -d -a 1 -n r/3 - lines-\n/usr/bin/wc -c bytes-* lines-*\n", "stdout": " 2 bytes-0\n 2 bytes-1\n 2 bytes-2\n 6 lines-0\n 0 lines-1\n 0 lines-2\n12 total\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/split-and-csplit-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### csplit on a marker

```example
{"id": "split-and-csplit-03", "title": "Cut before FOOT", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'HEAD\\n1\\n2\\nFOOT\\n' > doc\n/usr/bin/csplit -q -f part doc '/^FOOT/'\n/usr/bin/printf 'part00:\\n'\n/usr/bin/cat part00\n/usr/bin/printf 'part01:\\n'\n/usr/bin/cat part01\n", "stdout": "part00:\nHEAD\n1\n2\npart01:\nFOOT\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/split-and-csplit-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Drop empty pieces

```example
{"id": "split-and-csplit-04", "title": "csplit -z", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\n\\nb\\n' > blanks\n/usr/bin/csplit -z -q -f z blanks '/^$/' '{*}'\n/usr/bin/wc -c z*\n", "stdout": "2 z00\n3 z01\n5 total\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/split-and-csplit-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Shard a line-oriented log for parallel workers with `split -d -l 10000 -a 4 --additional-suffix=.log`. Workers must tolerate a boundary that is not a transaction boundary. If the transaction is multiple lines, `split` does not know. `csplit` can cut on a start marker you control.

`--filter='gzip > $FILE.gz'` compresses each piece. Test the filter on one small file before you point it at a disk you care about. A bad filter with `-` reading stdin can look like a hang.

## Tips and pitfalls

`split` of a file that is smaller than the chunk size still creates the pieces `-n` asked for, some of them empty in the round-robin case. Check sizes with `wc -c` before you launch a worker per file.

`csplit` without `-k` removes the output files if an error occurs mid-way. `-k` keeps them. The quiet flag `-q` suppresses the byte counts. Use it when the counts would pollute a log, and omit it when the counts are the verification.

Brace repetition `'{*}'` must be quoted so the shell does not expand it.

The other pieces are empty. That is line round-robin, not byte striping.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abcdef' | /usr/bin/split -d -a 1 -n r/3 - r\n/usr/bin/wc -c r*\n", "stdout": "6 r0\n0 r1\n0 r2\n6 total\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/split-and-csplit-ex02.sh"}

The second begins with END.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'one\\nEND\\n' > doc\n/usr/bin/csplit -q -f p doc '/^END/'\n/usr/bin/printf '0:\\n'\n/usr/bin/cat p00\n/usr/bin/printf '1:\\n'\n/usr/bin/cat p01\n", "stdout": "0:\none\n1:\nEND\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/split-and-csplit-ex03.sh"}

## Performance

`split` reads the input once and writes the pieces. The cost is the bytes, plus a directory update per piece. A million tiny pieces is a metadata storm, the same shape as the rm lesson's many unlinks. Choose a piece size that matches the consumer, not a piece size of one line for a multi-gigabyte log, unless you have a reason to pay for millions of inodes. `--filter` starts a process per piece. That startup dominates when the pieces are tiny and disappears when each piece is large. `csplit` scans for the pattern. It is not a search index. If you only need "bytes 0 to N", `dd` or `head -c` avoids the regex. There is no parallel flag on split in the sense of `--parallel` on sort. Parallelism comes from processing the pieces afterward, and only if the pieces are independent.

lessons.title: fmt, fold, expand, nl, and pr
lessons.summary: These tools reflow, wrap, expand tabs, number lines, and paginate. They are byte and column tools, and fold can split a UTF-8 character.
objectives: Reflow a paragraph with fmt and keep a prefix with -p
Show fold splitting the bytes of é
Expand and unexpand tabs at a chosen stop
Number every line with nl -ba and columnate with pr -t
lessons.gnuVsBsd: `fmt` and `fold` exist on BSD with different extra flags. GNU `fmt -p` is the prefix-preserving mode used below. `expand` and `unexpand` are POSIX-ish and the tabstop flags vary. `nl` and `pr` are in both worlds and their option letters are a portability hazard. `pr -t` to drop headers is what you want for a pipe; the default header includes a date and will not match across runs. Captured behavior is GNU 9.4.
lessons.markdown:
`fmt` joins and breaks lines so a paragraph fits a width. It is for prose. It will join short lines that look like one paragraph, which is the wrong thing to do to a table, a poem, or a source file. `-w` sets the width. `-p` keeps a leader such as `>` on mail quotes and reflows the text after it. The leader is not a comment syntax for every language. `fmt` does not know Markdown.

`fold` breaks lines that are already too long. `-w` is the width. `-s` prefers to break at spaces. `-b` counts bytes. On this UTF-8 locale, `fold -w 1` of the character `é` (bytes C3 A9) split the character across lines. The dump is in the example. Do not assume a "column" option keeps a multibyte character together. If you need a character-aware wrap, this is the wrong tool, and the observation belongs in the lesson so you do not discover it in a log file of names.

`expand` turns tabs into spaces. `-t 4` sets the stop. `-i` only converts leading tabs. `unexpand` does the reverse and will change a run of spaces into a tab only when it lands on a stop. Round-tripping is not identity unless the stops and the `-a` flag agree. A Makefile has meaningful tabs. Do not `expand` a Makefile and check it in.

`nl` numbers lines. The default body style skips blank lines. `-ba` is `-b a`, "number all lines", and it numbers the blanks too. `-w` sets the width of the number and `-s` the separator. It is a formatter for a listing you will read. It is not an index you should parse to edit the file.

`pr` paginates. The default page header includes the date and the filename, which makes output unstable. `-t` omits the header and trailer so the bytes can go to another filter. `-2` makes two columns. `-s,` sets the separator between columns. `pr` is not `paste` and not `join`. It fills columns down the page from one stream.

## Worked examples

### Reflow and a quoted prefix

```example
{"id": "wrap-and-number-01", "title": "fmt -w and fmt -p", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'one two three four\\n' | /usr/bin/fmt -w 10\n/usr/bin/printf '> a b c d e\\n' | /usr/bin/fmt -p '>' -w 8\n", "stdout": "one two\nthree\nfour\n> a b c\n> d e\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/wrap-and-number-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### fold splits é

```example
{"id": "wrap-and-number-02", "title": "fold -w 1 on U+00E9", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '\u00e9\u00e9\\n' | /usr/bin/fold -w 1 | /usr/bin/od -An -tx1\n", "stdout": " c3 0a a9 0a c3 0a a9 0a\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/wrap-and-number-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Tabs

```example
{"id": "wrap-and-number-03", "title": "expand and unexpand", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\tb\\n' | /usr/bin/expand -t 4 | /usr/bin/cat -A\n/usr/bin/printf 'a   b\\n' | /usr/bin/unexpand -t 4 | /usr/bin/cat -A\n", "stdout": "a   b$\na^Ib$\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/wrap-and-number-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Number every line and make two columns

```example
{"id": "wrap-and-number-04", "title": "nl -ba and pr -t", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\n\\nb\\n' | /usr/bin/nl -ba -w2 -s' '\n/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\nd\\n' | /usr/bin/pr -t -2 -s,\n", "stdout": " 1 a\n 2 \n 3 b\na,c\nb,d\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/wrap-and-number-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Prepare a commit message paragraph with `fmt -w 72` if your project asks for that width. Do not run it on the diff.

Show a tab that a test failed to preserve with `cat -A` after `expand`, so the failure is visible in a log that does not show a tab as whitespace.

Number a log excerpt you are pasting into a bug report with `nl -ba` so the other person can say "line 40".

## Tips and pitfalls

`pr` without `-t` puts the run date in the header. Two captures will differ. The example uses `-t`.

`fmt` treats a blank line as a paragraph break. A file of single-line records with no blanks may become one paragraph. Check.

`unexpand` can look like it did nothing when the spaces do not fill a tab stop. Dump with `cat -A` before you conclude the input had a tab.

The tab is gone.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '\\ta\\n' | /usr/bin/expand -t 4 | /usr/bin/cat -A\n", "stdout": "    a$\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/wrap-and-number-ex02.sh"}

The default nl style would have skipped the blank.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\n\\nb\\n' | /usr/bin/nl -ba\n", "stdout": "     1\ta\n     2\t\n     3\tb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/wrap-and-number-ex03.sh"}


## Performance

These tools are linear in the input and cheap next to a compiler. The performance issue is using them on data they will damage: `fmt` on a minified JSON line builds a "paragraph" and spends CPU to produce a file the parser rejects. `fold` on a multi-gigabyte minified line holds a long line. GNU tools do not impose a tiny line-length limit, so the memory cost is the line, not a fixed buffer you can ignore. `pr` with many columns buffers a page. For a huge file, cut the piece you need with `head` first. None of these is a parallel formatter. If you need a fast code formatter, it is not in coreutils.

lessons.title: cut, paste, and the CSV myth
lessons.summary: cut selects bytes, characters, or delimiter fields. It does not parse quotes. paste merges lines. Neither tool is a CSV library.
objectives: Select fields and a complement of fields with cut
Show a quoted comma breaking -d,
Compare cut -c and cut -b on a multibyte character
Merge files and join lines of one file with paste
lessons.gnuVsBsd: POSIX cut selects fields. GNU `--complement`, `--output-delimiter`, and `-z` are extensions. BSD cut will not accept the GNU long options. `paste -z` is GNU. The CSV failure is not GNU-specific: any delimiter cut that does not implement quotes will split `"a,b",c` the same way. This capture is GNU 9.4. A real CSV parser is not in coreutils.
lessons.markdown:
`cut -f2 -d,` prints the second comma-separated field. Fields are numbered from 1. `-d` is a single character. `--output-delimiter` changes what is printed between fields you kept, which is how you turn a comma file into a tab file without `tr` eating commas you meant to keep inside a field. `--complement` prints the fields you did not name. `-c` selects characters. `-b` selects bytes. On `é`, which is two bytes, `-c1` can yield the character and `-b1` yields the first byte, which is not a character. The od dump in the tr lesson is the same class of bug. Know which flag you passed.

The CSV myth is the sentence "I will just cut on commas". The input `"a,b",c` has a comma inside quotes. `cut -d, -f1` returns `"a` and `-f2` returns `b"`. The quotes are ordinary bytes. There is no escape syntax. A field that contains the delimiter cannot be represented in the format cut understands. If your Android manifest or your benchmark table is actually CSV with quotes, parse it in a language that has a CSV reader. If your file is a delimiter-separated file with a contract that the delimiter never appears inside a field, cut is appropriate and fast.

`paste` reads lines from each file and writes them side by side, separated by a tab by default. `-d,` uses a comma. `-s` serializes one file: it joins the lines of that file with the delimiter. `paste -s -d,` of three lines is one line. `paste` does not match keys. If the files are not in corresponding order, you silently zip the wrong rows. `join` is the tool that matches keys, and it requires sorted input. Use paste when the alignment is "line N with line N" and you created both files.

`-z` on cut and paste uses NUL as the line delimiter. That is the filename-safe mode. It does not make cut understand CSV quotes either.

## Worked examples

### Fields and the complement

```example
{"id": "cut-and-paste-01", "title": "Second field, and everything but the second", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a,b,c\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d, -f2\n/usr/bin/printf 'a,b,c\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d, -f2 --complement\n", "stdout": "b\na,c\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cut-and-paste-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Quotes do not protect a comma

```example
{"id": "cut-and-paste-02", "title": "cut is not a CSV parser", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '\"a,b\",c\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d, -f1\n/usr/bin/printf '\"a,b\",c\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d, -f2\n", "stdout": "\"a\nb\"\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cut-and-paste-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Character versus byte

```example
{"id": "cut-and-paste-03", "title": "cut -c and cut -b on \u00e9", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '\u00e9x' | /usr/bin/cut -c1 | /usr/bin/od -An -tx1\n/usr/bin/printf '\u00e9x' | /usr/bin/cut -b1 | /usr/bin/od -An -tx1\n", "stdout": " c3 0a\n c3 0a\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cut-and-paste-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### paste side by side and in series

```example
{"id": "cut-and-paste-04", "title": "paste columns and paste -s", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\n' > left\n/usr/bin/printf '1\\n2\\n' > right\n/usr/bin/paste left right\n/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\n' | /usr/bin/paste -s -d,\n", "stdout": "a\t1\nb\t2\na,b,c\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cut-and-paste-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Extract a column from a GNU `sha256sum` manifest with `cut -d' ' -f1` only after you know the format uses two spaces and the names do not contain newlines. The checksum lesson shows the actual line. For names with spaces, cut on the first field is the hash and the rest is not one simple field. Prefer `--zero` manifests when names are hostile.

Build a two-column report with `paste` from two lists you generated in the same order, for example a list of object files and a list of their sizes from a loop that printed one then the other. If the lists can diverge, stop and use `join`.

## Tips and pitfalls

`cut -f` without `-d` uses tab. A comma file stays one field. The output looks like cut "did nothing".

`-f1-3` is a range. `-f1,3` is a set. The comma in the flag is not the delimiter.

`paste` of files with different line counts pads the shorter side. You do not get an error. Count lines with `wc -l` if alignment matters. Remember the missing-newline trap when you count.

That is the demonstration to keep next to any script that claims to parse CSV with cut.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '\"a,b\",c\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d, -f1\n", "stdout": "\"a\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/cut-and-paste-ex02.sh"}



## Performance

`cut` and `paste` are single-pass and memory-light. They are faster than a spreadsheet and slower than a purpose-built parser only when the parser does more work, such as honoring quotes. Do not "speed up" CSV handling by switching to cut if the result is wrong. The cost of a wrong field is a bad Android versionName in a release note, not a saved millisecond. For a huge delimiter file that really is delimiter-safe, cut is appropriate and the bottleneck is reading the bytes, which a warm cache hides. The benchmark method on the benchmarks page is how you would time it. This lesson does not invent a cycles-per-byte figure.

lessons.title: join and comm
lessons.summary: join and comm require the same sort order. GNU checks by default. --nocheck-order will happily drop rows and exit 0.
objectives: Join two sorted files on a key
Read the partial output and non-zero status of an unsorted join
Show --nocheck-order returning 0 with a wrong answer
Read comm's three columns, including the tabs, with cat -A
lessons.gnuVsBsd: POSIX join and comm require sorted inputs. GNU join checks order unless you pass `--nocheck-order`, and it can still emit a partial line before exiting 1. BSD join often does not diagnose disorder and can mis-join quietly. `comm --check-order` is GNU. Column suppression `-1`, `-2`, `-3` is widely available. The unsorted captures below are GNU 9.4. They were not repeated on BSD.
lessons.markdown:
`join` merges lines that share a key. The default key is the first field, fields split on blanks. Both files must be sorted on the key with the same locale rules. `-t` sets a delimiter. `-1` and `-2` pick the key field on each side. `-a 1` keeps unpairable lines from file 1. `-e` fills a missing field. `-o` selects the output fields. This is a relational join only in the small sense of "sorted equijoin". It is not SQL.

GNU join checks that the input is sorted. On the unsorted file `b` then `a` joined to a sorted partner, this 9.4 build printed a joined line for `b`, wrote a diagnostic to stderr, and exited 1. You can see a plausible row and a failure in the same run. If a script discards stderr and does not check the status, it keeps the plausible row. `--nocheck-order` disables the check. The same unsorted input then exits 0 and still does not contain the row for `a`. That is a silent wrong answer. The flag is for the case where you have proved the order by some other means, not for making the error go away.

`comm` compares two sorted files line by line. Column 1 is lines only in file 1, column 2 is lines only in file 2, column 3 is lines in both. The columns are indented with tabs. A display that collapses tabs hides the structure. `cat -A` shows `^I`. `-1` suppresses column 1, so `comm -12` prints the intersection and `comm -13` prints lines only in file 2. GNU comm also checks order. An unsorted file produces a diagnostic and status 1, and it may already have printed something. Sort both files with the same `LC_ALL` before you comm them. `sort -u` if you need set semantics. comm does not unique the files for you; duplicate lines are part of the comparison.

Header lines break both tools. A header is an unsorted extra line at the top. Strip it with `tail -n +2` before sorting, or the check fails on line 1 for a boring reason.

## Worked examples

### A sorted join

```example
{"id": "join-and-comm-01", "title": "Both inputs sorted on field 1", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a 1\\nb 2\\n' > left\n/usr/bin/printf 'a x\\nb y\\n' > right\n/usr/bin/join left right\n", "stdout": "a 1 x\nb 2 y\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/join-and-comm-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### The check catches disorder and still prints

```example
{"id": "join-and-comm-02", "title": "Unsorted join", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'b 1\\na 2\\n' > messy\n/usr/bin/printf 'a x\\nb y\\n' > tidy\n/usr/bin/join messy tidy\n", "stdout": "b 1 y\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/join: messy:2: is not sorted: a 2\n/usr/bin/join: input is not in sorted order\n", "exitCode": 1, "download": "/downloads/examples/join-and-comm-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### nocheck-order is a wrong answer with status 0

```example
{"id": "join-and-comm-03", "title": "--nocheck-order hides the bug", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'b 1\\na 2\\n' > messy\n/usr/bin/printf 'a x\\nb y\\n' > tidy\n/usr/bin/join --nocheck-order messy tidy\n/usr/bin/printf 'status-was-zero\\n'\n", "stdout": "b 1 y\nstatus-was-zero\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/join-and-comm-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### comm columns

```example
{"id": "join-and-comm-04", "title": "Three columns, tabs made visible", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\n' > one\n/usr/bin/printf 'b\\nc\\nd\\n' > two\n/usr/bin/comm one two | /usr/bin/cat -A\n", "stdout": "a$\n^I^Ib$\n^I^Ic$\n^Id$\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/join-and-comm-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Compare two package lists: `sort -u` each, then `comm -13 old new` for additions and `comm -23 old new` for removals. Keep `LC_ALL=C` if the lists are byte identifiers such as package names that should not be collated as dictionary words. Document the locale next to the sort.

Join a two-column size table onto a two-column name table only after both are `sort -k1,1`. If the key is numeric and the other fields must keep their original order among ties, `sort -k1,1 -s`.

## Tips and pitfalls

A join key with extra spaces is a different key. `-t $'\t'` is the strict separator if the fields are tab-separated. The default blank splitting collapses runs of spaces and will glue a sentence into the wrong fields.

`comm` of files that are sorted in different locales fails the check or, if you disable it, lies. One `LC_ALL` for both sorts and the comm.

Do not pipe `comm` to `cut` on tabs without looking at `cat -A` first. The leading tabs are the column identity.

Both inputs must be sorted. These letters already are.", "solution": "`b` and `c`.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\n' > l\n/usr/bin/printf 'b\\nc\\nd\\n' > r\n/usr/bin/comm -12 l r\n", "stdout": "b\nc\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/join-and-comm-ex03.sh"}


## Performance

Both tools are linear after the sort. The sort is the expensive part and it is the part with `-S`, `-T`, and `--parallel`. A join that re-sorts on every run of a build is paying N log N to avoid storing the data in order. If the producer can emit sorted output, skip the sort. `--nocheck-order` is not a performance feature you turn on to save the check. The check is cheap next to a wrong release diff. Locale collation makes the sort slower and the join correct only if both sides match. The sort benchmark measures collation cost. Use it before you claim `LC_ALL=C` is required for speed; use `LC_ALL=C` anyway when the keys are bytes.
