lessons.title: test and expr
lessons.summary: test and [ are the same coreutils program. expr evaluates an expression and uses exit status as a boolean. The shell builtins shadow both.
objectives: Compare /usr/bin/test, the [ binary, and the bash builtin
Check a file exists and a string is non-empty
Use expr for a small arithmetic comparison and read its status
Keep test out of a hot loop
lessons.gnuVsBsd: POSIX specifies `test` and `[`. GNU `test` and `[` are the same program. Bash provides builtins of both, so a script that writes `test` may never exec coreutils. GNU `expr` has operators BSD also has, plus GNU-only extensions. `expr` matching uses basic regular expressions. Status conventions differ from C++: `expr` exits 1 when the result is 0 or null, and 2 on error. This lesson used `/usr/bin/test`, `/usr/bin/[`, and `/usr/bin/expr` so the binary is unambiguous.
lessons.markdown:
`/usr/bin/test` evaluates an expression and exits 0 for true, 1 for false, and 2 when the expression itself is an error. It prints nothing on success. `/usr/bin/[` is the same program with a required closing `]`. The reference page for `[` uses the slug `bracket` because a directory named `[` breaks the static export. The manual node is still "test invocation".

In bash, `test` and `[` are builtins. `type test` says so. `type /usr/bin/test` names the file. The builtins are faster and they are not the bytes this course is teaching. Write the path in examples. In a script that must behave when `/bin/sh` is not bash, POSIX `test` is the contract, and the coreutils binary is a fine implementation of it.

Useful predicates: `-e` exists, `-f` regular file, `-d` directory, `-s` non-empty file, `-z` empty string, `-n` non-empty string, `=` string equal, `-eq` integer equal. Quote the operands. `test -n $name` is a syntax error when `name` is empty because the operand disappears. `test -n "$name"` is false and well-formed.

`expr` prints a result and uses status as a second channel. `expr 1 + 2` prints `3` and exits 0. `expr 1 = 2` prints `0` and exits 1. `expr 1 = 1` prints `1` and exits 0. A pipeline that checks only the printed text will treat a false comparison as the string `0`, which is easy to misread as success. Check `$?`. Shell arithmetic `$((1+2))` does not fork. Prefer it when you are in bash and the lesson is not "what does coreutils expr do".

The manual lists `expr` among the utilities whose exit status is not the plain 0-or-1 rule, because 2 means an error. `test` is on that list too.

## Worked examples

### The binary and the builtin

```example
{"id": "test-and-expr-01", "title": "type test versus /usr/bin/test", "companion": "", "script": "type test\ntype /usr/bin/test\n/usr/bin/test -d /usr && /usr/bin/printf 'usr-is-dir\\n'\n", "stdout": "test is a shell builtin\n/usr/bin/test is /usr/bin/test\nusr-is-dir\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/test-and-expr-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A missing file

```example
{"id": "test-and-expr-02", "title": "test -e", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/test -e ./no-such-file\n/usr/bin/printf 'exists:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "exists:1\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/test-and-expr-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Bracket form

```example
{"id": "test-and-expr-03", "title": "[ is test", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/[ -n 'hello' ] && /usr/bin/printf 'nonempty\\n'\n", "stdout": "nonempty\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/test-and-expr-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### expr status

```example
{"id": "test-and-expr-04", "title": "expr equality", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/expr 1 = 1\n/usr/bin/printf 'eq:%s\\n' $?\n/usr/bin/expr 1 = 2\n/usr/bin/printf 'ne:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "1\neq:0\n0\nne:1\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/test-and-expr-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Guard a destructive command with `test` and an explicit path. `test -d "$build" && rm -rf -- "$build"` still requires `$build` to be a path you computed, not a path a user typed as `/`. The remove lesson's preserve-root default does not apply to `rm -rf -- "$build"` when the variable expands to something you did not intend. Test the prefix as well: a case statement that rejects empty, `/`, and paths without the expected parent.

Use `expr` when a strictly POSIX `sh` must do a match and you cannot assume bash `[[ ]]`. For everything else, the language you are already writing (C++, Rust) has the comparison.

## Tips and pitfalls

`[` without the space before `]` is a different command name. `/usr/bin/[` expects `]` as the last argument. Forgetting it is status 2.

`test` of too many arguments is an error, not a false result. Quote, and do not pass unquoted globs.

`expr` needs spaces around operators. `expr 1+2` is a string, not addition.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id": "test-and-expr-ex01", "title": "Confirm a directory", "prompt": "Use `/usr/bin/test -d /tmp` and print `yes` only if it is true.", "hint": "`&&` runs the next command when the status is 0.", "solution": "`yes` is printed. /tmp exists on this host.", "script": "/usr/bin/test -d /tmp && /usr/bin/printf 'yes\\n'\n", "stdout": "yes\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/test-and-expr-ex01.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "test-and-expr-ex02", "title": "Empty string is not -n", "prompt": "Show the status of `/usr/bin/test -n \"\"`.", "hint": "False is status 1. Use set +e so the script continues.", "solution": "Status 1. The quotes kept the empty operand.", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/test -n \"\"\n/usr/bin/printf 'status:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "status:1\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/test-and-expr-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "test-and-expr-ex03", "title": "Add with expr", "prompt": "Print `expr 20 + 22`.", "hint": "Spaces around `+`.", "solution": "`42`.", "script": "/usr/bin/expr 20 + 22\n", "stdout": "42\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/test-and-expr-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

Forking `/usr/bin/test` or `/usr/bin/expr` inside a per-file loop is the slow part. The predicate itself is a stat or a compare. The shell builtin `test` avoids the exec and is the right call when you are writing bash and you have already learned which binary you meant. A million stats is a million stats either way: the syscall remains. Batch the decision in one program when the loop is the product, not the lesson. `expr` on short strings is noise. `expr` with a pathological regular expression is a CPU sink. Do not pass untrusted patterns to it.

lessons.title: env, timeout, stdbuf, nice, nohup, nproc
lessons.summary: These six programs do not transform files. They change the environment, the clock, the stdio policy, the niceness, the hangup signal, or they report how many processors the scheduler will give you.
objectives: Run one command in another directory and with a variable removed
Bound a sleep with timeout and read statuses 124 and 143
Explain why stdbuf -iL is rejected and where libstdbuf.so comes in
Treat nproc as a hint for job count, not as a benchmark result
lessons.gnuVsBsd: `timeout`, `stdbuf`, `nproc`, and GNU `env -C` / `-S` are GNU extensions. macOS needs Homebrew `gtimeout` and has no `stdbuf`. `nice` and `nohup` exist in both userlands, but a negative niceness adjustment needs privilege on both, and the diagnostic text differs. This lesson captured GNU coreutils 9.4. The niceness warning and the 124/143 statuses are from this host, not from a BSD run.
lessons.markdown:
`env` is how you exec a program with a different environment without editing the parent shell. `-C` changes the working directory for that child only. `-u NAME` removes one variable. `-i` starts from an empty environment, which is the right way to prove a build does not depend on a stray `CFLAGS` from your prompt. You must then pass `PATH` if the child needs to find binaries. `-S` splits a single argument into a command, which is useful in a shebang line and easy to quote wrong in a lesson, so the examples use `-C`, `-u`, and `-i` instead.

`timeout` starts a command and sends it a signal when the duration elapses. The default signal is TERM. The default status, when timeout itself decides the command ran too long, is 124. `--preserve-status` makes timeout exit with the status the signal produced. On this host `timeout --preserve-status 1 sleep 3` exits 143, which is 128 plus SIGTERM (15). That distinction matters in a test harness: 124 means "the wrapper fired", and 143 means "the child died of TERM" if you asked to preserve status. A command that finishes in time returns its own status, and timeout stays out of the way.

`stdbuf` adjusts buffering for programs that use stdio. It does this by arranging `LD_PRELOAD` of `libstdbuf.so` from the coreutils libexec directory before the child starts. `-oL` requests line buffering on stdout, which is the setting you want when a progress line should appear before the pipe fills. `-iL` is rejected: the manual and the binary agree that line buffering stdin is meaningless, and the status is 125, one of the special statuses the exit-status node lists for `stdbuf`. `cat` and `dd` are called out in the manual because they do not use stdio for the data path, so stdbuf does not change their block size. `tee` resets buffering on its own. The buffering benchmark in this course measures a program that does use stdio, and it reports the numbers it measured. It does not claim a universal speedup.

`nice` adds to the niceness of a command. A positive adjustment makes the process more willing to yield. On this host `nice -n 5 true` exits 0. A negative adjustment asks to be less nice, which an ordinary user cannot do. `nice -n -1 true` prints "cannot set niceness: Permission denied" and still runs the command. The status is the command's status, so `true` yields 0 and `false` yields 1. The warning is not a failed command unless you treat stderr as fatal. Do not wrap `nice` around a benchmark and then claim the elapsed time changed because of the warning. This course does not rank nice levels.

`nohup` arranges for the child to ignore SIGHUP and, if stdout is a terminal, redirects it to `nohup.out`. When stdout is already redirected, `nohup` does not create that file. The example redirects to `redirected.out` and lists the directory so you can see the absence. `nohup` is not a service manager. A child that ignores hangup still dies when the machine reboots, and it still needs `timeout` if it can hang.

`nproc` prints how many processors are available to the current process, after considering affinity and cgroup limits the kernel reports. `--all` prints the installed count. `--ignore=N` subtracts N, which is the usual way to leave one processor for the desktop while a compile runs. On the capture host the three numbers were 4, 4, and 3 in the order `nproc`, `nproc --all`, `nproc --ignore=1`. Your laptop can differ. Use the value as a starting `-j` for a build. It is not a measurement of memory bandwidth, and a machine with 4 processors and 2 GiB of RAM will thrash if every job is a linking C++ binary. The performance lesson and the benchmark page are where resource tradeoffs are stated with inputs attached.

## Worked examples

### A different directory and a removed variable

```example
{"id": "process-wrappers-01", "title": "env -C, -u, and -i", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/env -C /tmp /usr/bin/pwd\nset +e\n/usr/bin/env -u HOME /usr/bin/printenv HOME\n/usr/bin/printf 'home_status:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n/usr/bin/env -i PATH=/usr/bin /usr/bin/printf 'clean\\n'\n", "stdout": "/tmp\nhome_status:1\nclean\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/process-wrappers-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### timeout statuses

```example
{"id": "process-wrappers-02", "title": "124 versus preserve-status", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/timeout 1 /usr/bin/sleep 3\n/usr/bin/printf 'default:%s\\n' $?\n/usr/bin/timeout --preserve-status 1 /usr/bin/sleep 3\n/usr/bin/printf 'preserved:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "default:124\npreserved:143\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/process-wrappers-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### nice without privilege

```example
{"id": "process-wrappers-03", "title": "Positive nice works, negative nice warns", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/nice -n 5 /usr/bin/true\n/usr/bin/printf 'raised:%s\\n' $?\nset +e\n/usr/bin/nice -n -1 /usr/bin/true\n/usr/bin/printf 'lower:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "raised:0\nlower:0\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/nice: cannot set niceness: Permission denied\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/process-wrappers-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### nohup does not invent nohup.out when stdout is redirected

```example
{"id": "process-wrappers-04", "title": "Redirected nohup", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/nohup /usr/bin/printf 'hi\\n' > redirected.out\n/usr/bin/ls -1\n/usr/bin/cat redirected.out\n", "stdout": "redirected.out\nhi\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/process-wrappers-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Processor count and the stdbuf library

```example
{"id": "process-wrappers-05", "title": "nproc and libstdbuf.so", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/nproc\n/usr/bin/nproc --all\n/usr/bin/nproc --ignore=1\n/usr/bin/ls -l /usr/libexec/coreutils/libstdbuf.so\n", "stdout": "4\n4\n3\n-rwxr-xr-x. 1 root root 14632 Aug 25 15:09 /usr/libexec/coreutils/libstdbuf.so\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/process-wrappers-05.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Wrap a flaky integration test with `timeout 30` and treat 124 as "the test hung", which is a failure, not a skip. Use `--preserve-status` only when you need to distinguish the signal the child actually died from.

Start a one-off data transform from a service directory with `env -C "$workdir" -u DISPLAY` so the child cannot see a variable it should not, and so relative paths resolve where you think they do. Clear the environment with `-i` in a packaging script, then add back the four variables you intend.

Pick a build job count with `nproc --ignore=1` on a workstation and plain `nproc` in CI where the cgroup is already the limit. Write it into a variable once. Do not call `nproc` inside the inner loop.

## Tips and pitfalls

`timeout` of a pipeline applies to the command you named, not to every stage, unless you pass a shell. `timeout 1 bash -c 'sleep 10 | sleep 10'` is the form that covers both. `timeout 1 sleep 10 | sleep 10` only bounds the first sleep.

`stdbuf` cannot line-buffer a program that writes with `write(2)` and never calls stdio. If the progress line still arrives late, the program is not a stdio program. Read the manual's list before you file a bug.

`nohup command &` in an interactive shell still leaves a job. Redirect stdin from `/dev/null` as well if the child might try to read a terminal that is going away.

`env -i` without `PATH` cannot find `printf` by name. The example passes `PATH=/usr/bin` and an absolute `printf` so either spelling works.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id": "process-wrappers-ex01", "title": "Change directory for one command", "prompt": "Print the working directory of `pwd` when `env -C /tmp` runs it.", "hint": "The parent shell's directory does not change.", "solution": "The printed path is `/tmp`.", "script": "/usr/bin/env -C /tmp /usr/bin/pwd\n", "stdout": "/tmp\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/process-wrappers-ex01.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "process-wrappers-ex02", "title": "Let timeout fire", "prompt": "Run `timeout 1 sleep 3` and allow the wrapper status.", "hint": "124 means the duration elapsed. It is not sleep's own status.", "solution": "Status 124. The command is stopped because of the wrapper.", "script": "/usr/bin/timeout 1 /usr/bin/sleep 3\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 124, "download": "/downloads/solutions/process-wrappers-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "process-wrappers-ex03", "title": "Reject line-buffered stdin", "prompt": "Run `stdbuf -iL true` and let it fail.", "hint": "Status 125 is the stdbuf usage error.", "solution": "stderr says line buffering stdin is meaningless.", "script": "/usr/bin/stdbuf -iL /usr/bin/true\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "/usr/bin/stdbuf: line buffering stdin is meaningless\nTry '/usr/bin/stdbuf --help' for more information.\n", "exitCode": 125, "download": "/downloads/solutions/process-wrappers-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

`env`, `nice`, and `nohup` add one process and almost no steady-state cost. They are not levers for a tight loop. `timeout` adds a process that sleeps until the deadline or until the child exits. The cost is the extra process and the signal, which is noise next to a compile and relevant next to a microbenchmark that times a millisecond command. Do not put `timeout` inside the timed section of a benchmark unless the deadline is the subject.

`stdbuf` changes when bytes cross into the pipe, which changes latency and can change how much CPU a downstream reader spends waking up. It does not change how many bytes a checksum must read. The buffering benchmark is the place that records a first-byte delay with a fixed program. Read that page before you generalize. A line-buffered producer can be slower in throughput because it writes more often. "Faster" depends on whether you are waiting for the first line or for the last byte.

`nproc` is a number of processors, not a number of jobs that will finish sooner. Past the point where jobs fit in cache and RAM, more jobs increase elapsed time. This course does not publish a universal `-j` winner. It tells you to start from `nproc`, watch RSS, and stop raising the count when the machine swaps.

lessons.title: tee, mktemp, pathchk, and mkfifo
lessons.summary: tee splits a stream without rereading it. mktemp makes an unguessable scratch name. pathchk rejects names that will not travel. mkfifo is a pipe with a filesystem entry.
objectives: Write one stream to two files with tee
Create a scratch file and a scratch directory with mktemp
Reject a newline in a portable name with pathchk -p
See timeout report 124 when cat waits on an empty fifo
lessons.gnuVsBsd: POSIX specifies `tee`, `mktemp`, `pathchk`, and `mkfifo`. GNU `mktemp` template rules match the usual `XXXXXX` spelling. BSD `mktemp` exists and the flag letters for dry-run and suffixes differ. GNU `pathchk -p` checks the POSIX portable character set and a 255-byte name limit. `tee -p` (operate on pipes, ignore write errors to a pipe) is a GNU behavior to read in `--help` before you rely on it. This lesson did not run BSD tee.
lessons.markdown:
`tee` reads stdin once and writes the same bytes to stdout and to every file you name. That is how you keep a log of a pipeline without running the producer twice. `printf 'ab\n' | tee a.txt b.txt` creates two files of three bytes and also writes those three bytes to stdout. `-a` appends. Without `-a`, tee truncates each file at the start, the same way a shell redirect does. The order of writes to the files and to stdout is not a transaction: a full disk on the second file can leave the first file complete and the pipeline failing. Check the status.

The manual notes that `tee` is one of the programs that resets its own buffering. Putting `stdbuf` in front of `tee` does not give you a free line-buffered split. If you need a line to appear in a log before a later stage finishes, look at the producer, not at a second stdbuf wrapped around tee.

`mktemp` creates a file or, with `-d`, a directory, using a template that ends in at least six `X` characters. It replaces the `X`s with random characters and creates the object with `O_EXCL`, so two racing scripts do not share the name. The course runner already gives every example a private directory. You still want `mktemp` inside a script that a person will run on their own machine, because `/tmp/out` is a shared name and a symlink attack. Print the name mktemp prints. Do not invent a parallel "random" name with `date` alone. The clock is a poor unique id when two jobs start in the same second.

`pathchk` answers a different question: would this name be legal and portable? `-p` checks the POSIX portable filename character set. A newline fails. `pathchk` does not create the file and does not look at whether you have permission. It is the check you run on a name you are about to embed in a release tarball, not a substitute for `mkdir`.

`mkfifo` creates a named pipe. Opening it for reading blocks until a writer opens it, and the reverse. `timeout 1 cat fifo` with no writer exits 124. That is the same timeout status as the process-wrapper lesson, applied to a pipe that nobody is writing. Named pipes are useful in a demo of "this command waits" and a poor place to store data. A fifo has a name and no contents you can `ls` the size of in a useful way. The size stays zero. The bytes exist only while a reader and a writer are both connected.

## Worked examples

### One stream, two files

```example
{"id": "tee-mktemp-pathchk-01", "title": "tee duplicates stdin", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'ab\\n' | /usr/bin/tee a.txt b.txt >/dev/null\n/usr/bin/wc -c a.txt b.txt\n", "stdout": "3 a.txt\n3 b.txt\n6 total\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/tee-mktemp-pathchk-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Append

```example
{"id": "tee-mktemp-pathchk-02", "title": "tee -a", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'one\\n' > log.txt\n/usr/bin/printf 'two\\n' | /usr/bin/tee -a log.txt >/dev/null\n/usr/bin/cat log.txt\n", "stdout": "one\ntwo\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/tee-mktemp-pathchk-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Scratch names

```example
{"id": "tee-mktemp-pathchk-03", "title": "mktemp file and directory", "companion": "", "script": "file=$(/usr/bin/mktemp ./item.XXXXXX)\ndir=$(/usr/bin/mktemp -d ./dir.XXXXXX)\n/usr/bin/printf 'z\\n' > \"$file\"\n/usr/bin/printf 'file=%s\\n' \"$(/usr/bin/basename \"$file\")\"\n/usr/bin/printf 'dir_is_dir:'\n/usr/bin/test -d \"$dir\" && /usr/bin/printf 'yes\\n'\n", "stdout": "file=item.kN5Ysn\ndir_is_dir:yes\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/tee-mktemp-pathchk-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Portable names and a fifo that nobody writes

```example
{"id": "tee-mktemp-pathchk-04", "title": "pathchk and a waiting fifo", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/pathchk -p 'ok_name'\nset +e\n/usr/bin/pathchk -p \"$(/usr/bin/printf 'bad\\nname')\"\n/usr/bin/printf 'path_status:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n/usr/bin/mkfifo fifo\nset +e\n/usr/bin/timeout 1 /usr/bin/cat fifo\n/usr/bin/printf 'fifo_status:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "path_status:1\nfifo_status:124\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/pathchk: non-portable character \u2018\\n\u2019 in file name 'bad'$'\\n''name'\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/tee-mktemp-pathchk-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Record a long build log and still watch it with `command 2>&1 | tee build.log`. The shell redirect applies to the whole pipeline's display. tee is what copies the bytes into the file. Add `-a` only when you mean to continue yesterday's log.

Create a work directory with `work=$(mktemp -d)` and remove it in an `EXIT` trap. Put intermediates there. A fixed path in `$HOME` collides with the previous run and survives a crash in a way that hides bugs.

Run `pathchk -p` on every filename a code generator emits before you write the file. A C++ header named with a space will build on your laptop and fail in a tool that splits on whitespace. Fail the generator.

## Tips and pitfalls

`mktemp` with a template that does not end in `XXXXXX` fails. Six `X` characters is the minimum. A template in a directory you cannot write also fails. The status is non-zero and no name is printed.

`tee` of a file you are also reading is a classic truncation bug. `tee file < file` empties the file. Write to a new name and `mv` it.

`pathchk` accepting a name does not mean the filesystem will accept it. A too-long UTF-8 name can pass a character-set check and still fail in `open`. `pathchk` without `-p` also checks length against the filesystem. Use both checks when the name is destined for this machine and for a tarball.

A fifo left in a directory looks like a file. `rm` removes the name. Do not `cp` a fifo and expect bytes. There are no stored bytes.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id": "tee-mktemp-pathchk-ex01", "title": "Duplicate a line", "prompt": "Write `hi` plus a newline through tee into `one.txt` and show the file.", "hint": "Redirect tee's stdout to /dev/null if you only want the file.", "solution": "`one.txt` contains `hi` and a newline. tee also wrote that to stdout if you did not redirect it.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'hi\\n' | /usr/bin/tee one.txt >/dev/null\n/usr/bin/cat one.txt\n", "stdout": "hi\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/tee-mktemp-pathchk-ex01.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "tee-mktemp-pathchk-ex02", "title": "Accept a portable name", "prompt": "Run `pathchk -p` on `ok_name` and print `ok` if it accepts the name.", "hint": "Status 0 means the check passed.", "solution": "`ok` is printed. The name uses letters and an underscore.", "script": "/usr/bin/pathchk -p 'ok_name' && /usr/bin/printf 'ok\\n'\n", "stdout": "ok\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/tee-mktemp-pathchk-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "tee-mktemp-pathchk-ex03", "title": "Make a scratch directory", "prompt": "Create a directory with `mktemp -d` using a template in the current directory, and write `note` into `note.txt` inside it.", "hint": "Capture the directory name. It is not a fixed string.", "solution": "The file exists under the generated directory. The directory name ends with the characters mktemp substituted.", "script": "dir=$(/usr/bin/mktemp -d ./work.XXXXXX)\n/usr/bin/printf 'note\\n' > \"$dir/note.txt\"\n/usr/bin/cat \"$dir/note.txt\"\n", "stdout": "note\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/tee-mktemp-pathchk-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

`tee` doubles the writes and does not double the reads. That is the point. A pipeline that runs the producer twice to "save a copy" pays the producer's CPU and the input reads twice. tee pays the output writes twice and the input once. On a large stream the extra write is the cost. If one destination is a slow disk and the other is a terminal, the slow destination back-pressures the whole pipeline, including the terminal. tee does not have a side buffer that hides that.

`mktemp` is one create. Calling it per line of a million-line file is the wrong shape. Create one directory and write the million files inside it with names you control, or, better, do not create a million files. `pathchk` is also a once-per-name check. Run it on the generator's pattern, not on every file of a tree you already wrote, unless you are auditing.

A fifo has no throughput advantage over an anonymous pipe. It exists so two unrelated processes can meet at a path. The timeout example spends about a second waiting, and that second is the deadline, not work. Do not benchmark `cat` on an idle fifo.

lessons.title: Identity, the host, and what is not a terminal
lessons.summary: id, whoami, uname, and hostid describe the account and the kernel. users, who, logname, and tty describe a login session this capture does not have. SELinux tools fail closed here.
objectives: Read the user and groups from id without confusing them with a login session
Print a kernel line with uname -srm and keep the nodename out of it
Interpret empty users output and a failing logname and tty
See id -Z and runcon fail because SELinux is not enabled
lessons.gnuVsBsd: POSIX specifies `id`, `uname`, `logname`, `tty`, and `who`. `whoami` is ubiquitous and not the same spelling everywhere in older systems. GNU `id -Z` and `runcon` / `chcon` are SELinux interfaces. BSD uses different mandatory-access tools and does not accept `-Z`. GNU `uname` field selectors match the letters this lesson uses. `stty` exists in both userlands. This course does not point `stty` at the session terminal, because it changes terminal modes. No BSD identity command was executed.
lessons.markdown:
`id` prints the user and group identifiers of the process. `id -un` prints the name only. `whoami` prints that same name. On this capture both print the sandbox account, which is the account the runner used, not a student name and not a machine name. `groups` lists the supplementary groups. Those groups are why a process can read plugdev or sudo-owned files. They are not a list of logged-in people.

`uname -srm` prints the kernel name, the release, and the machine. This host produced a line beginning `Linux` and ending `x86_64`. The lesson uses `-srm` on purpose. `-n` would print the nodename, and a nodename is often a hostname you did not mean to publish in a course page or a bug report. `arch` prints the machine hardware name and matches the trailing field of that `uname` line on this host. Neither command reads `/etc/hostname`. The `hostname` binary on Ubuntu is a different package, documented with the companions.

`users` and `who` read the login accounting files. In this capture there is no logged-in user in that table. `users` prints nothing and exits 0. `who` prints nothing and exits 0. An empty success is not "the command is broken". It is "the table is empty". `pinky` prints a header and no rows in the same situation. `logname` asks for the login name associated with the terminal and fails here with "no login name", status 1. `tty` prints "not a tty" and exits 1, because the runner's stdout is a pipe, not a terminal. The exit-status node lists `tty` as a command whose non-zero status is an answer. A script that does `set -e` and then calls `tty` will stop on a pipe, which is often what you want when you were about to launch an interactive pager.

`hostid` prints a 32-bit hex identifier. The captured value on this host is `007f0100`. Treat it as a host tag the binary printed, not as a credential and not as proof of a particular network address. Do not key a license check on it. It is stable enough to confuse you and weak enough to be the wrong authenticator.

`printenv` prints the environment. It is the inspection tool that matches `env`, which modifies the environment for a child. `printenv HOME` prints the sandbox home the runner set. `printenv` of an unset name exits 1. That status is one of the exceptions in the exit-status node.

SELinux is not enabled on this kernel. `id -Z` exits 1 and says `--context` works only on an SELinux-enabled kernel. `chcon` cannot apply a partial context to an unlabeled file. `runcon` exits 125 and says it may be used only on an SELinux kernel. The course records those failures so you do not copy a Fedora snippet onto this Ubuntu image and treat the failure as a mystery. `stty` is installed and is the tool that changes terminal settings. The examples do not run it against a terminal. `--help` is as far as this lesson goes, because a stray `stty` in a captured session can change echo and erase for the person watching.

## Worked examples

### Account and groups

```example
{"id": "identity-and-host-01", "title": "id, whoami, and groups", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/id -un\n/usr/bin/whoami\n/usr/bin/groups\n", "stdout": "ubuntu\nubuntu\nubuntu adm dialout cdrom floppy sudo audio dip video plugdev\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/identity-and-host-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Kernel line without the nodename

```example

```


## Recipes

Put `uname -srm` and `id -un` in a bug report, plus the coreutils version from the orientation lesson. Leave the nodename out unless the bug is about the name. Add `tty` status when the bug is "it behaves differently in CI", because CI is usually not a terminal and your laptop is.

Before a script calls `logname` or opens `/dev/tty`, check `tty` and branch. A pipeline that assumes a terminal will fail in the course runner, in cron, and in a GitHub Actions job for the same reason.

Do not gate a feature on `id -Z` succeeding. Test for SELinux explicitly and skip the context commands when the kernel says they do not apply. The statuses above are the skip signal on this image.

## Tips and pitfalls

`whoami` and `logname` answer different questions. `whoami` is the effective user of the process. `logname` is the user who logged in on the terminal. They diverge under `su` and they diverge here because there is no terminal login at all.

`users` exiting 0 with an empty line is success. A monitor that alerts on empty stdout will false-alarm. Alert on status, or on a parsed count you printed yourself.

`pinky` is a friendlier `who`. It still reads the same kind of accounting data. An empty body under a header is the same fact as `who` printing zero lines.

`stty -a` on a real terminal dumps settings and is harmless. `stty raw` or `stty -echo` is not harmless. This course does not run those. If you experiment, run them in a terminal you can close, and remember `reset` from ncurses is the usual recovery. `reset` is not coreutils.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id": "identity-and-host-ex01", "title": "Print the user name", "prompt": "Print `id -un` and `whoami` on separate lines.", "hint": "Both read the process owner.", "solution": "The two lines match. On this runner they are the sandbox account.", "script": "/usr/bin/id -un\n/usr/bin/whoami\n", "stdout": "ubuntu\nubuntu\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/identity-and-host-ex01.sh"}

There is no `-n`.", "solution": "Three fields. The machine field matches `arch` on this host.", "script": "/usr/bin/uname -srm\n", "stdout": "Linux 6.12.113+ x86_64\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/identity-and-host-ex02.sh"}
```

That is expected here.", "script": "/usr/bin/tty\n", "stdout": "not a tty\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 1, "download": "/downloads/solutions/identity-and-host-ex03.sh"}


## Performance

These commands are lookups. `id` and `uname` are single syscalls plus formatting. `who` and `users` read a small accounting file. None of them belong in a per-file loop. Call them once, store the string, and reuse it in a banner. `hostid` is also a single call and still the wrong thing to hash on every request of a service.

`tty` is cheap and worth calling once at startup of an interactive tool. Calling it per line to decide whether to colorize is unnecessary once you know the answer does not change mid-process, unless you reopened stdout. The performance question for identity commands is not their CPU cost. It is the cost of logging too much: a nodename and a hostid in every line of a high-volume log is bytes you pay to store and a privacy problem, not a speedup.

lessons.title: Mechanisms that decide speed
lessons.summary: Locale collation, stdio buffering, external sort, sparse files, and reflink decide cost. This lesson shows the mechanisms with captured behavior and points at the benchmark page for numbers.
objectives: Contrast LC_ALL=C byte order with a locale sort of the same four lines
Read wc -l as a newline count, including a file that has none
Show a sparse file's apparent size against its allocated size
Watch cp --reflink=always fail on this filesystem and --reflink=auto fall back
lessons.gnuVsBsd: `LC_ALL=C` selects the POSIX collation on both GNU and BSD, but the name of the UTF-8 locale and the default sort differ. GNU `cp --reflink` is a GNU and Linux feature. BSD `cp` on macOS uses `clonefile` under different flags, and a failure mode from ext4 does not transfer. GNU `wc` and BSD `wc` both count newlines for `-l`, which is the fact this lesson uses. No timing number in this lesson was copied from a BSD machine, and none was invented. Measured trials live on the benchmark page.
lessons.markdown:
Speed in coreutils is a property of a bottleneck, not a property of a flag you can memorize as "the fast one". The same `sort` is cheap on a thousand integers and expensive when it spills. The same `cp` is a metadata operation when the filesystem can share extents, and a full read-write when it cannot. The same `wc -l` is a streaming scan that never builds a line list. This lesson fixes the mechanisms. The benchmark page is where a fixed input, a seed, five trials, and a median are recorded, with the version, the filesystem, and the warm-cache limit written next to the numbers. If a gap there is smaller than the spread of the trials, the page says not to rank the variants. This lesson does not add a second, quieter ranking.

Collation is the first mechanism people trip over. `LC_ALL=C` compares bytes. `en_US.UTF-8` groups case and applies the locale's weights, so the same four letters come out in a different order. The work is not "more flags". The work is a heavier comparison function, called once per pair the algorithm needs, and it cannot be skipped by `-S` or `--parallel`. Those flags change memory and thread count for the external merge. They do not switch the comparator. `sort -S` sets the main buffer. The manual's unit rules are picky: a bare number is 1024-byte units, `K` is 1024, `M` is 1048576, `%` is a percent of memory. The buffer can still grow to hold a long line. `-T` chooses the spill directory and overrides `TMPDIR`. `--parallel` defaults to the available processors and is capped at 8, and the manual warns that the merge wants memory that grows with the thread count. `--compress-program` must compress stdin to stdout and decompress with `-d`. All of that is in the sort lesson with a captured spill log. The benchmark page repeats the comparison on a fixed input and reports medians. A single interactive run is not that page.

Buffering is the second mechanism. A program that uses stdio and writes to a pipe uses a large block buffer by default. The reader sees nothing until the block fills or the writer exits. `stdbuf -oL` requests a line buffer by preloading `libstdbuf.so`. It does not apply to `cat` and `dd`, which do not use stdio for their data, and `tee` resets its own buffering. The latency you care about in a progress pipe is time-to-first-byte. The throughput you care about in a checksum is bytes per second of the hash, and line buffering can make that worse by issuing more writes. The buffering benchmark records a first-byte delay. Read it as a delay, not as a claim that line buffering is faster.

`wc` is the model of a streaming tool. `wc -l` counts newline bytes. `printf 'abc' | wc -l` is 0. `wc -c` on the same bytes is 3. `wc -m` counts characters and has to decode UTF-8, so it is the slower mode when the locale is multibyte and the file is large. The benchmark page runs `-c`, `-l`, and `-m` on one generated ASCII file so the difference is the scan, not a different input. Do not quote those medians as the cost of Unicode. The input is ASCII on purpose.

Filesystem shape is the fourth mechanism. `truncate -s 1M` creates a hole. `stat` shows a large size and zero allocated blocks on this filesystem. `du -b` reports the apparent size. `du -B1` reports the allocation, which is 0 for that fresh hole. A backup tool that reads the apparent size copies a megabyte of zeros. A tool that copies extents can keep the hole. `cp --reflink=always` on this ext4 asks for a clone and fails with "Operation not supported". `--reflink=auto` falls back to a copy and exits 0. The benchmark page compares a plain copy with `dd` on an 8 MiB file and says the filesystem up front. It does not claim reflink won, because reflink did not work here.

Caches sit under all of this. The course creates inputs and rereads them. The page cache holds the data. Nobody ran `drop_caches`, and an ordinary user cannot. A second trial is warmer than a first trial on a quiet machine and still not a cold-disk number. RSS is Linux `ru_maxrss` in kibibytes, taken from a short Python helper that waits for the child, so the elapsed time includes the helper. Compare variants that share the helper. Do not publish the absolute seconds as the cost of `sort` alone.

NUL-terminated names, `sort -z`, and `find -print0` (find is findutils) avoid a class of correctness bugs that become performance bugs when a script splits names on newlines and then reruns. They are not faster. They are the version that processes the names you actually have.

## Worked examples

### The same four lines, two collations

```example
{"id": "performance-mechanisms-01", "title": "C byte order and locale order", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'b\\nA\\na\\nB\\n' | LC_ALL=C /usr/bin/sort\n/usr/bin/printf '---\\n'\n/usr/bin/printf 'b\\nA\\na\\nB\\n' | LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 /usr/bin/sort\n", "stdout": "A\nB\na\nb\n---\na\nA\nb\nB\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/performance-mechanisms-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### wc counts newlines

```example
{"id": "performance-mechanisms-02", "title": "No newline means zero lines", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abc' | /usr/bin/wc -l\n/usr/bin/printf 'abc' | /usr/bin/wc -c\n", "stdout": "0\n3\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/performance-mechanisms-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A hole is not a megabyte of allocation

```example
{"id": "performance-mechanisms-03", "title": "truncate, stat, and du", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/truncate -s 1M hole\n/usr/bin/stat -c 'size=%s blocks=%b' hole\n/usr/bin/du -b hole\n/usr/bin/du -B1 hole\n", "stdout": "size=1048576 blocks=0\n1048576\thole\n0\thole\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/performance-mechanisms-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Reflink is a request, not a promise

```example
{"id": "performance-mechanisms-04", "title": "cp --reflink=always and --reflink=auto", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'data\\n' > src\nset +e\n/usr/bin/cp --reflink=always src dst\n/usr/bin/printf 'always:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n/usr/bin/cp --reflink=auto src dst2\n/usr/bin/wc -c dst2\n", "stdout": "always:1\n5 dst2\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/cp: failed to clone 'dst' from 'src': Operation not supported\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/performance-mechanisms-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

When a sort in a script starts hitting the disk, look at `-S` and `-T` and the comparator before you look at `--parallel`. A locale comparator on short keys is a different bottleneck from a merge that spilled to a small `/tmp`. The sort lesson's compress-program example shows the spill as a count of compressor invocations, not as a made-up duration.

When a copy of a build tree is slow, check whether the files are many and small. The cost is metadata. Reflink would not have removed the per-file syscall even on a filesystem that supports it. `du -d 1` tells you which directory dominates. `df` tells you whether the filesystem has room. They answer different questions, and the du lesson keeps them apart.

When a pipeline "hangs" and the CPU is idle, suspect a block buffer. Reproduce with a slow producer and `stdbuf -oL` on the stage that uses stdio. If nothing changes, the stage is not an stdio program.

## Tips and pitfalls

A flag that helps a spill hurts a sort that already fit in RAM, because compression and threads have overhead. The benchmark page is allowed to show a tie. A tie is a result.

`LC_ALL=C` changes more than sort. It changes `ls` order, character classes, and the decimal point. Set it for the one command that needs byte order, not for an entire build, unless you mean it.

Apparent size and allocated size are both "the size". Say which one you measured. A chart that mixes `du -b` and `du -B1` without labels is how a sparse image looks like it doubled.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id": "performance-mechanisms-ex01", "title": "Sort four letters in the C locale", "prompt": "Sort `b`, `A`, `a`, `B` with `LC_ALL=C`.", "hint": "Byte order puts uppercase before lowercase.", "solution": "`A`, `B`, `a`, `b` on four lines.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'b\\nA\\na\\nB\\n' | LC_ALL=C /usr/bin/sort\n", "stdout": "A\nB\na\nb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/performance-mechanisms-ex01.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "performance-mechanisms-ex02", "title": "Count lines of a string with no newline", "prompt": "Pipe `printf 'abc'` through `wc -l` and `wc -c`.", "hint": "`-l` counts newline bytes.", "solution": "The line count is 0. The byte count is 3.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abc' | /usr/bin/wc -l\n/usr/bin/printf 'abc' | /usr/bin/wc -c\n", "stdout": "0\n3\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/performance-mechanisms-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "performance-mechanisms-ex03", "title": "Ask for a clone and record the fallback", "prompt": "Copy `src` with `--reflink=auto` after writing `data` and a newline. Print the byte count of the destination.", "hint": "`auto` may copy. `always` is allowed to fail on this filesystem.", "solution": "The destination is 5 bytes. The status of `--reflink=auto` is 0 here even though a forced clone is not supported.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'data\\n' > src\n/usr/bin/cp --reflink=auto src dst\n/usr/bin/wc -c dst\n", "stdout": "5 dst\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/performance-mechanisms-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

There is no closing trick that makes every coreutils command faster. The levers that exist are real and local. Use a byte-order locale when the comparator is the cost and the order is allowed to be byte order. Give `sort` a buffer and a spill disk when the input does not fit, and do not assume more threads help once the cap and the memory formula are against you. Stream with `wc`, `cut`, and `tr` instead of loading the file. Copy extents only when the filesystem says yes, and time the fallback you will actually run. Keep names NUL-terminated so you do not redo the job after a split. Measure with the benchmark scripts, five trials, a median, and the disclosure block. A number without that block is a story. This course refuses the story.

lessons.title: Pipelines that fail closed
lessons.summary: Spaces, newlines, empty variables, and SIGPIPE are how a short script deletes the wrong tree or reports success after a writer died. The fixes are quoting, explicit targets, and pipefail.
objectives: Create and name a file that contains a space without letting the shell split it
Show a newline inside a name with ls --quoting-style=shell-escape
Delete a relative build directory you just created, and refuse an empty target
Read status 141 from yes | head when pipefail is on
lessons.gnuVsBsd: POSIX quoting rules are shared. GNU `ls --quoting-style=shell-escape` is the GNU spelling. BSD `ls` uses different flags to reveal a newline in a name. GNU `rm --preserve-root` is the default, and `--no-preserve-root` exists. This lesson never runs `rm` against `/`. `set -o pipefail` is a bash/ksh feature, not a coreutils flag, and it is how the SIGPIPE from `yes` becomes visible. Status 141 is 128+SIGPIPE on Linux. A macOS shell reports the signal with its own spelling. No destructive BSD command was run.
lessons.markdown:
A pipeline is safe when every name is one word, every deletion has a target you computed, and a dead writer is allowed to fail the script. Coreutils will do exactly what the shell asks after the shell has already split the words. Most "rm disasters" are word-splitting and empty variables, not a bug in `rm`.

Quoting comes first. `printf 'hello world\n' > "my file"` creates one file. The same redirect without quotes creates `my` and then tries to write `world` as a command, or worse, passes two operands to a later `rm`. The quoting lesson covers globs. This lesson is the part where you apply it to destruction. Double quotes allow expansions and prevent splitting. Single quotes prevent expansions. A name you got from a variable is always quoted: `"$path"`.

Newlines in names are legal on Linux. `ls` with the default quoting can hide them or render them as a question mark depending on version and options. `--quoting-style=shell-escape` prints a form you can tell is one name. `ls --zero` emits NUL separators so a reader does not have to parse the escape. `find -print0` and `xargs -0` are the findutils pair, not coreutils, and they are the right producer when the walk is recursive. Coreutils tools that support `-z` (`sort -z`, `uniq -z`, `comm` has related options you should read in `--help` before you assume them) keep the NUL boundary. The filename lesson is the longer treatment. The rule to remember here is: if you pipe `ls` to anything, you have already given up, unless you used `--zero` and a reader that understands it.

Deletion comes second. `rm -rf -- "$dir"` is safe only when `$dir` is the directory you created. The double dash stops a name that begins with `-` from becoming a flag. `--preserve-root` is the default, which blocks `rm -rf /` specifically. It does not block `rm -rf /tmp` or `rm -rf "$dir"` when `dir` is empty. An empty expansion of an unquoted variable vanishes. An empty expansion of a quoted variable is an empty argument, and `rm` will complain. Test the string before you call `rm`. Refuse empty. Refuse `/`. Prefer to `cd` into a parent you created and delete a relative name. The example creates `build/obj`, removes `build`, and checks that the name is gone. It does not touch the real root.

`rm -I` asks once when you pass more than three files, and with an empty stdin it removes nothing and exits 0. That status is easy to misread as "I deleted them". The remove lesson captures it. If you need a prompt, also check that the files are gone. Do not use `-I` as your only safety check.

SIGPIPE is the third failure. `yes | head -n 2` prints two lines and then `yes` is killed because `head` closed the pipe. With `set -o pipefail` the pipeline status is 141. Without it, the status is `head`'s status, which is 0, and a script reports success for a writer that died. The printf lesson shows the same pipeline. Turn pipefail on in any script whose middle stage is not allowed to fail quietly. `set -e` does not by itself give you pipefail.

A final habit: run the script once in a scratch directory. The course runner does that for every example. Your laptop should do it too, with `mktemp -d`, before you point a command at a source tree.

## Worked examples

### A space is part of the name

```example
{"id": "safe-pipelines-01", "title": "Quoted filename", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'hello world\\n' > \"my file\"\n/usr/bin/ls --quoting-style=shell-escape\n/usr/bin/wc -c \"my file\"\n", "stdout": "'my file'\n12 my file\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/safe-pipelines-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A newline inside a name

```example
{"id": "safe-pipelines-02", "title": "shell-escape quoting", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir nest\n/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > \"$(/usr/bin/printf 'nest/a\\nb')\"\n/usr/bin/ls --quoting-style=shell-escape nest\n", "stdout": "'a'$'\\n''b'\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/safe-pipelines-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Delete a tree you just made

```example
{"id": "safe-pipelines-03", "title": "Relative rm of a scratch build", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir -p build/obj\n/usr/bin/printf 'o\\n' > build/obj/a.o\n/usr/bin/rm -rf -- build\n/usr/bin/test ! -e build && /usr/bin/printf 'gone\\n'\n", "stdout": "gone\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/safe-pipelines-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### pipefail sees SIGPIPE

```example
{"id": "safe-pipelines-04", "title": "yes and head", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\nbash -c 'set -o pipefail; yes | /usr/bin/head -n 2'\n/usr/bin/printf 'pipefail:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "y\ny\npipefail:141\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/safe-pipelines-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

Generate a path, then guard it.

```bash
dir=${1:-}
if test -z "$dir" || test "$dir" = / || test "$dir" = .; then
  printf 'refuse %s\n' "$dir" >&2
  exit 1
fi
```

That fragment is the shape. The exercise runs the empty case and prints `refuse` without calling `rm`. Add the `rm` only after the guard, and only on a relative directory you created in the same script.

Log a pipeline with `tee` and keep pipefail so a failing producer is not hidden by tee's success. `set -o pipefail` applies to the shell running the pipeline. A shell that execs another shell needs the option in the inner shell, which is why the example uses `bash -c`.

Walk names with `find -print0` when you must recurse. The companion lesson shows the command. Do not convert the NUL stream back to lines with `tr '\0' '\n'` and then split again. You have reintroduced the bug.

## Tips and pitfalls

`rm -rf -- "$dir/"` with a trailing slash still deletes the directory's contents when the variable is set. The slash is not a safety feature. The guard is the safety feature.

`ls` output is not a file list API. `--quoting-style=shell-escape` is for human eyes and for reproducing a name in a shell snippet. `--zero` is for programs. Mixing them up produces a list that still contains escapes a later tool will treat as literal characters.

`yes` exists to feed a prompt. Bound it. An unbounded `yes` into a command that never closes stdin fills a disk. `head` or `timeout` is the bound. The status under pipefail will be non-zero. Decide whether that non-zero is acceptable and handle it, rather than turning pipefail off for the whole script.

GNU `rm` refuses to operate on `.` and `..` as the final path component in the cases the manual describes. Do not rely on that as permission to build paths by string concatenation without checking the parent.

## Exercises

The file is one name.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'hello world\\n' > \"my file\"\n/usr/bin/wc -c \"my file\"\n", "stdout": "12 my file\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/safe-pipelines-ex01.sh"}


```exercise
{"id": "safe-pipelines-ex02", "title": "Refuse an empty target", "prompt": "Set `target` to empty and print `refuse` when it is empty or `/`. Do not call rm.", "hint": "`test -z` and `test \"$target\" = /`.", "solution": "The script prints `refuse` and never deletes anything.", "script": "target=\"\"\nif test -z \"$target\" || test \"$target\" = /; then\n  /usr/bin/printf 'refuse\\n'\nelse\n  /usr/bin/printf 'would-delete\\n'\nfi\n", "stdout": "refuse\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/safe-pipelines-ex02.sh"}
```

```exercise
{"id": "safe-pipelines-ex03", "title": "Remove a relative directory", "prompt": "Create `scratch/file`, remove `scratch` with `rm -rf --`, and print `gone` if the name is absent.", "hint": "`test ! -e`.", "solution": "`gone` is printed. The double dash is what you keep when the name might start with a dash.", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir -p scratch\n/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > scratch/file\n/usr/bin/rm -rf -- scratch\n/usr/bin/test ! -e scratch && /usr/bin/printf 'gone\\n'\n", "stdout": "gone\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/safe-pipelines-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

Quoting and `pipefail` do not slow a pipeline down in any way that matters next to the work. The unsafe version is the one that gets rerun after it splits names wrong, and a rerun of `sort` on a large file is the expensive part. NUL-safe tools pass the same bytes with a different delimiter. `sort -z` is not a faster sort. It is the sort that does not break the key in half at a newline.

`rm -rf` of a tree of small files is a metadata storm: one unlink per file, plus directory updates. It is slow on a cold cache and it is not made faster by `-f`. `-f` only changes the prompt. If you need to delete millions of files often, the design problem is the millions of files, not the flags. A new directory and an atomic `mv` of the parent, followed by a background delete, keeps the publisher fast. The delete itself still costs the unlinks.

`yes | head` is a terrible benchmark. The 141 status is a signal, and the elapsed time is dominated by process startup. Use the benchmark scripts when you want a median.

lessons.title: Tools that are not coreutils
lessons.summary: find, xargs, grep, sed, awk, and tar sit beside the toolbox and are easy to misfile as coreutils. hostname, kill, and uptime are in the GNU manual and still belong to other Ubuntu packages. rsync, perf, and GNU time are not installed here.
objectives: Mark find, grep, sed, awk, and tar as other packages while using them for one real task
Walk a filename that contains a space with find -print0 and xargs -0
Show which package owns hostname, kill, and uptime on this image
Record that rsync, perf, and /usr/bin/time are absent
lessons.gnuVsBsd: BSD base systems ship their own find, grep, sed, awk, and tar, with different extended flags. GNU find is findutils. GNU grep is grep. On this Ubuntu image awk is mawk via alternatives, not gawk. The GNU coreutils manual documents hostname, kill, and uptime, but dpkg attributes those paths to other packages here. macOS `hostname` is not the hostname package this lesson queries. rsync and perf were not installed, so this lesson does not demonstrate their flags. No BSD companion was executed.
lessons.markdown:
Coreutils is a bounded set. The introduction in the manual describes that set. Everything else you type in a shell is a guest. Guests are useful. Calling them coreutils leads to the wrong manual, the wrong bug tracker, and a script that assumes a flag the package never shipped. This lesson runs the guests and names the package.

`find` and `xargs` come from findutils. `find` walks a tree. `find -print0` ends each path with a NUL. `xargs -0` reads those paths and builds argument lists. Together they are the recursive form of the NUL-safe habit in the filename lesson. `xargs` has its own failure rules: by default a command that exits 255 can stop the whole run, and without `-0` it splits on blanks. A space in `my file` is the test. `wc -c` from coreutils can count the file once xargs has passed the name through intact.

`grep` searches. Coreutils does not. `grep -n` prints the line number. It is the right tool for "which line contains this token" and the wrong tool to cite as a coreutils one-liner. The remove lesson uses grep only as a companion to find a phrase in `rm --help`.

`sed` is a stream editor with its own language. `sed -n '2p'` prints the second line. `tail` and `head` can slice by count. They cannot apply an edit script. When you need the second line only, `sed -n '2p'` or `tail -n +2 | head -n 1` both work. The second form stays inside coreutils. Prefer it when the lesson is coreutils. Use sed when you are already in a sed script, and say so.

`awk` is a field language. On this host `/usr/bin/awk` is mawk, selected by the alternatives system, not GNU awk. A script that uses gawk-only features will fail here even though `awk` exists. The example prints the second field of one line and the version line mawk reports. `cut` is the coreutils field tool, and it splits on a single character. It does not evaluate an awk expression, and it does not understand CSV quotes. That limit has its own cookbook recipe.

`tar` writes a tape archive. `cp -a` copies a tree and is not an archive format. The example creates a one-file tar and lists it. Compression flags belong to tar and to gzip, not to coreutils. This course does not teach tar's format beyond "it is a different package".

`hostname`, `kill`, and `uptime` have nodes in the GNU coreutils manual because the upstream project documents them. Ubuntu packages them elsewhere. `dpkg -S` on the three paths shows the owning packages. The orientation lesson made the same point with the version of coreutils you do have. Read the manual node only after you have checked which binary answered.

`rsync` is not installed. `perf` is not installed. `/usr/bin/time` is not installed. The shell keyword `time` is bash, and it does not print maximum RSS. The benchmark helper uses Python's `resource` module for that counter and says so in the disclosure. Do not paste a GNU time format string into this environment and expect a binary to appear.

## Worked examples

### grep is its own package

```example
{"id": "companion-tools-01", "title": "A line number from grep", "companion": "grep", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'alpha\\nbeta\\n' | /usr/bin/grep -n beta\n", "stdout": "2:beta\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/companion-tools-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A space survives -print0

```example
{"id": "companion-tools-02", "title": "find and xargs", "companion": "find", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir box\n/usr/bin/printf 'x\\n' > \"box/my file\"\n/usr/bin/find box -type f -print0 | /usr/bin/xargs -0 /usr/bin/wc -c\n", "stdout": "2 box/my file\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/companion-tools-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### sed and mawk

```example
{"id": "companion-tools-03", "title": "Second line, second field", "companion": "sed", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\n' | /usr/bin/sed -n '2p'\n/usr/bin/printf 'field:'\n/usr/bin/printf 'a b\\n' | /usr/bin/awk '{print $2}'\n/usr/bin/awk -W version > awk-version.txt\n/usr/bin/head -n 1 awk-version.txt\n", "stdout": "b\nfield:b\nmawk 1.3.4 20240123\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/companion-tools-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### tar lists a member

```example
{"id": "companion-tools-04", "title": "tar is not cp", "companion": "tar", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\n' > file.txt\n/usr/bin/tar -cf bundle.tar file.txt\n/usr/bin/tar -tf bundle.tar\n", "stdout": "file.txt\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/companion-tools-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Manual chapters this Ubuntu image attributes elsewhere

```example
{"id": "companion-tools-05", "title": "hostname, kill, uptime, and the absent tools", "companion": "", "script": "dpkg -S /usr/bin/hostname\ndpkg -S /usr/bin/kill\ndpkg -S /usr/bin/uptime\nset +e\ncommand -v rsync >/dev/null\n/usr/bin/printf 'rsync_status:%s\\n' $?\ncommand -v perf >/dev/null\n/usr/bin/printf 'perf_status:%s\\n' $?\ncommand -v /usr/bin/time >/dev/null\n/usr/bin/printf 'gnu_time_status:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "hostname: /usr/bin/hostname\nprocps: /usr/bin/kill\nprocps: /usr/bin/uptime\nrsync_status:1\nperf_status:1\ngnu_time_status:1\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/companion-tools-05.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

In a C++ or Rust repository the usual walk is `find . -name '*.rs' -print0` or the build system's own file list. Prefer the build system. When you shell out, keep `-print0`. Count lines with `wc -l` only after each file is a separate argument or a separate redirection, so a filename cannot become an extra line of source.

Checksum an NDK zip with `sha256sum`, which is coreutils, and search the zip listing with tools that are not. Write the package name in the script comment. The next person will thank you when `awk` is mawk and their gawk function is missing.

When a blog shows `time -v`, check `command -v /usr/bin/time` before you port the flag. On this image the check fails. Use the benchmark helper or a language runtime counter.

## Tips and pitfalls

`command -v time` in bash finds the keyword and prints `time`, status 0. That is not GNU time. Test the path `/usr/bin/time`.

`xargs` without `-0` and without `-d` splits on spaces. The example's whole point disappears if you drop `-0` and also drop `-print0`. Drop them together or not at all.

`grep -r` is a walk plus a search. It is still not coreutils, and it has its own symlink and binary-file rules. Coreutils `grep` does not exist. There is nothing to fall back to inside `ls`.

`dpkg -S` can match several packages when the argument is a fragment. The example passes absolute paths. Keep that.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id": "companion-tools-ex01", "title": "Find a numbered line", "prompt": "Print the grep line number of `beta` in a two-line stream.", "hint": "`grep -n`. This is not a coreutils binary.", "solution": "The line begins with `2:`.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'alpha\\nbeta\\n' | /usr/bin/grep -n beta\n", "stdout": "2:beta\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/companion-tools-ex01.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "companion-tools-ex02", "title": "Print the second field with awk", "prompt": "Pipe `a b` through awk and print field 2.", "hint": "mawk is the awk on this host.", "solution": "`b`. The tool is a companion.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a b\\n' | /usr/bin/awk '{print $2}'\n", "stdout": "b\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/companion-tools-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "companion-tools-ex03", "title": "Show who owns hostname", "prompt": "Run `dpkg -S` on `/usr/bin/hostname`.", "hint": "The path is absolute so the match is the binary.", "solution": "The owning package is not coreutils. Read the captured line.", "script": "dpkg -S /usr/bin/hostname\n", "stdout": "hostname: /usr/bin/hostname\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/companion-tools-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

`find` is a directory walk, like `du`, and it does not read file bodies unless the predicate asks it to. `grep` reads bodies. Pointing `grep` at a tree of build artifacts reads those artifacts. Restrict the walk. `xargs` exists to batch arguments so you do not pay one exec per file, and also so you do not overflow `ARG_MAX`. A batch that is too large fails. A batch of one is a slow loop. The default batching is the feature. Do not replace it with a shell `while read` unless you need the loop, and if you do, read NUL with `read -d ''`.

`sed` and `awk` on a multi-gigabyte log are streaming and usually fine. They become the bottleneck when the script captures groups back into the shell once per line. Do the whole transform in one awk process. mawk and gawk differ in speed and in features. This course does not publish a winner, because the installed awk is mawk and gawk is not here to time.

`tar` of a tree of small files is metadata plus content. It is not a benchmark of `cp`. `rsync` would be a different algorithm and it is not installed, so any claim about its speed on this host would be fiction. The copy benchmark uses `cp` and `dd` only.

lessons.title: A small build, install, and checksum
lessons.summary: The daily path for a C++, Rust, or Android tree is install, nproc, sha256sum, and timeout. This lesson runs that path on a one-file C program and a payload manifest.
objectives: Compile a one-file program and place it with install -D -m 755
Record a sha256sum manifest and check it
Read nproc as a starting job count
Bound a command with timeout and keep a non-zero status visible
lessons.gnuVsBsd: POSIX `install` is not the same program as GNU `install`. BSD install uses different flag letters for the mode and for creating parents. GNU `install -D` creates missing parent directories. `sha256sum` is GNU. BSD environments often spell the tool `shasum -a 256` or `sha256`. `nproc` and `timeout` are GNU. A macOS CI job needs the Homebrew equivalents or it needs to call different tools. This lesson ran gcc and GNU coreutils on Ubuntu. It did not run an Android SDK, and it did not claim an NDK zip was present.
lessons.markdown:
A developer workstation uses coreutils in the gaps around the compiler. The compiler is not coreutils. `gcc` is not coreutils. `rustc` and `gradle` are not coreutils. The tools that place the binary, count the processors, hash the artifact, and stop a hung test are coreutils, and they are the ones a build script gets wrong when it uses `cp` and hopes.

`install -D -m 755 src/app dest/bin/app` copies the file, creates `dest/bin` if needed, and sets the mode. `-D` is the difference from `cp` followed by a separate `mkdir` and `chmod` that can race. `-m 755` is applied after the install umask handling the manual describes. The permissions lesson covers `install -C`, which preserves the mtime when the content matches, and the non-portable warning on `cp -n`. This lesson uses the plain install that a prefix expects. The mode in the capture is whatever `stat -c '%a'` prints. Read it. Do not assume a blog's `chmod` line ran.

A checksum is the artifact's identity. `sha256sum blob > MANIFEST` writes a line the same tool can check with `-c`. The check prints `OK` and exits 0 when the bytes match. A wrong digest exits non-zero. The checksum lesson shows a deliberately bad line. Here the manifest matches, because a release script that cannot round-trip a good file is not ready for a bad one. Hash the bytes you ship. Hashing a filename list without the contents does not catch a corrupt object file.

`nproc` is the starting point for `-j` in make, ninja, or cargo. `--ignore=1` leaves a processor for everything that is not the build. The number is local. The capture prints it. A linking C++ job can use more RAM than a processor count suggests, and an Android gradle build can saturate disk before it saturates CPUs. Raise the job count until RSS or the disk queue says stop. The performance lesson states that rule without a fake timing table.

`timeout` belongs around tests and around network fetches a build should not wait on forever. `timeout 2` of a program that returns immediately passes the program's status through. `timeout 1 sleep 3` returns 124. A CI script that treats every non-zero as "the compiler failed" will mis-file a hang. Branch on 124.

The shell around these tools still has the quoting rules from the previous lesson. A prefix in a variable is quoted. An empty prefix is refused. `install` will happily write to a relative `dest` you created in the scratch directory. That is the shape to copy. A script that `install`s into `/` because a variable was empty is the shape to reject before the command runs.

Rust and Android fit the same pattern even though this capture does not invoke them. `cargo build --release` writes a binary you then `install` into a prefix. An NDK archive you downloaded is a file you `sha256sum -c` against the digest the vendor published. `timeout` bounds the emulator test. None of those products are coreutils. The four commands around them are.

## Worked examples

### install into a prefix

```example
{"id": "developer-workflow-01", "title": "Compile and install -D", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir -p src\n/usr/bin/printf '%s\\n' 'int main(void) { return 0; }' > src/main.c\ngcc -o src/app src/main.c\n/usr/bin/install -D -m 755 src/app dest/bin/app\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%a %n' dest/bin/app\ndest/bin/app\n/usr/bin/printf 'ran:%s\\n' $?\n", "stdout": "755 dest/bin/app\nran:0\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/developer-workflow-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A manifest that checks

```example
{"id": "developer-workflow-02", "title": "sha256sum -c", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'payload\\n' > blob\n/usr/bin/sha256sum blob > MANIFEST\n/usr/bin/sha256sum -c MANIFEST\n", "stdout": "blob: OK\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/developer-workflow-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### Job count

```example
{"id": "developer-workflow-03", "title": "nproc as a starting point", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/nproc\n/usr/bin/nproc --ignore=1\n", "stdout": "4\n3\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/developer-workflow-03.sh", "truncated": false}
```


### A hang is status 124

```example
{"id": "developer-workflow-04", "title": "timeout distinguishes a quick program from a sleeper", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir -p src\n/usr/bin/printf '%s\\n' 'int main(void) { return 0; }' > src/main.c\ngcc -o src/app src/main.c\nset +e\n/usr/bin/timeout 2 src/app\n/usr/bin/printf 'quick:%s\\n' $?\n/usr/bin/timeout 1 /usr/bin/sleep 3\n/usr/bin/printf 'sleeper:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "quick:0\nsleeper:124\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/developer-workflow-04.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Recipes

A prefix script for a small C or C++ tool:

```bash
prefix=${1:-}
if test -z "$prefix" || test "$prefix" = /; then
  printf 'refuse prefix\n' >&2
  exit 1
fi
jobs=$(nproc --ignore=1)
make -j "$jobs"
install -D -m 755 app "$prefix/bin/app"
sha256sum "$prefix/bin/app" > "$prefix/bin/app.sha256"
```

The capture does not run `make`. It runs the same `install` and `sha256sum` on a scratch binary so you can see the bytes. Quote `$prefix`. Refuse `/`.

For a downloaded archive, verify before you unpack. `sha256sum -c` the vendor file. Then `tar` (a companion) extracts. A failed check should stop the script because `set -e` is on. Do not unpack and then check.

Put `timeout` on the test binary, not on the compiler, unless you have a reason to believe the compiler hangs. A killed compiler leaves a partial object that the next incremental build may trust. Delete the partial output in the failure branch when you do wrap the compiler.

## Tips and pitfalls

`install` without `-D` will not create `dest/bin`. The error is "no such file", and the binary you compiled is still in the build tree. The example uses `-D` because a prefix install that requires a manual mkdir is one more step to forget.

`sha256sum -c` reads the manifest's filenames relative to the current directory. Run it from the directory you will ship, or put paths in the manifest that match how you will check. A check from the wrong directory fails even when the bytes are fine.

`nproc` inside a container reports the container's limit when the runtime sets it. It can also report the host count when the runtime does not. Print it in the CI log so the job count you used is visible next to the failure.

`gcc` in the example is the system compiler, used only to produce a binary worth installing. The course is not a C tutorial. The interesting lines are `install`, `sha256sum`, `nproc`, and `timeout`.

## Exercises

```exercise
{"id": "developer-workflow-ex01", "title": "Install a binary into bin", "prompt": "Create a tiny C program, compile it to `src/app`, and `install -D -m 755` it to `dest/bin/app`. Print the mode.", "hint": "`-D` creates the parent directory.", "solution": "`stat` prints `755` and the path. The parent `dest/bin` did not need a separate mkdir.", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir -p src\n/usr/bin/printf '%s\\n' 'int main(void) { return 0; }' > src/main.c\ngcc -o src/app src/main.c\n/usr/bin/install -D -m 755 src/app dest/bin/app\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%a' dest/bin/app\n", "stdout": "755\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/developer-workflow-ex01.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "developer-workflow-ex02", "title": "Check a matching manifest", "prompt": "Write `payload` and a newline to `blob`, save `sha256sum` output, and check it.", "hint": "`-c` reads the file you just wrote.", "solution": "The check prints `OK` and exits 0.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'payload\\n' > blob\n/usr/bin/sha256sum blob > MANIFEST\n/usr/bin/sha256sum -c MANIFEST\n", "stdout": "blob: OK\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/developer-workflow-ex02.sh"}
```


```exercise
{"id": "developer-workflow-ex03", "title": "Bound a sleep", "prompt": "Run `timeout 1 sleep 3`.", "hint": "124 is the wrapper.", "solution": "The status is 124 because the sleep outlasts the deadline.", "script": "/usr/bin/timeout 1 /usr/bin/sleep 3\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 124, "download": "/downloads/solutions/developer-workflow-ex03.sh"}
```


## Performance

`install` of one binary is a copy plus metadata. It is noise next to a C++ link. `install` of a tree of thousands of headers is a metadata walk, and `-C` avoids rewriting a file whose contents did not change, which keeps dependent mtimes stable. The permissions lesson demonstrates `-C` on a small file. Use it when a stamp file would otherwise change every build and pull the whole incremental graph with it.

`sha256sum` of a large artifact is a streaming read and a CPU-bound hash. The checksum benchmark times `md5sum`, `sha256sum`, and `b2sum` on one 8 MiB input and reports medians. Use that page for a comparison. Do not infer the winner from a single release zip on a laptop with a warm cache. For an Android archive the hash cost is usually smaller than the download. Still hash it. A skipped check is not a performance optimization you can defend after a corrupt file spends an hour unpacking.

`nproc` costs nothing. The jobs it encourages cost RAM. If the build swaps, lower the job count before you change compilers. `timeout` adds a process. Around a multi-minute test it is invisible. Around a microbenchmark it is part of the measurement, so keep it outside the timed section. The benchmark scripts already separate the helper's overhead by comparing variants that share it.

examples.title: Compile and install -D
examples.script:

/usr/bin/printf '%s\n' 'int main(void) { return 0; }' > src/main.c
