cookbook.title: Collapse repeated log lines
cookbook.summary: sort and uniq -c show which lines repeat. sort -u drops duplicates when the whole line is the key.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: POSIX `sort` and `uniq` exist on BSD. GNU `sort -u` is not the same as `sort | uniq` when the sort key is narrower than the whole line. BSD sort keys use a different flag spelling for field separators. This recipe ran GNU sort and uniq only.
cookbook.markdown:
A log that repeats the same line a thousand times is hard to read and easy to count. `sort` groups identical lines together. `uniq -c` prefixes each group with the count. `sort -u` prints each distinct line once and is the right tool when you want the set of lines and you are sorting the whole line. It is the wrong tool when a key flag ignores part of the line: `sort -u` still emits one row per key, and `sort | uniq` only collapses rows that are entirely identical after the sort. The sort lesson demonstrates that difference. This recipe uses the whole line, so the two forms agree.

The input has to be sorted for `uniq` to see a run of duplicates. `uniq` does not search the whole file for a match that occurred earlier. That is why the pipeline is `sort | uniq` and not `uniq` alone on a raw log. If you need the original order, you are outside what this pair promises. A language with an ordered set is the honest tool then, or `awk` (a companion, and mawk on this host) with an associative array.

Counts from `uniq -c` are padded. `sort -n` orders those count lines numerically if you want the noisiest line first. The padding is spaces, so a plain lexical sort of the count output is the wrong order once counts reach two digits.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "dedupe-a-log-01", "title": "Count duplicate lines", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'b\\na\\nb\\nb\\na\\n' > log\n/usr/bin/sort log | /usr/bin/uniq -c\n", "stdout": "      2 a\n      3 b\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/dedupe-a-log-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "dedupe-a-log-02", "title": "One copy of each line", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'b\\na\\nb\\nb\\na\\n' > log\n/usr/bin/sort -u log\n", "stdout": "a\nb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/dedupe-a-log-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "dedupe-a-log-ex01", "title": "Count three identical lines", "prompt": "Write `err` three times and print `uniq -c` after sorting.", "hint": "The count is the first field.", "solution": "One output line, count 3, text `err`.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'err\\nerr\\nerr\\n' > log\n/usr/bin/sort log | /usr/bin/uniq -c\n", "stdout": "      3 err\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/dedupe-a-log-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

Sorting is the expensive part once the log no longer fits in the sort buffer. `uniq` is a linear scan of an already ordered stream. Do not run `sort | uniq` and then `sort -u` on the same huge file if you only needed one of them. Give `sort` a `-T` directory on a filesystem with room when the log is large. The benchmark page measures sort with a fixed input and does not measure your production log. Locale collation changes both the order and the CPU cost. `LC_ALL=C` is appropriate when the lines are byte strings and you do not need dictionary order.

cookbook.title: Compare two sorted sets with comm
cookbook.summary: comm prints lines only in the first file, only in the second, and in both. The inputs have to be sorted or the result is a partial lie.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: POSIX `comm` is shared. GNU comm checks that the inputs look ordered and can exit 1 while still printing. `--nocheck-order` disables the check and can pair the wrong lines. BSD comm may not perform the same check. This recipe ran GNU comm on sorted inputs.
cookbook.markdown:
`comm` is the set operation for line-oriented files. Column one is lines only in the first file. Column two is lines only in the second. Column three is lines in both. `-1`, `-2`, and `-3` suppress columns, so `comm -12` is the intersection and `comm -13` is "in the second file but not the first" when you remember which digit you deleted. The files must be sorted with the same locale you use for `comm`. A file sorted under `en_US.UTF-8` and compared under `LC_ALL=C` is not ordered in the way comm expects.

GNU comm notices unsorted input, prints a diagnostic, and exits 1. It may already have printed some lines. That partial output is not a complete answer. `--nocheck-order` exits 0 and can still pair lines incorrectly. Do not use it to silence a real order bug. Sort both files in the pipeline that feeds comm, with an explicit `LC_ALL` so the CI locale matches your laptop.

Blank lines and duplicate lines are data. `comm` does not unique them unless you did. If you wanted sets, run `sort -u` first and accept that you threw away multiplicity.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "compare-sets-01", "title": "Three columns", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\n' > left\n/usr/bin/printf 'b\\nc\\nd\\n' > right\n/usr/bin/comm left right\n", "stdout": "a\n\t\tb\n\t\tc\n\td\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/compare-sets-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "compare-sets-02", "title": "Intersection only", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\n' > left\n/usr/bin/printf 'b\\nc\\nd\\n' > right\n/usr/bin/comm -12 left right\n", "stdout": "b\nc\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/compare-sets-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "compare-sets-ex01", "title": "Lines only on the right", "prompt": "Print lines that are in `right` and not in `left` for the sets a,b,c and b,c,d.", "hint": "Suppress columns 1 and 3.", "solution": "The remaining line is `d`.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\n' > left\n/usr/bin/printf 'b\\nc\\nd\\n' > right\n/usr/bin/comm -13 left right\n", "stdout": "d\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/compare-sets-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

`comm` is a linear merge. It does not build a hash set. The cost is the two sorts you did to prepare the files, plus a single pass. Sorting twice and then comm is cheaper than a nested shell loop that greps one file per line of the other, and it is correct for duplicates in a way the loop usually is not. The files should already be sorted from the producer when you can arrange that, so you do not pay the sort again. There is no parallel flag worth reaching for at this size. If the inputs are huge, the sort spill is the bill. Point `sort -T` at a disk with space and read the sort lesson before you add `--parallel`.

cookbook.title: Join two sorted tables on a key
cookbook.summary: join merges sorted files on a field. Unsorted input is diagnosed. --nocheck-order hides the diagnosis and can emit a wrong join.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: POSIX `join` requires sorted inputs. GNU join checks order by default, writes a diagnostic, and exits 1, sometimes after partial stdout. BSD join may omit that check. Field numbers and the default separator are shared. This recipe used GNU join.
cookbook.markdown:
`join` matches lines that share a key and writes one line with the key and the remaining fields. The default key is field one. The default separator is whitespace. Both files must be sorted on that key. `printf '1 red\n2 blue\n'` joined with `printf '1 apple\n2 berry\n'` yields two lines. The same files with a key out of order make GNU join complain. The complaint can arrive after some output has already been written, and the status is 1. `--nocheck-order` suppresses the check, exits 0, and can miss pairs. A green status from that flag is not evidence the join is complete.

Keys that appear only on one side are omitted by default. `-a 1` or `-a 2` keeps the unpaired lines, which is the closest join has to an outer join. It is still not SQL. There is no quoting, no numeric coercion, and no "last field" syntax. If the key is field 2 you pass `-1 2 -2 2` and you sort on field 2 as well, with `sort -k2,2`. Sorting on the whole line and joining on field 2 is a mismatch.

Empty fields and repeated keys multiply rows. Two left rows with key `1` and two right rows with key `1` produce four output rows. Know your cardinality before you treat the output as a lookup.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "join-tables-01", "title": "Join on field one", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '1 red\\n2 blue\\n' > colors\n/usr/bin/printf '1 apple\\n2 berry\\n' > fruit\n/usr/bin/join colors fruit\n", "stdout": "1 red apple\n2 blue berry\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/join-tables-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "join-tables-02", "title": "Unsorted input is an error", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/printf '2 blue\\n1 red\\n' > colors\n/usr/bin/printf '1 apple\\n2 berry\\n' > fruit\n/usr/bin/join colors fruit\n/usr/bin/printf 'status:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "2 blue berry\nstatus:1\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/join: colors:2: is not sorted: 1 red\n/usr/bin/join: input is not in sorted order\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/join-tables-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself



## Performance

`join` is a merge, linear in the number of lines, after the sorts. The sort is the part that spills. Do the sort once and keep the files if you will join them again. A database is the right tool when you need indexes, unsorted inserts, and repeated joins. Coreutils join is the right tool when you already have two sorted exports and you want no server. `--nocheck-order` does not make the merge faster in a way that pays for a wrong answer. Leave the check on. If it fires, sort the input and rerun rather than timing the broken run.

cookbook.title: cut splits on a character, not on CSV quotes
cookbook.summary: A comma inside quotes is still a comma to cut. Field two of a,"b,c",d is not the quoted cell.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: POSIX `cut` selects bytes, characters, or fields. GNU cut adds `--complement` and `-z`. Neither GNU nor BSD cut implements RFC 4180 quotes. A CSV parser is a different program. This recipe shows the GNU split.
cookbook.markdown:
`cut -d, -f2` takes the second comma-separated field. It does not know that a double quote can protect a comma. The line `a,"b,c",d` has four comma-separated fields: `a`, `"b`, `c"`, and `d`. Field two is quote-b, not the cell b,c. Any script that extracts a column from an export "because it is a csv" with `cut` will silently shift columns the first time a description contains a comma. That is a correctness bug that looks like clean data.

`cut` is still the right tool for files that really are single-character-separated and contain no quoted separators: `/etc/passwd` with `-d:`, or a log you generated yourself with a delimiter you know cannot appear. `--complement` drops the fields you name and keeps the rest, which is useful for removing a column without renumbering. `-z` uses NUL as the line delimiter when the upstream tool produced NUL records. None of those flags add a quote parser.

If the file is real CSV, use a parser in the language you are shipping (Python's csv module, a Rust crate, a C++ library). `awk` with `FPAT` is a GNU awk feature, and this host's awk is mawk, so a blog snippet that depends on `FPAT` will not run here anyway. Do not "fix" cut by deleting quotes with `tr` first. Embedded quotes and escaped quotes will still break, and you will have destroyed data you needed.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "cut-is-not-csv-01", "title": "The comma inside quotes still splits", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a,\"b,c\",d\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d, -f1\n/usr/bin/printf 'a,\"b,c\",d\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d, -f2\n/usr/bin/printf 'a,\"b,c\",d\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d, -f3\n/usr/bin/printf 'a,\"b,c\",d\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d, -f4\n", "stdout": "a\n\"b\nc\"\nd\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cut-is-not-csv-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "cut-is-not-csv-02", "title": "A delimiter that cannot appear is fine", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d: -f1,7\n", "stdout": "root:/bin/bash\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cut-is-not-csv-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "cut-is-not-csv-ex01", "title": "Show field two of a quoted comma", "prompt": "Print field 2 of `a,\"b,c\",d` split on commas.", "hint": "Do not expect `b,c`.", "solution": "The field is `\"b` including the quote. The comma ended the field.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a,\"b,c\",d\\n' | /usr/bin/cut -d, -f2\n", "stdout": "\"b\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/cut-is-not-csv-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

`cut` is a streaming scan. It is cheap compared with a CSV parser that counts quotes and allocations, and that cheapness is why people reach for it. The cost of a wrong column in a data export is not saved CPU. Use cut when the format matches the tool, and pay for a parser when it does not. `cut -c` on a multibyte locale counts characters. `cut -b` counts bytes and can split a UTF-8 sequence. For ASCII field files the difference is invisible. For logs in UTF-8, decide which one you meant. Neither mode makes CSV quotes work.

cookbook.title: Record and check a SHA-256 digest
cookbook.summary: sha256sum writes a digest line and sha256sum -c reads it back. The three bytes abc are the usual test vector.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: GNU `sha256sum` prints two spaces and then the name in text mode, or a space and an asterisk for binary mode. BSD `sha256` prints a different label. `cksum -a sha256 --tag` is the GNU way to get a BSD-style line. This recipe uses GNU sha256sum text mode. The digest of the bytes `abc` is a published test vector. The capture confirms this binary.
cookbook.markdown:
`sha256sum` reads bytes and writes a hex digest, two spaces, and the name. `sha256sum -c` reads that line back, rereads the file, and prints `OK` or `FAILED`. The status is 0 only when every line you asked it to check matches. A missing file and a wrong digest are both failures. The checksum lesson shows a bad line made of 64 `a` characters. This recipe keeps the good path, because a release script should prove the round trip before you depend on the failure path.

The three bytes `a`, `b`, and `c` with no newline are the SHA-256 test vector everyone publishes. Including a newline, which `echo` often adds and `printf 'abc'` does not, produces a different digest. The example uses `/usr/bin/printf 'abc'` so the newline is absent. If your check fails against a published vector, dump the file with `od -An -tx1` and count the bytes before you blame the hash.

Text mode and binary mode matter on platforms that translate newlines. On GNU/Linux they hash the same bytes and the marker in the output differs: two spaces versus a space and an asterisk. Check with the same mode you wrote. A manifest generated on Linux and checked with a tool that expects the BSD label will fail at parse time, before any byte is compared.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "checksum-a-blob-01", "title": "Digest of abc", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abc' > blob\n/usr/bin/sha256sum blob\n", "stdout": "ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad  blob\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/checksum-a-blob-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "checksum-a-blob-02", "title": "Check the manifest", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abc' > blob\n/usr/bin/sha256sum blob > MANIFEST\n/usr/bin/sha256sum -c MANIFEST\n", "stdout": "blob: OK\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/checksum-a-blob-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "checksum-a-blob-ex01", "title": "Round-trip a digest", "prompt": "Write `abc` with no newline, save sha256sum output, and check it.", "hint": "`printf`, not echo.", "solution": "The check prints `blob: OK`.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'abc' > blob\n/usr/bin/sha256sum blob > MANIFEST\n/usr/bin/sha256sum -c MANIFEST\n", "stdout": "blob: OK\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/checksum-a-blob-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

SHA-256 of a small file is startup noise. SHA-256 of a multi-gigabyte image is a streaming read and a CPU-bound compression of that read into 32 bytes. It does not benefit from locale settings. Running it twice to "be sure" doubles the read and does not change the mathematics. The checksum benchmark on the benchmark page compares algorithms on one 8 MiB input, warm cache, five trials, and tells you not to treat the absolute seconds as a disk measurement. Pick SHA-256 for a new manifest unless you are matching a vendor file that already published a different algorithm. Matching the vendor is more important than the microbenchmark.

cookbook.title: Split a log into fixed line counts
cookbook.summary: split -l writes pieces with a prefix. split -n and split -n r/N do not mean the same thing when lines are uneven.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: POSIX `split` supports line and byte counts. GNU `split -n` and `-n r/N` are GNU extensions for byte chunks and line round-robin. BSD split does not accept the same `-n` syntax. A one-line input given to `-n r/3` stays in the first piece. This recipe ran GNU split.
cookbook.markdown:
`split -l 2` reads a text file and writes new files with at most two lines each. The prefix you pass becomes the start of each name, and the suffix is `aa`, `ab`, and so on unless you change it. The pieces are ordinary files. Nothing in split deletes the original. You can checksum the pieces, upload them, or feed them to workers. You should also know how you will put them back: `cat part_*` works when the names sort in order, which they do for the default suffixes until you pass a few hundred pieces and need `-d` numeric suffixes to keep lexical order honest. `split -d` uses numbers. Prefer it when a later `sort` of the names would otherwise surprise you. The default alphabetic suffixes are fine for a handful of chunks.

`split -n 3` divides the file into three byte ranges. It can cut a line in half. `split -n r/3` round-robins lines, and a file with one line puts that entire line in the first piece. The split lesson captured both. Use `-l` or `-n l/N` when the consumer must see whole lines. Use byte splits only when the consumer is a byte tool, such as a parallel checksum of ranges you will concatenate in order.

An empty input creates no glory and may create empty pieces depending on the mode. Check the names with `ls` and the line counts with `wc -l` before you launch a fleet of workers on empty files.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "split-a-log-01", "title": "Two lines per piece", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '1\\n2\\n3\\n4\\n5\\n' > log\n/usr/bin/split -l 2 log part_\n/usr/bin/ls part_*\n/usr/bin/wc -l part_*\n", "stdout": "part_aa\npart_ab\npart_ac\n 2 part_aa\n 2 part_ab\n 1 part_ac\n 5 total\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/split-a-log-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "split-a-log-02", "title": "One line round-robin stays in the first piece", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'only\\n' > one\n/usr/bin/split -n r/3 one rr_\n/usr/bin/wc -c rr_*\n", "stdout": "5 rr_aa\n0 rr_ab\n0 rr_ac\n5 total\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/split-a-log-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "split-a-log-ex01", "title": "Split five lines", "prompt": "Split a file of five lines into pieces of two lines and list the piece names.", "hint": "`split -l 2` and a prefix.", "solution": "Three pieces. The last one holds the leftover line.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '1\\n2\\n3\\n4\\n5\\n' > log\n/usr/bin/split -l 2 log part_\n/usr/bin/ls part_*\n", "stdout": "part_aa\npart_ab\npart_ac\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/split-a-log-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

`split` reads the input once and writes the pieces once. It is disk-bound on a large log and cheap on a small one. Splitting into thousands of tiny files creates a metadata storm that can cost more than the bytes. Choose a piece size that a worker can process without drowning the directory. Round-robin line split is still one read. It does not parallelize the split itself. The parallelism, if any, is the later workers. Concatenating the pieces in the wrong order is a correctness bug, not a performance feature. Numeric suffixes (`-d`) keep the order obvious.

cookbook.title: Count a file whose name contains a space
cookbook.summary: find -print0 and xargs -0 keep a space inside one filename. find and xargs are findutils, not coreutils. wc is coreutils.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: GNU find `-print0` and GNU xargs `-0` are the NUL pair. BSD find and xargs also support them. A POSIX-only `xargs` without `-0` splits on blanks. `wc` is in both userlands. This recipe marks find as a companion and ran it on Ubuntu.
cookbook.markdown:
A space in a filename is ordinary on a desktop and fatal in a shell pipeline that splits words. `my file` is one directory entry. An unquoted expansion or a newline-oriented `xargs` treats it as two arguments, and `wc` then reports that `my` does not exist. The durable fix is to end each name with a NUL byte, which cannot appear inside a path, and to read names the same way.

`find` is findutils. `xargs` is findutils. `wc` is coreutils. The pipeline `find box -type f -print0 | xargs -0 wc -c` is a collaboration, and the example badge says so. Dropping either `-print0` or `-0` reintroduces the split. `ls` piped to `xargs` is the version that fails the space test even before newlines. GNU `ls --zero` exists when you already have a non-recursive listing and you refuse to switch to find. Recursive walks belong to find or to your build system.

Coreutils filters that accept `-z` (`sort -z`, `uniq -z`) keep the same boundary once find has produced it. Converting NUL to newline with `tr` so you can use a tool that lacks `-z` brings the original bug back the moment a name contains a newline. Prefer a tool that understands NUL, or do the walk in the language that will process the files.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "nul-safe-names-01", "title": "A space survives NUL framing", "companion": "find", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir box\n/usr/bin/printf 'hello\\n' > \"box/my file\"\n/usr/bin/find box -type f -print0 | /usr/bin/xargs -0 /usr/bin/wc -c\n", "stdout": "6 box/my file\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/nul-safe-names-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "nul-safe-names-02", "title": "The quoting style a human can see", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir box\n/usr/bin/printf 'hello\\n' > \"box/my file\"\n/usr/bin/ls --quoting-style=shell-escape box\n", "stdout": "'my file'\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/nul-safe-names-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```

```exercise

The space stayed inside one argument.", "script": "/usr/bin/mkdir box\n/usr/bin/printf 'hello\\n' > \"box/my file\"\n/usr/bin/find box -type f -print0 | /usr/bin/xargs -0 /usr/bin/wc -c\n", "stdout": "6 box/my file\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/nul-safe-names-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

NUL framing adds one byte per name and no measurable CPU next to reading the file. The win is that you do not rerun the job after `wc` skipped half the tree. `xargs` batches names so `wc` starts once per batch instead of once per file. That exec saving matters when the files are tiny and disappears when each file is hundreds of megabytes, because the read dominates. `find` itself is a metadata walk. It is slow on a cold directory cache and fast on a warm one. This recipe does not drop caches, and it does not claim a timing. The safe pipeline is the one you can finish.

cookbook.title: Measure a hole instead of copying it
cookbook.summary: truncate -s 1M creates a sparse file. du -b reports the apparent size. du -B1 reports the allocation, which is zero on this filesystem.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: GNU `du --apparent-size` and `-b` are the logical size. macOS `du` uses different flags. GNU `truncate -s` is the GNU/BSD-ish spelling to check in `--help` before you port it. A hole that `du` reports as zero blocks here can allocate differently on another filesystem. This recipe recorded ext4 behavior on the capture host and did not run BSD du.
cookbook.markdown:
A sparse file has a logical size larger than the blocks the filesystem has allocated. `truncate -s 1M hole` sets the size to one mebibyte and does not write a mebibyte of zeros. `stat -c 'size=%s blocks=%b'` shows the size and the allocated-block count. On this capture the block count is 0 for a fresh hole. `du -b` is apparent size in bytes, so it prints 1048576. `du -B1` prints the allocation, 0. Both numbers are "the size". A script that alerts on one of them and a human who reads the other will disagree, and both will be quoting the tool correctly.

Copying the file decides whether the hole survives. A naive read of every byte materializes the zeros. `cp --sparse=always` tries to keep holes. A transfer that does not, including some archive tools and some network copies, turns the hole into real blocks and the disk fills. Check `du -B1` after the copy, not only `ls -l`.

`df` will not move by a mebibyte when you create this hole, because the blocks were never allocated. It will move if a later write fills the hole. That is the same distinction the du lesson draws between a tree walk and a filesystem query.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "sparse-apparent-size-01", "title": "Apparent size and allocation", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/truncate -s 1M hole\n/usr/bin/stat -c 'size=%s blocks=%b' hole\n/usr/bin/du -b hole\n/usr/bin/du -B1 hole\n", "stdout": "size=1048576 blocks=0\n1048576\thole\n0\thole\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/sparse-apparent-size-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "sparse-apparent-size-02", "title": "The directory listing shows the logical size", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/truncate -s 1M hole\n/usr/bin/ls -l hole\n", "stdout": "-rw-r--r-- 1 ubuntu ubuntu 1048576 Nov  8 16:09 hole\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/sparse-apparent-size-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "sparse-apparent-size-ex01", "title": "Report both sizes", "prompt": "Create a 1 MiB hole and print `du -b` and `du -B1`.", "hint": "`-b` is apparent size. `-B1` is allocated bytes.", "solution": "Apparent size is 1048576. Allocated size is 0 on this filesystem for a new hole.", "script": "/usr/bin/truncate -s 1M hole\n/usr/bin/du -b hole\n/usr/bin/du -B1 hole\n", "stdout": "1048576\thole\n0\thole\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/sparse-apparent-size-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

Creating the hole is a metadata update. Reading it back as zeros is a megabyte of generated bytes per mebibyte of logical size, and it will dominate if a backup does it. The fast path is the one that copies extents or skips holes, and it exists only when the filesystem and the tool agree. This host's `cp --reflink=always` fails. Sparseness and reflink are different features. Time the copy you will actually run, on a file large enough to see, and include `du -B1` of the destination in the notes so a materialized hole is visible. The course benchmark does not use a sparse input for the copy trial. It uses an 8 MiB dense file and says so.

cookbook.title: Ask for a reflink and accept a real copy
cookbook.summary: cp --reflink=always fails on this filesystem. --reflink=auto copies and exits 0. The fallback is the behavior a script can ship.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: GNU `cp --reflink=always` and `--reflink=auto` are Linux clone requests. macOS `cp` uses a different clone flag and a different failure text. A script that requires `always` will exit 1 on this ext4. This recipe captured that failure and the auto fallback. It did not run BSD cp.
cookbook.markdown:
A reflink is a request that the filesystem share extents between two directory entries instead of reading and writing every byte. `cp --reflink=always` makes the request mandatory. On this capture host the kernel returns "Operation not supported" and cp exits 1. Nothing is left that you can treat as a successful clone. `cp --reflink=auto` makes the same request and, when the filesystem refuses, copies the bytes and exits 0. The destination then has the same contents and its own allocated blocks.

A build script that uses `always` on a developer laptop with btrfs and in CI on ext4 will be green on the laptop and red in CI, or the reverse. `auto` is the portable request inside GNU cp when a clone is a nice speedup and a copy is acceptable. `always` belongs in a test that is specifically asserting "this filesystem can clone", where a failure is the result you want to see.

Check the copy. `wc -c` or `sha256sum` of both files tells you the bytes arrived. A reflink and a plain copy look the same to `cat`. They do not look the same to `du -B1` once the file is large and the clone shares blocks. This recipe uses a five-byte file, so allocation differences are smaller than a block and are the wrong thing to assert. The status and the byte count are the assertion.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "reflink-fallback-01", "title": "A mandatory clone fails here", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'data\\n' > src\nset +e\n/usr/bin/cp --reflink=always src dst\n/usr/bin/printf 'always:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "always:1\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/cp: failed to clone 'dst' from 'src': Operation not supported\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/reflink-fallback-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "reflink-fallback-02", "title": "auto falls back to a copy", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'data\\n' > src\n/usr/bin/cp --reflink=auto src dst\n/usr/bin/wc -c dst\n/usr/bin/sha256sum src dst\n", "stdout": "5 dst\n6667b2d1aab6a00caa5aee5af8ad9f1465e567abf1c209d15727d57b3e8f6e5f  src\n6667b2d1aab6a00caa5aee5af8ad9f1465e567abf1c209d15727d57b3e8f6e5f  dst\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/reflink-fallback-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "reflink-fallback-ex01", "title": "Copy with an optional reflink", "prompt": "Write `data` and a newline and copy it with `--reflink=auto`. Print the destination size.", "hint": "`auto` exits 0 on this host.", "solution": "The size is 5. The digests of source and destination match.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'data\\n' > src\n/usr/bin/cp --reflink=auto src dst\n/usr/bin/wc -c dst\n", "stdout": "5 dst\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/reflink-fallback-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

When a clone works, the elapsed time stays near the cost of a metadata update and does not grow with the file size. When it falls back, the elapsed time is a read and a write of every byte. This host takes the second path. The copy benchmark compares `cp --reflink=never` with `dd` on an 8 MiB dense file so the fallback is what is measured, and it says the cache is warm. Do not quote a btrfs clone benchmark as the speed of `cp` on this ext4. If you change filesystems, rerun the measurement. A script that logs whether the `always` probe failed is more honest than a script that hides the fallback inside `auto` and then claims the copy was free.

cookbook.title: Stop a command that ignores the clock
cookbook.summary: timeout returns 124 when it kills the child. --preserve-status returns 143 for SIGTERM on this host. A command that finishes in time keeps its own status.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: `timeout` is GNU. macOS does not ship it in the base system. Status 124 is GNU timeout's "timed out" code. `--preserve-status` instead reports the signal status, 143 for SIGTERM here (128+15). BSD has no identical wrapper. This recipe ran GNU timeout.
cookbook.markdown:
A test that waits forever is a stuck CI job. `timeout DURATION COMMAND` starts the command and sends TERM when the duration elapses. If the command is still running when the signal fires, timeout exits 124 unless you passed `--preserve-status`. With that flag, this host exits 143, because the child died from SIGTERM and 128+15 is 143. If the command finishes early, you see the command's status and timeout does not invent 124.

Pick the status your harness can branch on. 124 is easier to recognize as "the wrapper fired". 143 is easier when you already have a signal table and you want the wrapper to be invisible. Use one convention in a repository and document it. Do not treat both as "non-zero, so the build failed" without a message. A compiler error and a hang want different retries.

`timeout` applies to the process it execs. A pipeline is not one process. `timeout 1 sleep 5 | sleep 5` bounds only the first sleep. Wrap the pipeline in `timeout 1 bash -c '...'` when every stage must share the deadline. The process-wrapper lesson records the same statuses. This recipe is the short form you can paste above a test binary.

The examples use `sleep` because it is predictable. A real test binary replaces `sleep`. Keep the duration longer than a healthy run and shorter than the job's overall budget.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "bound-a-hung-command-01", "title": "Default status is 124", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/timeout 1 /usr/bin/sleep 3\n/usr/bin/printf 'timed_out:%s\\n' $?\n/usr/bin/timeout 2 /usr/bin/true\n/usr/bin/printf 'finished:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "timed_out:124\nfinished:0\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/bound-a-hung-command-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "bound-a-hung-command-02", "title": "preserve-status reports the signal", "companion": "", "script": "set +e\n/usr/bin/timeout --preserve-status 1 /usr/bin/sleep 3\n/usr/bin/printf 'preserved:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "preserved:143\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/bound-a-hung-command-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "bound-a-hung-command-ex01", "title": "Let the wrapper fire", "prompt": "Run `timeout 1 sleep 3`.", "hint": "124 is timeout's own status.", "solution": "The command does not sleep for three seconds. The status is 124.", "script": "/usr/bin/timeout 1 /usr/bin/sleep 3\n", "stdout": "", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 124, "download": "/downloads/solutions/bound-a-hung-command-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

`timeout` costs one extra process and a sleep until the child exits or the deadline hits. Next to a multi-minute test, that is noise. Next to a microbenchmark, it is part of the number, so keep it outside the timed region. The one-second examples in this recipe spend about one second each because that is the deadline. They are not a measurement of `sleep` accuracy. A deadline that is tighter than the scheduler's jitter will flake. Leave margin. Killing a process does not roll back its partial output. If the hung command was writing an artifact, delete the artifact in the 124 branch before the next retry, or the next step will trust a short file.

cookbook.title: Label IEC units with numfmt
cookbook.summary: 2048 bytes is 2.0K in IEC and 2.1K in SI. numfmt --field formats one column and leaves the rest of the line alone.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: `numfmt` is GNU. BSD has no matching binary. `--to=iec` uses powers of 1024. `--to=si` uses powers of 1000. The one-decimal rounding of 2048 to `2.1K` in SI is the trap. This recipe ran GNU numfmt 9.4.
cookbook.markdown:
Human-readable sizes are where capacity graphs go wrong. `numfmt --to=iec` scales by 1024. `numfmt --to=si` scales by 1000. The integer 2048 is exactly 2 × 1024, so IEC prints `2.0K`. The same integer divided by 1000 is 2.048, and one-decimal SI rounding prints `2.1K`. A dashboard that mixes the flags will show a file growing when nobody wrote to it. Pick one unit system, label the column, and pass the matching flag.

`--field=2` formats the second whitespace-separated field and copies the others. That is how you pretty-print a `du -B1` report without turning the path into a number. `--from=si` parses a suffixed value back to a count when you must sort numerically. Sorting the suffixed text with `sort` is wrong. `sort -h` knows human suffixes and is the other honest option. The sort manual describes `-h`. Prefer raw bytes in the file you sort, and format only the display copy.

`--invalid=ignore` leaves a bad token in place and exits 0. The default is to fail. A header line such as `BYTES name` fails a conversion. Strip headers with `tail -n +2` before you format, or the first bad field aborts the pipeline under `set -e`.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "format-byte-counts-01", "title": "IEC and SI disagree on 2048", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '2048\\n' | /usr/bin/numfmt --to=iec\n/usr/bin/printf '2048\\n' | /usr/bin/numfmt --to=si\n", "stdout": "2.0K\n2.1K\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/format-byte-counts-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "format-byte-counts-02", "title": "Format one field", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '2048 payload\\n' | /usr/bin/numfmt --field=1 --to=iec\n", "stdout": "2.0K payload\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/format-byte-counts-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "format-byte-counts-ex01", "title": "Format 4096 as IEC", "prompt": "Pipe `4096` through `numfmt --to=iec`.", "hint": "4096 is 4 \u00d7 1024.", "solution": "`4.0K`.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf '4096\\n' | /usr/bin/numfmt --to=iec\n", "stdout": "4.0K\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/format-byte-counts-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

`numfmt` is a formatting pass over text. It does not stat files and it does not change how full the disk is. The expensive mistake is human: an operator deletes the wrong tree because SI and IEC were mixed. Format once at the edge of a report. Keep the bytes integer in the log you will grep later. There is no parallel mode worth invoking. If you are formatting the output of `du` on a million-file tree, the walk inside `du` is the cost and numfmt is a rounding error on top of it.

cookbook.title: Sort version-like names with sort -V
cookbook.summary: Lexical sort puts a10 before a2. sort -V treats the digit runs as version numbers and prints a1, a2, a10.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: GNU `sort -V` is a GNU version-sort. BSD sort does not use `-V` for the same algorithm. The order is not the same as numeric `-n`, and it is not locale dictionary order. This recipe shows GNU sort 9.4 on three names. It is not a claim about every version scheme a package manager accepts.
cookbook.markdown:
Lexical sort compares characters. The name `a10` and the name `a2` share the prefix `a`, and then `1` is before `2`, so `a10` sorts first. That is the correct byte order and the wrong version order. `sort -V` recognizes runs of digits and compares those runs as version numbers, so the same three names come out `a1`, `a2`, `a10`. Package filenames, kernel tags, and `ls` of `app-1.2` versus `app-1.10` are why the flag exists.

Version sort is not a general semver parser. It does not apply every rule of a particular ecosystem's pre-release tags. Debian and RPM disagree with each other and with `-V` on some suffixes. Use `-V` for the "digits should compare as integers" problem. Use the package manager's own comparison when you are ordering real package versions for an upgrade decision.

`ls -v` is the listing form of a similar idea. `sort -V` is the filter you can put in a pipeline. Set the locale deliberately. Version sort still has text parts, and those parts follow rules the version-sort node describes. If the names are pure integers, `sort -n` is the simpler tool and the one readers expect.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "version-sort-01", "title": "Lexical order", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a1\\na10\\na2\\n' | /usr/bin/sort\n", "stdout": "a1\na10\na2\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/version-sort-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "version-sort-02", "title": "Version order", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a1\\na10\\na2\\n' | /usr/bin/sort -V\n", "stdout": "a1\na2\na10\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/version-sort-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```



## Performance

`-V` is a more expensive comparison than an unsigned byte compare. On a short list of release names you will not measure it. On a multi-million-line file, a heavier comparator shows up in CPU, and `--parallel` does not remove that cost. If you only needed integer order on one field, `-n` or `-k` with `-n` is cheaper and clearer. The sort benchmarks on this site use a fixed key and a byte or locale collation. They do not time `-V`. Do not cite them as the cost of version sort. For a directory of a few hundred build artifacts, either flag finishes before you can read the help text.

cookbook.title: Repeat a shuffle with --random-source
cookbook.summary: shuf has no --seed flag. The same --random-source file produces the same permutation. /dev/zero is deterministic and is not entropy.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: GNU `shuf` takes randomness from `--random-source`, a file it reads as a byte stream. There is no `--seed` in coreutils 9.4. BSD `jot -r` and other shufflers use different flags. `/dev/zero` makes the run repeatable and is a terrible secret. This recipe ran GNU shuf.
cookbook.markdown:
`shuf` prints a permutation of its input. Two runs without a fixed random source differ, which is what you want for a real sample and what you do not want for a test. There is no `--seed` option in this version. Reproducibility is `--random-source=FILE`. The file is read as raw bytes. The same file and the same input produce the same permutation, which the recipe checks with `sha256sum` of the two outputs. `/dev/zero` is a convenient infinite file of zero bytes. It is deterministic. It is not a secret and it is not a high-quality random stream. Use it for tests. Use `/dev/urandom`, or a file you generated once and checked in, when you understand which of those you need.

`sort -R` is the other GNU tool that shuffles, and it also accepts `--random-source`. Its order is not required to match `shuf` even with the same source. Pick one tool and keep it. Do not mix them in a golden test.

`shuf -n 2` prints a sample of two lines rather than a full permutation. The sample is still a function of the random source. A test that only checks the count, not the identity, can use `-n`. A test that checks the identity must fix the source.

An empty input produces empty output and exits 0. A missing random source fails. Quote the path if it contains spaces. The source is a filename, not a seed integer, so do not pass `20261108` and expect it to be parsed as a number. That string would be opened as a file and fail.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "reproducible-shuf-01", "title": "Two shuffles from /dev/zero match", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\nd\\n' > names\n/usr/bin/shuf --random-source=/dev/zero names > one\n/usr/bin/shuf --random-source=/dev/zero names > two\n/usr/bin/sha256sum one two\n", "stdout": "cf2c7f63055d2e84af6e3f01ac1bb7fce598d20cf213fab2b56b8e8047b46ced  one\ncf2c7f63055d2e84af6e3f01ac1bb7fce598d20cf213fab2b56b8e8047b46ced  two\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/reproducible-shuf-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "reproducible-shuf-02", "title": "A short sample still uses the source", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\nd\\n' > names\n/usr/bin/shuf -n 2 --random-source=/dev/zero names\n", "stdout": "a\nb\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/reproducible-shuf-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "reproducible-shuf-ex01", "title": "Repeat a four-line shuffle", "prompt": "Shuffle `a` through `d` twice with `--random-source=/dev/zero` and hash both outputs.", "hint": "The digests match because the source bytes match.", "solution": "`sha256sum` prints one digest twice. `/dev/zero` is not entropy.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'a\\nb\\nc\\nd\\n' > names\n/usr/bin/shuf --random-source=/dev/zero names > one\n/usr/bin/shuf --random-source=/dev/zero names > two\n/usr/bin/sha256sum one two\n", "stdout": "cf2c7f63055d2e84af6e3f01ac1bb7fce598d20cf213fab2b56b8e8047b46ced  one\ncf2c7f63055d2e84af6e3f01ac1bb7fce598d20cf213fab2b56b8e8047b46ced  two\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/reproducible-shuf-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

Shuffling a few lines is instant. Shuffling a file larger than memory is a disk problem, because `shuf` has to hold the permutation. `-n` with a reservoir is the mode that avoids storing every line when you only want a sample, and the manual describes the limits. Do not read `/dev/zero` as a performance trick. It is an infinite file of zeros, and shuf only reads as many bytes as its algorithm needs. Pointing a cryptographic generator at a unit test slows the test and does not make the assertion stronger once the source is fixed. The benchmark seed on this site (`20261108`) belongs to the benchmark scripts, which do not call `shuf`.

examples.title: Two shuffles from /dev/zero match
examples.script:
/usr/bin/printf 'a\nb\nc\nd\n' > names
/usr/bin/shuf --random-source=/dev/zero names > one
/usr/bin/shuf --random-source=/dev/zero names > two
/usr/bin/sha256sum one two

cookbook.title: Place a program in a prefix with install -D
cookbook.summary: install -D -m 755 creates the destination directory and sets the mode in one step. An empty prefix is refused before any copy.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: GNU `install -D` creates missing parents. BSD `install` uses a different set of flags and often requires the directory to exist. `-m 755` is the executable mode this recipe requests. The source here is `/usr/bin/true`, copied into a scratch prefix. This is GNU install from coreutils 9.4.
cookbook.markdown:
`install` is the tool a build uses to publish a binary into a prefix. `cp` copies bytes. `install -D -m 755` copies bytes, creates the parent directory, and sets the mode. `-D` is what saves you from a separate `mkdir -p` that a later edit forgets. The mode is the one you pass, not whatever umask did to a `cp` followed by a forgotten `chmod`.

The recipe copies `/usr/bin/true` into `prefix/bin/true` inside the scratch directory. That is a stand-in for the binary your compiler just linked. Running the installed path shows the mode is executable. `stat -c '%a'` prints `755`. Refuse an empty prefix and refuse `/` before you call install. The guard is ordinary `test`. `install` will not save you from a variable that expanded to the real root. `--preserve-root` is an `rm` feature, not an `install` feature.

`install -C` skips the write when the content is unchanged, which keeps the mtime stable and stops an incremental build from rebuilding the world. The permissions lesson measures that on a small file. Use `-C` when stamps matter. Use plain `-D` when you always want the mode reapplied and you have not read the `-C` comparison rules yet.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "install-a-prefix-01", "title": "Create bin and set the mode", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/install -D -m 755 /usr/bin/true prefix/bin/true\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%a %n' prefix/bin/true\nprefix/bin/true\n/usr/bin/printf 'ran:%s\\n' $?\n", "stdout": "755 prefix/bin/true\nran:0\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/install-a-prefix-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "install-a-prefix-02", "title": "Refuse an empty prefix", "companion": "", "script": "prefix=\"\"\nif test -z \"$prefix\" || test \"$prefix\" = /; then\n  /usr/bin/printf 'refuse\\n'\nelse\n  /usr/bin/printf 'would-install\\n'\nfi\n", "stdout": "refuse\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/install-a-prefix-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "install-a-prefix-ex01", "title": "Install true into a prefix", "prompt": "Use `install -D -m 755` to copy `/usr/bin/true` to `prefix/bin/true` and print the mode.", "hint": "`-D` creates `prefix/bin`.", "solution": "The mode is `755`. The command runs and returns 0.", "script": "/usr/bin/install -D -m 755 /usr/bin/true prefix/bin/true\n/usr/bin/stat -c '%a' prefix/bin/true\n", "stdout": "755\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/install-a-prefix-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

Installing one binary is a copy. Installing thousands of headers is a metadata walk. `-C` avoids dirtying mtimes when the bytes did not change, and that saving shows up as fewer downstream rebuilds, not as a faster `install` process. The copy benchmark measures `cp` and `dd`, not `install`. Expect `install` of a large binary to cost about what a copy costs, plus a chmod. Do not put `install` on a network filesystem and then blame the flag for the latency. The network is the bottleneck. A local prefix on the same filesystem can at least be a rename of a finished file, which is the move lesson's publish pattern: write the temp name beside the final name, then `mv -T`.

examples.title: Create bin and set the mode
Refuse an empty prefix
examples.script:
prefix=""
if test -z "$prefix" || test "$prefix" = /; then
  /usr/bin/printf 'refuse\n'
else
  /usr/bin/printf 'would-install\n'
fi

cookbook.title: Verify a manifest before you trust the file
cookbook.summary: sha256sum -c is the gate. A matching file prints OK. A rewritten file fails the check and the script stops.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: GNU `sha256sum -c` understands the two-space text-mode line this recipe writes. BSD check tools want their own label. A mismatch exits non-zero and prints FAILED. This recipe ran GNU sha256sum. It does not download anything.
cookbook.markdown:
The point of a manifest is the check you run before the next step, not the file you printed and forgot. `sha256sum blob > MANIFEST` records the digest and the name. `sha256sum -c MANIFEST` recomputes it. With `set -e`, a failed check stops the script, which is what you want in a build that is about to unpack an NDK archive or flash an image. The recipe does both the good check and a deliberate mismatch so the statuses are visible.

The mismatch is local. The script writes `payload`, records the digest, overwrites the file with `other`, and checks. The failed check prints `FAILED` and a warning about the computed digest. The status is non-zero. The example uses `set +e` only so it can print that status and continue. A real script leaves `set -e` on and does not continue.

Paths in the manifest are relative to the directory you run `-c` from. Generate and check in the same directory, or write the paths you will actually use. A check that fails because you changed directories is still a failed check. Fix the path. Do not pass `--ignore-missing` to paper over a file you thought you had.

`md5sum` has the same shape and a weaker hash. Use it when you are matching an old vendor file. Use SHA-256 when you are choosing. The checksum lesson lists the algorithms this `cksum` supports. `cksum` without `-a` is the traditional CRC, not SHA-256. Read the label before you compare it to a web page.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "verify-a-manifest-01", "title": "A matching file", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'payload\\n' > blob\n/usr/bin/sha256sum blob > MANIFEST\n/usr/bin/sha256sum -c MANIFEST\n", "stdout": "blob: OK\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/verify-a-manifest-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "verify-a-manifest-02", "title": "A rewritten file fails", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'payload\\n' > blob\n/usr/bin/sha256sum blob > MANIFEST\n/usr/bin/printf 'other\\n' > blob\nset +e\n/usr/bin/sha256sum -c MANIFEST\n/usr/bin/printf 'status:%s\\n' $?\nset -e\n", "stdout": "blob: FAILED\nstatus:1\n", "stderr": "/usr/bin/sha256sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match\n", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/verify-a-manifest-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "verify-a-manifest-ex01", "title": "Check a fresh manifest", "prompt": "Write `payload` plus a newline, record sha256sum, and check it.", "hint": "Do not modify the file between the two commands.", "solution": "The line says `blob: OK`.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'payload\\n' > blob\n/usr/bin/sha256sum blob > MANIFEST\n/usr/bin/sha256sum -c MANIFEST\n", "stdout": "blob: OK\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/verify-a-manifest-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

Checking a digest reads the whole file once. That read is the lower bound on "are these the bytes I hashed". Skipping it saves the read and accepts corruption. For a small artifact the read is cheaper than the outage. For a huge disk image the read is minutes, and those minutes are still cheaper than flashing the wrong image. The algorithm benchmark compares hash functions on 8 MiB so you can see CPU differences without pretending the ranking survives a different file size and a cold disk. Run one check, not two, unless the two files are different. `sha256sum -c` already recomputes.

examples.title: A rewritten file fails
examples.script:
/usr/bin/printf 'payload\n' > blob
/usr/bin/sha256sum blob > MANIFEST
/usr/bin/printf 'other\n' > blob
set +e
/usr/bin/sha256sum -c MANIFEST
/usr/bin/printf 'status:%s\n' $?
set -e
examples.stderr: /usr/bin/sha256sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match

cookbook.title: Move a file onto another filesystem
cookbook.summary: mv between the sandbox and /dev/shm cannot be a pure rename. stat -c %d shows two device ids. The scratch file is removed on exit.
cookbook.gnuVsBsd: When `rename` returns EXDEV, `mv` copies and then unlinks. That is POSIX behavior, not a GNU invention. GNU `mv -T` and `-t` are GNU spellings. Device numbers differ by host. This recipe uses `/dev/shm` on Linux and deletes the file in an EXIT trap. It does not run BSD mv and it does not leave the scratch file behind.
cookbook.markdown:
`mv` on one filesystem is a rename. The directory entry changes and the bytes stay where they are. `mv` across filesystems cannot do that. The kernel returns EXDEV, and `mv` copies, then unlinks the source. The copy is not atomic. A crash can leave both names, or the new name with a short file. Scripts that publish a finished artifact should `mv` within one filesystem: write a temporary name in the destination directory, then `mv -T` it onto the public name.

You can see the boundary with `stat -c '%d'`. The sandbox and `/dev/shm` have different device numbers on this host. The recipe prints both, moves a small file, prints the destination, and removes it with a trap. `/dev/shm` is outside the course runner's scratch directory. The trap is what deletes it. Copy the trap if you adapt the recipe. Do not point it at a directory you care about. The destination path includes the shell pid so two runs do not share a name.

Same-filesystem publish is still the pattern to prefer. Cross-device move is the pattern to recognize when a build directory and a deploy mount are different disks. If you need the copy to keep holes or modes, read the cp flags `mv` will use on the fallback, and test them. Do not assume every attribute survived because the exit status was 0.

## Steps

```example
{"id": "cross-device-move-01", "title": "Two device ids and a move", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'payload\\n' > local\ndest=\"/dev/shm/cuwb-cb-$$\"\ntrap 'rm -f \"$dest\"' EXIT\n/usr/bin/stat -c 'src_dev=%d' .\n/usr/bin/stat -c 'shm_dev=%d' /dev/shm\n/usr/bin/mv local \"$dest\"\n/usr/bin/cat \"$dest\"\n", "stdout": "src_dev=65056\nshm_dev=47\npayload\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cross-device-move-01.sh", "truncated": false}
```


```example
{"id": "cross-device-move-02", "title": "A same-directory rename", "companion": "", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'payload\\n' > local\n/usr/bin/mv local published\n/usr/bin/cat published\n/usr/bin/test ! -e local && /usr/bin/printf 'source-gone\\n'\n", "stdout": "payload\nsource-gone\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/examples/cross-device-move-02.sh", "truncated": false}
```


## Check yourself

```exercise
{"id": "cross-device-move-ex01", "title": "Rename inside the sandbox", "prompt": "Write `payload` and a newline to `local`, rename it to `published`, and print the file.", "hint": "Same directory means a rename, not a cross-device copy.", "solution": "The body is unchanged. `local` is gone.", "script": "/usr/bin/printf 'payload\\n' > local\n/usr/bin/mv local published\n/usr/bin/cat published\n", "stdout": "payload\n", "stderr": "", "exitCode": 0, "download": "/downloads/solutions/cross-device-move-ex01.sh"}
```


## Performance

A rename is a directory update and does not move bytes. A cross-device `mv` is a full copy plus a delete, so it costs read bandwidth, write bandwidth, and then the unlink. Measuring `mv` without recording whether the device ids matched measures two different operations and calls them one name. Print the device ids in the log when a publish step is slow. If they differ, write the file on the destination filesystem in the first place, or copy with the cp flags you actually want and then rename into place on the destination. The copy benchmark's 8 MiB trial is the dense-copy cost on this host, warm cache, and it is the right order of magnitude for the fallback. It is not a rename.

exercises.title: Rename inside the sandbox
exercises.prompt: Write `payload` and a newline to `local`, rename it to `published`, and print the file.
exercises.hint: Same directory means a rename, not a cross-device copy.
