reference.summary: Exit with the status determined by EXPRESSION.
reference.note: This is the coreutils test command under another name. Bash also provides [ as a builtin, so type [ before you trust a flag. The manual lists it among utilities whose exit status is the answer, not a simple success bit.

reference.name: arch
reference.summary: Print machine architecture.
reference.note: Prints the machine hardware name, the same class of fact as uname -m. It is a tiny GNU program. macOS often has no arch from coreutils; uname -m is the portable question.

reference.name: b2sum
reference.summary: Print or check BLAKE2b (512-bit) checksums.
reference.note: BLAKE2b checksums with the same check-file interface as sha256sum. A faster median than SHA-256 on one host is not a reason to change a manifest format. Length can be shortened with -l; do that only when the consumer expects it.

reference.name: base32
reference.summary: Base32 encode or decode FILE, or standard input, to standard output.
reference.note: RFC 4648 base32. GNU base32 wraps at 76 columns unless -w 0. Decode with -d. It is not on stock macOS; basenc --base32 is the same alphabet inside coreutils.

reference.name: base64
reference.summary: Base64 encode or decode FILE, or standard input, to standard output.
reference.note: RFC 4648 base64. -w sets the wrap column and -d decodes. macOS base64 uses -D and a different default wrap. Whitespace on decode needs -i. This is encoding, not encryption.

reference.name: basename
reference.summary: Print NAME with any leading directory components removed.
reference.note: Strips the directory prefix and an optional trailing suffix. It reads operands, not stdin. GNU basename accepts -a and -z. Quoting still matters because the shell expands the argument first.

reference.name: basenc
reference.summary: basenc encode or decode FILE, or standard input, to standard output.
reference.note: One binary for base16, base32, base32hex, base64, base64url, base2msbf, base2lsbf, and z85 in coreutils 9.4. There is no --base58 in this version. z85 input length must be a multiple of 4.

reference.name: cat
reference.summary: Concatenate FILE(s) to standard output.
reference.note: Streams files to stdout. -A shows tabs, ends, and other nonprinting bytes. The manual says cat does not use C FILE streams, so stdbuf does not change its buffering. It is the wrong tool for random access.

reference.name: chcon
reference.summary: Change the SELinux security context of each FILE to CONTEXT.
reference.note: Changes an SELinux security context. This capture host has no SELinux-enabled kernel, and chcon fails on unlabeled files. Do not treat a failure here as a permissions-bit problem; chmod is a different mechanism.

reference.name: chgrp
reference.summary: Change the group of each FILE to GROUP.
reference.note: Changes group ownership. Without privilege you can only move a file to a group you belong to. --reference copies the group from another file. BSD chgrp does not take GNU long options.

reference.name: chmod
reference.summary: Change the mode of each FILE to MODE.
reference.note: Changes mode bits with an octal mode or a symbolic mode. --reference copies a mode. It does not change the owner. Recursive -R on a tree you do not mean to publish is the usual accident.

reference.name: chown
reference.summary: Change the owner and/or group of each FILE to OWNER and/or GROUP.
reference.note: Changes user and group. On this sandbox, chown to root fails with Operation not permitted. --from avoids racing with another owner. GNU --reference is not a BSD flag.

reference.name: cksum
reference.summary: Print or verify checksums.
reference.note: The historical CRC plus byte count is still the default. -a selects md5, the SHA-2 family, blake2b, sm3, and the old sum algorithms. --tag is how cryptographic digests print a BSD-style line; the CRC line stays numeric.

reference.name: comm
reference.summary: Compare sorted files FILE1 and FILE2 line by line.
reference.note: Compares two sorted files line by line and prints three columns. GNU comm checks order and exits 1 when it is wrong, after it may already have written lines. Suppress columns with -1, -2, and -3.

reference.name: cp
reference.summary: Copy SOURCE to DEST, or multiple SOURCE(s) to DIRECTORY.
reference.note: Copies files and trees. -a is -dR --preserve=all. --reflink=always fails on this ext4 filesystem; --reflink=auto falls back to a read/write copy. --sparse controls holes. -n is marked non-portable in 9.4; use --update=none.

reference.name: csplit
reference.summary: Output pieces of FILE separated by PATTERN(s) to files 'xx00', 'xx01', ...,
reference.note: Splits a file at context lines rather than at a fixed size. Patterns are basic regular expressions. -z suppresses empty pieces. It is not a CSV or JSON parser. Stock macOS does not ship GNU csplit.

reference.name: cut
reference.summary: Print selected parts of lines from each FILE to standard output.
reference.note: Selects byte, character, or field ranges. -d sets a single-byte delimiter. It does not understand quotes, so a CSV comma inside quotes is still a separator. --complement and --output-delimiter are GNU extensions.

reference.name: date
reference.summary: Display date and time in the given FORMAT.
reference.note: Formats and parses dates. -d takes a date string, including @epoch. BSD date uses -v and -f instead. --debug explains a parse. The clock resolution reported by --resolution is a property of this host.

reference.name: dd
reference.summary: Copy a file, converting and formatting according to the operands.
reference.note: Copies blocks. status=progress and status=none are GNU. conv=sparse seeks over NUL blocks. iflag=fullblock matters when reading a pipe that returns short reads. Never point of= at a device in an example you have not identified.

reference.name: df
reference.summary: Show information about the file system on which each FILE resides,
reference.note: Reports filesystem free space from statfs, not by walking files. GNU df -T prints the type. On BSD, df -T filters by type instead. --output and -T cannot be combined. This host's df -T says ext4 where stat -f says ext2/ext3.

reference.name: dir
reference.summary: List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
reference.note: dir is ls with a different default format, still the same coreutils binary family. Scripts should call ls with explicit options so a dir default never becomes part of the contract.

reference.name: dircolors
reference.summary: Output commands to set the LS_COLORS environment variable.
reference.note: Prints shell commands that set LS_COLORS. The database is not consulted unless the shell evaluates that output. Color is a display hint. It does not change the bytes ls writes when --color=never.

reference.name: dirname
reference.summary: Output each NAME with its last non-slash component and trailing slashes
reference.note: Prints everything through the last slash. Multiple operands are allowed. -z changes the output delimiter; it does not make dirname read NUL-separated stdin. A path with no slash yields '.'.

reference.name: du
reference.summary: Summarize device usage of the set of FILEs, recursively for directories.
reference.note: Walks a tree and sums allocated space, counting a hard link once unless -l is set. --apparent-size or -b reports the logical size, which is what sparse files make diverge from du without that flag. df does not walk the tree.

reference.name: echo
reference.summary: Echo the STRING(s) to standard output.
reference.note: The manual recommends printf for anything that must be portable. Bash's builtin echo ignores --help and prints the word. /usr/bin/echo is coreutils, and -E (no escapes) is its default. -e is a GNU behavior, not POSIX.

reference.name: env
reference.summary: Set each NAME to VALUE in the environment and run COMMAND.
reference.note: Runs a command with a modified environment. -i starts empty, -u removes a name, -C changes directory, and -S splits a string for shebangs. The manual lists env among commands with special exit statuses. BSD env lacks -S.

reference.name: expand
reference.summary: Convert tabs in each FILE to spaces, writing to standard output.
reference.note: Turns tabs into spaces. -t sets tab stops. -i affects only leading tabs. It does not reflow paragraphs; fmt does that. Tabs inside the data are bytes, not a table layout.

reference.name: expr
reference.summary: Print the value of EXPRESSION to standard output.  A blank line below
reference.note: Evaluates an expression and prints it. A true comparison prints 1 and exits 0. A false comparison prints 0 and exits 1. That inversion surprises people who treat the printed number as the exit status. Prefer test or shell arithmetic for new scripts.

reference.name: factor
reference.summary: Print the prime factors of each specified integer NUMBER.  If none
reference.note: Prints prime factors of arbitrary-precision integers. factor 1 and factor 0 print the number and no factors. It is not a general cryptography library and it is not a reason to invent timing claims.

reference.name: false
reference.summary: Exit with a status code indicating failure.
reference.note: Exits with status 1. Bash also has a builtin false. /usr/bin/false --version identifies coreutils. The manual lists false as an ordinary failure status, unlike test's use of 1 as an answer.

reference.name: fmt
reference.summary: Reformat each paragraph in the FILE(s), writing to standard output.
reference.note: Reflows paragraphs to a width. -w sets the width and -p keeps a mail-style prefix. It is not a code formatter and it will join short lines that look like a paragraph. BSD fmt exists with a different option set.

reference.name: fold
reference.summary: Wrap input lines in each FILE, writing to standard output.
reference.note: Wraps lines at a width. On this UTF-8 locale, fold -w 1 split the two bytes of U+00E9. Do not assume a column width keeps a multibyte character intact; check with od. -b counts bytes. -s breaks at spaces.

reference.name: groups
reference.summary: Print group memberships for each USERNAME or, if no USERNAME is specified, for
reference.note: Prints the groups of a user. With no operand it describes the current process. It reads the account database, not the file mode bits. id -Gn is the related coreutils form.

reference.name: head
reference.summary: Print the first 10 lines of each FILE to standard output.
reference.note: Prints a prefix. GNU head -n -5 prints all but the last five lines; BSD head rejects a negative count. -c counts bytes. -z uses NUL as the line delimiter. It does not follow a growing file; tail -f does.

reference.name: hostid
reference.summary: Print the numeric identifier (in hexadecimal) for the current host.
reference.note: Prints a hexadecimal identifier, historically derived from an address. It is not a UUID and not a secret you should publish as an authenticator. Treat the captured value as a fact about this machine only.

reference.name: id
reference.summary: Print user and group information for each specified USER,
reference.note: Prints uid, gid, and groups. -u and -g print numbers. -Z asks for an SELinux context and fails on this kernel. Scripts that parse the default sentence are brittle; use the numeric options.

reference.name: install
reference.summary: This install program copies files (often just compiled) into destination
reference.note: Copies a file and sets its mode, creating parent directories with -D. -C skips the write when the content already matches, which keeps the destination mtime. BSD install uses a different flag set. It is the right tool for placing a built binary into a prefix.

reference.name: join
reference.summary: For each pair of input lines with identical join fields, write a line to
reference.note: Joins two files on a shared field. Both inputs must be sorted on that field. The default GNU check exits 1 on disorder but can still emit a partial line. --nocheck-order returns 0 and can silently drop rows.

reference.name: link
reference.summary: Call the link function to create a link named FILE2 to an existing FILE1.
reference.note: Creates a hard link with link(2) and no extra flags. It will not replace an existing name and it will not link a directory for an unprivileged user. ln is the tool with -s, -f, and -r. unlink is the matching removal call.

reference.name: ln
reference.summary: In the 1st form, create a link to TARGET with the name LINK_NAME.
reference.note: Makes hard and symbolic links. -s is a symlink. GNU -r / --relative rewrites the target as a relative path. -sfn retargets a symlink even when the destination name exists. BSD ln has no --relative.

reference.name: logname
reference.summary: Print the user's login name.
reference.note: Prints the name from the login utmp record. In this non-login sandbox it fails. whoami reads the effective uid instead and still works. Do not use logname as a synonym for the account that owns the files.

reference.name: ls
reference.summary: List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
reference.note: Lists names and, with -l, metadata. The shell expands globs before ls sees them. --quoting-style=shell-escape makes odd names visible. --zero delimits with NUL. GNU -T is tab size; BSD ls -T is a time format. dir and vdir are related entry points.

reference.name: md5sum
reference.summary: Print or check MD5 (128-bit) checksums.
reference.note: MD5 checksums in the GNU text/binary line format. Fine for accidental corruption checks in old manifests. Not a collision-resistant choice for new ones. --check and --status match the other *sum tools. md5sum.textutils is a symlink, not a second algorithm.

reference.name: mkdir
reference.summary: Create the DIRECTORY(ies), if they do not already exist.
reference.note: Creates directories. -p creates parents and does not fail if the leaf exists. -m applies to the final component created in that invocation; parents are created under the current umask, which is 0022 here, so they land at 755 when -m 700 is asked.

reference.name: mkfifo
reference.summary: Create named pipes (FIFOs) with the given NAMEs.
reference.note: Creates a named pipe. Opening it blocks until the other end is opened. A lesson that reads a fifo must bound the wait with timeout, or the sandbox hangs. mkfifo does not copy bytes; the readers and writers do.

reference.name: mknod
reference.summary: Create the special file NAME of the given TYPE.
reference.note: Creates fifos, and device nodes when you pass a type and numbers. Device nodes need privileges this course does not use. Prefer mkfifo for a named pipe. Do not run mknod against /dev in examples.

reference.name: mktemp
reference.summary: Create a temporary file or directory, safely, and print its name.
reference.note: Creates a temporary file or directory with a unique name. The template must end in at least six X characters. -d makes a directory. --suffix appends a suffix after the X's. Leaving the default /tmp is fine; the course scripts also set TMPDIR to the sandbox.

reference.name: mv
reference.summary: Rename SOURCE to DEST, or move SOURCE(s) to DIRECTORY.
reference.note: Renames, or copies and unlinks when the destination is another filesystem. -n refuses to overwrite and, on this GNU version, exits 1. -t collects sources into a directory. There is no cross-device rename system call; EXDEV is why the copy happens.

reference.name: nice
reference.summary: Run COMMAND with an adjusted niceness, which affects process scheduling.
reference.note: Adjusts niceness and runs a command. The manual says a negative adjustment without privilege prints a warning and continues as if the adjustment were zero. The exit status is the command's status, not the warning. renice is a different program and is not coreutils.

reference.name: nl
reference.summary: Write each FILE to standard output, with line numbers added.
reference.note: Numbers lines. -ba is -b a, which numbers every line including blanks. The default body style skips blanks. It is a formatter, not a way to address lines for editing. BSD nl differs in style names.

reference.name: nohup
reference.summary: Run COMMAND, ignoring hangup signals.
reference.note: Runs a command immune to SIGHUP and, if stdout is a terminal, redirects it to nohup.out. When stdout is already redirected, nohup.out is not created. It does not daemonize, and it does not change niceness.

reference.name: nproc
reference.summary: Print the number of processing units available to the current process,
reference.note: Prints the number of processing units available to the process, which can be less than --all when the affinity mask is smaller. --ignore subtracts from that count. GNU documents the default sort --parallel cap in terms of available processors. nproc is not in BSD base.

reference.name: numfmt
reference.summary: Reformat NUMBER(s), or the numbers from standard input if none are specified.
reference.note: Formats numbers with SI or IEC suffixes. 2048 becomes 2.0K in IEC (1024) and 2.1K in SI (1000) because of rounding. --field selects a column. It is GNU-only. It does not change sort's numeric comparison; sort -h has its own rules.

reference.name: od
reference.summary: Write an unambiguous representation, octal bytes by default,
reference.note: Dumps bytes in hex, octal, or named characters. Use it when cat -A is not enough, especially for NULs and encoding mistakes. -An drops the address. -w sets the width. hexdump is a different program and is not coreutils.

reference.name: paste
reference.summary: Write lines consisting of the sequentially corresponding lines from
reference.note: Merges lines from files, or, with -s, joins lines of one file. -d sets the delimiter. -z uses NUL as the record separator. It does not sort or match keys; join does that.

reference.name: pathchk
reference.summary: Diagnose invalid or non-portable file names.
reference.note: Checks whether a name is portable. -p applies the POSIX portable character set and a length limit. A name containing | fails -p. It does not create the file and it does not tell you whether the directory is writable.

reference.name: pinky
reference.summary: in short format
reference.note: A lightweight who. With nobody recorded in utmp it prints a header and no rows, which is what this sandbox shows. It is GNU-specific. who reads the same kind of login records.

reference.name: pr
reference.summary: Paginate or columnate FILE(s) for printing.
reference.note: Paginates and columns text. -t drops the header and footer so the output can go to another filter. -s sets a column separator. It is not a table join. Default headers include the date, so scripts that need stable bytes pass -t.

reference.name: printenv
reference.summary: Print the values of the specified environment VARIABLE(s).
reference.note: Prints the environment or one variable. A missing name exits non-zero, which the manual calls out. -0 uses NUL delimiters. env runs a command; printenv only displays.

reference.name: printf
reference.summary: Print ARGUMENT(s) according to FORMAT, or execute according to OPTION:
reference.note: Formats operands. Bash also has a builtin printf. Use /usr/bin/printf when you need the coreutils binary, including %q for shell quoting. The format string is not a filename. Prefer printf over echo for escapes and missing newlines.

reference.name: ptx
reference.summary: Output a permuted index, including context, of the words in the input files.
reference.note: Builds a permuted index. It is a specialized text tool, not a sort replacement. The output columns are easy to misread; the manual's ptx section documents the format. Most developer workflows never need it.

reference.name: pwd
reference.summary: Print the full filename of the current working directory.
reference.note: Prints the working directory. Bash's builtin pwd is what you get if you type pwd. /usr/bin/pwd is coreutils. -P resolves symlinks; -L follows the logical $PWD. The builtin and the binary agree on this sandbox because the directory is not reached through a link.

reference.name: readlink
reference.summary: Print value of a symbolic link or canonical file name
reference.note: Prints the target of a symlink, or, with -f, a canonical path. -f allows the final component to be missing and still exits 0. -e requires every component to exist. GNU -f is not what older BSD readlink implemented.

reference.name: realpath
reference.summary: Print the resolved absolute file name;
reference.note: Prints an absolute path. The default allows a missing final component. -e requires the path to exist. -m allows missing middle components. --relative-to prints a path relative to a base. Older macOS installs did not ship realpath.

reference.name: rm
reference.summary: Remove (unlink) the FILE(s).
reference.note: Removes directory entries. GNU defaults include --preserve-root. -I prompts once before removing more than three items or descending recursively; an EOF answer left the files in place and still exited 0 in this sandbox. -i prompts per file. It does not shred data.

reference.name: rmdir
reference.summary: Remove the DIRECTORY(ies), if they are empty.
reference.note: Removes empty directories. A non-empty directory and a regular file both fail, with different messages. -p removes parent components if they become empty. Use rm -r only when you mean to delete contents.

reference.name: runcon
reference.summary: Run a program in a different SELinux security context.
reference.note: Runs a command in a different SELinux context. It needs a kernel with SELinux. This host does not have one. It is not a substitute for sudo and not a coreutils permission bit.

reference.name: seq
reference.summary: Print numbers from FIRST to LAST, in steps of INCREMENT.
reference.note: Prints a sequence of numbers. -w equalizes width and -s sets the separator. The floating-point section of the manual applies. On 9.4, seq 0 0.1 1 prints 11 values ending at 1.0 for this particular step; that is not a proof that every step is exact.

reference.name: sha1sum
reference.summary: Print or check SHA1 (160-bit) checksums.
reference.note: SHA-1 checksums, 160-bit, same interface as sha256sum. Collision attacks against SHA-1 are practical. Do not choose it for a new manifest. The manual groups it with the SHA-2 tools even though SHA-1 is not SHA-2.

reference.name: sha224sum
reference.summary: Print or check SHA224 (224-bit) checksums.
reference.note: SHA-224, a truncated SHA-256 variant with a different initial state. Same -c interface. Rare in download pages. Prefer sha256sum unless a protocol names SHA-224.

reference.name: sha256sum
reference.summary: Print or check SHA256 (256-bit) checksums.
reference.note: SHA-256 checksums. This is the usual coreutils tool for a download manifest. --check reads the GNU line format. A wrong hash prints FAILED and exits 1. The digest of the three bytes abc is a known test vector used in the lesson.

reference.name: sha384sum
reference.summary: Print or check SHA384 (384-bit) checksums.
reference.note: SHA-384, the truncated SHA-512 variant. Same command-line shape as sha256sum. Choose it when a protocol says SHA-384, not because the name looks longer than SHA-256.

reference.name: sha512sum
reference.summary: Print or check SHA512 (512-bit) checksums.
reference.note: SHA-512. The digest is longer and the implementation processes 64-bit words. On a small file the runtime difference may sit inside the noise. Use the benchmark if you need a number, and do not generalize it.

reference.name: shred
reference.summary: Overwrite the specified FILE(s) repeatedly, in order to make it harder
reference.note: Overwrites a file, and -u unlinks it afterward. The manual's assumption is that the filesystem and the device overwrite in place. Journals, snapshots, compression, RAID, and SSD wear leveling break that assumption. One pass in a lesson only shows the user interface.

reference.name: shuf
reference.summary: Write a random permutation of the input lines to standard output.
reference.note: Writes a random permutation. There is no --seed. Reproducible draws use --random-source with a file of bytes. -i ranges over integers and -n limits the count. shuf is GNU-only; it is not a sort.

reference.name: sleep
reference.summary: Pause for NUMBER seconds.  SUFFIX may be 's' for seconds (the default),
reference.note: Pauses for a duration. GNU sleep accepts a decimal and the suffixes s, m, h, and d. An invalid interval exits non-zero. It is not a scheduler. timeout is the tool that stops another command.

reference.name: sort
reference.summary: Write sorted concatenation of all FILE(s) to standard output.
reference.note: Orders lines. -s disables the last-resort full-line comparison. -S sets the initial memory buffer (default unit 1024 bytes; M is 1,048,576). -T sets the temporary directory. --parallel defaults to available CPUs capped at 8. Exit status 1 means a -c check failed; 2 means an error.

reference.name: split
reference.summary: Output pieces of FILE to PREFIXaa, PREFIXab, ...;
reference.note: Splits by lines, bytes, or into N chunks. -d uses numeric suffixes. -n r/N round-robins lines, so a file with one line puts everything in the first piece. --filter runs a command per piece. BSD split does not have this -n syntax.

reference.name: stat
reference.summary: Display file or file system status.
reference.note: Prints metadata with a format string. GNU uses -c. BSD uses -f for the format, which is the single most common portability break. stat -f here means filesystem status, and %T can say ext2/ext3 on ext4.

reference.name: stdbuf
reference.summary: Run COMMAND, with modified buffering operations for its standard streams.
reference.note: Adjusts C FILE buffering by preloading libstdbuf.so. The binary contains the strings LD_PRELOAD and libstdbuf.so. cat and dd do not use FILE streams. tee resets its own buffering. -iL is rejected with status 125. It is ELF-only and GNU-only.

reference.name: stty
reference.summary: Print or change terminal characteristics.
reference.note: Changes or prints terminal settings. This course does not run stty against the session terminal, because a bad mode breaks the terminal. Read the manual before using it in a script. It is not a file-permission tool.

reference.name: sum
reference.summary: Print or check BSD (16-bit) checksums.
reference.note: Historic BSD (-r) and System V (-s) checksums. cksum -a bsd and cksum -a sysv cover the same algorithms. Do not use sum for a new integrity check. The output width and algorithm differ between -r and -s.

reference.name: sync
reference.summary: Synchronize cached writes to persistent storage
reference.note: Asks the kernel to flush cached writes. With no operand it syncs all filesystems the process may sync. -f syncs the filesystems that contain the named files. It does not prove a drive's firmware finished the write.

reference.name: tac
reference.summary: Write each FILE to standard output, last line first.
reference.note: Prints lines in reverse. It is GNU-only; BSD users often use tail -r. -s sets a separator, and the separator stays attached to the record, which makes the reversed bytes look surprising until you inspect them with od.

reference.name: tail
reference.summary: Print the last 10 lines of each FILE to standard output.
reference.note: Prints a suffix, or follows a file with -f. -F follows by name and retries. -n +K starts at line K. GNU negative counts on head are a different feature. Follow mode runs until it is killed; bound it with timeout.

reference.name: tee
reference.summary: Copy standard input to each FILE, and also to standard output.
reference.note: Copies stdin to stdout and to files. -a appends. The manual notes that tee adjusts its own buffering, so stdbuf does not control it. It is the coreutils way to save a copy of a pipeline without a shell process substitution.

reference.name: test
reference.summary: Exit with the status determined by EXPRESSION.
reference.note: Evaluates an expression and exits 0 or 1. Bash's builtin test shadows /usr/bin/test. -s is true only for a non-empty file. The manual lists test among the commands whose 0 and 1 are answers. Use spaces around operators.

reference.name: timeout
reference.summary: Start COMMAND, and kill it if still running after DURATION.
reference.note: Runs a command and sends it a signal when the duration elapses. The default exit status is 124 if the command was signaled. --preserve-status returns 128 plus the signal, 143 for SIGTERM. It is GNU-only. macOS users install gtimeout.

reference.name: touch
reference.summary: Update the access and modification times of each FILE to the current time.
reference.note: Updates timestamps or creates an empty file. -d takes a date string and -r copies a timestamp from another file. -c does not create. BSD touch uses -t for a timestamp and does not accept GNU -d.

reference.name: tr
reference.summary: Translate, squeeze, and/or delete characters from standard input,
reference.note: Translates or deletes bytes from stdin. It has no file operands. Character classes such as [:upper:] are locale-sensitive. A UTF-8 character is more than one byte, and tr will rewrite each byte that appears in the set. It is not sed.

reference.name: true
reference.summary: Exit with a status code indicating success.
reference.note: Exits with status 0. The shell builtin is what an unadorned true usually runs. /usr/bin/true --version prints the coreutils banner. Useful as the command argument to nice or timeout when you need a known status.

reference.name: truncate
reference.summary: Shrink or extend the size of each FILE to the specified size
reference.note: Sets a file to a size. Extending a file creates a hole when the filesystem allows it, which is why du and stat then disagree. Shrinking discards the tail from the directory entry's point of view. It is GNU; it is not dd.

reference.name: tsort
reference.summary: Write totally ordered list consistent with the partial ordering in FILE.
reference.note: Topological order of a list of pairs. Input is one pair per line. A cycle makes it fail. It is the coreutils tool for a dependency order, not a general sort, and the input is not a Makefile.

reference.name: tty
reference.summary: Print the file name of the terminal connected to standard input.
reference.note: Prints the terminal name connected to stdin, or fails when stdin is not a terminal. Pipelines and this capture environment are not terminals, so tty exits non-zero. The manual lists tty among special exit statuses.

reference.name: uname
reference.summary: Print certain system information.  With no OPTION, same as -s.
reference.note: Prints kernel and machine facts. -srm is enough to identify the capture class without a hostname. -a includes the nodename. It does not print the coreutils version; ls --version does that.

reference.name: unexpand
reference.summary: Convert blanks in each FILE to tabs, writing to standard output.
reference.note: Turns runs of spaces into tabs. -a converts all runs, not only leading ones. -t must match the tab stops expand used, or the round trip changes columns. It is byte-oriented.

reference.name: uniq
reference.summary: Filter adjacent matching lines from INPUT (or standard input),
reference.note: Collapses adjacent matching lines. It does not search the whole file; sort first. -c counts, -d prints duplicates, -u prints uniques. -i folds case. GNU -z matches sort -z. sort -u is not the same once keys are involved.

reference.name: unlink
reference.summary: Call the unlink function to remove the specified FILE.
reference.note: Removes one name with unlink(2). It does not remove directories. It does not take -r. If another hard link remains, the data remains. rm is the tool with prompts and recursion.

reference.name: users
reference.summary: Output who is currently logged in according to FILE.
reference.note: Prints login names from utmp. This sandbox has no logged-in users, so the output is empty and the status is still 0. An empty line is not an error. who shows the same records with more columns.

reference.name: vdir
reference.summary: List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
reference.note: vdir is ls -l under another name, from the same package. Use it only when you want that default. Scripts should call ls -l so the format is explicit on systems where vdir is absent.

reference.name: wc
reference.summary: Print newline, word, and byte counts for each FILE, and a total line if
reference.note: Counts newlines, words, characters, bytes, and the longest line. -l counts newline bytes, so a file with no trailing newline can have a last line that -l does not count. --files0-from reads NUL-separated names. --total controls the total line.

reference.name: who
reference.summary: Print information about users who are currently logged in.
reference.note: Prints utmp records. With no logins it prints nothing and exits 0. It is coreutils on this Ubuntu. uptime is not, even though people mention them together. Do not parse who to authorize a user.

reference.name: whoami
reference.summary: Print the user name associated with the current effective user ID.
reference.note: Prints the effective user name. It still works when logname fails. It does not print the uid; id -u does. It is not a security boundary.

reference.name: yes
reference.summary: Repeatedly output a line with all specified STRING(s), or 'y'.
reference.note: Repeats a string until the pipe closes. The usual close is SIGPIPE. With pipefail the pipeline can exit 141. Without pipefail the status is the reader's status. Bound it with head. It is not a load generator you should leave running.

companions.name: find
companions.note: Recursive directory search. Not coreutils. GNU find is findutils. It is the usual producer of NUL-terminated names via -print0.

companions.name: xargs
companions.note: Builds argument lists from stdin. Not coreutils. GNU xargs is findutils. Use -0 with NUL names. It is a different failure model from a coreutils filter.

companions.name: grep
companions.note: Content search. Not coreutils. The grep package owns this binary. Coreutils can slice bytes; it does not search patterns.

companions.name: sed
companions.note: Stream editor. Not coreutils. Useful, and a different language. Do not describe a sed script as a coreutils one-liner.

companions.name: awk
companions.note: Field language. On this host /usr/bin/awk is mawk via the alternatives system, not GNU awk, and not coreutils.

companions.name: tar
companions.note: Archive format. Not coreutils. tar reads and writes its own format; cp -a does not.

companions.name: rsync
companions.note: Delta file copy. Not coreutils and not installed in the capture environment. cp has no equivalent of rsync's block algorithm.

companions.name: time
companions.note: The shell keyword `time` is not GNU time and does not print max RSS. The GNU time package is not installed here. Benchmarks use Python resource stats instead.

companions.name: perf
companions.note: Linux performance counters. Not coreutils and not installed here. Nothing in this course samples hardware counters.

companions.name: hostname
companions.note: The GNU manual documents hostname, but Ubuntu's /usr/bin/hostname is the hostname package, version string separate from coreutils.

companions.name: kill
companions.note: The GNU manual documents kill, but /usr/bin/kill on this Ubuntu image is procps. This course does not teach it as coreutils.

companions.name: uptime
companions.note: The GNU manual's uptime node is not the binary on this system. /usr/bin/uptime is procps.
